alt.ex: Alternative medicine is used instead of conventional treatment.
w: Adding acupuncture to physical therapy for back pain
Used with conventional care, this is complementary medicine.
Treating back pain with surgery and pain medication
This is conventional Western medicine.
Using massage along with prescribed medication for back pain
Combined with conventional care, this is complementary medicine.

alt.q: A patient with chronic back pain skips the surgery her surgeon recommended and uses acupuncture instead. Her choice is an example of _____.
alt.ex: Using a nonconventional therapy in place of conventional treatment is alternative medicine.
w: complementary medicine
Complementary therapies are used along with conventional care, not instead.
Western medicine
She rejected the conventional Western treatment.
integrative medicine
Integrative medicine combines conventional and complementary care.

items.q: An 86-year-old person has fallen twice in the last six months. Their child is worried that their parent should not be living alone in their home. What type of facility would be most appropriate?
items.ex: Assisted living offers housing with help and supervision for people unsafe living alone.
w: Wellness center
Wellness centers promote fitness and prevention; they provide no housing.
Skilled nursing facility
Skilled nursing is for patients needing round-the-clock skilled care, not just supervision.
Hospice
Hospice is for terminally ill patients, not someone at risk of falls.
tf: Assisted living residences provide housing with help and supervision for people who can no longer safely live alone.
Assisted living residences are mainly for patients who need 24-hour skilled nursing care.
Round-the-clock skilled care is the role of skilled nursing facilities.

alt.q: An elderly parent who has fallen twice in six months may no longer be safe living alone. Which setting is MOST appropriate?
alt.ex: Assisted living offers housing with help and supervision for people unsafe alone.
w: Wellness center
Wellness centers promote fitness and provide no housing.
Skilled nursing facility
Skilled nursing is for round-the-clock skilled care, not just supervision.
Hospice
Hospice is for terminally ill patients.

alt.q: A 90-year-old woman mostly cares for herself but forgets her medications and recently fell at home. Her son wants her somewhere with help available. Which option fits BEST?
alt.ex: Assisted living provides housing plus help and supervision for daily needs.
w: Hospice
Hospice is for dying patients, not fall risk.
Ambulatory surgery center
Surgery centers provide outpatient procedures, not housing.
Transitional care unit
A TCU is a short-term hospital unit; she is not hospitalized.

items.q: A growing trend in health care is to emphasize preventing diseases rather than simply curing them.
items.ex: Health care increasingly emphasizes prevention and wellness to improve health and reduce costs.
items.ww: Prevention and wellness are a major, growing focus in health care today.

alt.q: Health care is increasingly focused on keeping people from getting sick, not just treating illness.
alt.ex: Prevention and wellness are a growing emphasis in health care.
alt.ww: Prevention is a major, growing trend, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Health care today is moving away from prevention to focus only on curing disease.
alt.ex: The trend is toward more emphasis on prevention, not less.
alt.ww: Prevention and wellness are growing, not shrinking, priorities.

items.q: Yoga is used as a health practice by at least 10% of Americans.
items.ex: Surveys show more than 10% of U.S. adults practice yoga for health.
items.ww: Yoga is one of the most widely used complementary practices, used by over 10% of Americans.

alt.q: At least one in ten Americans practices yoga for their health.
alt.ex: Surveys show more than 10% of U.S. adults use yoga for health.
alt.ww: Yoga is among the most widely used practices, over 10% of Americans.

alt.q: Fewer than 1% of Americans use yoga as a health practice.
alt.ex: At least 10% of Americans use yoga as a health practice.
alt.ww: Yoga use is far higher than 1%.

items.q: With the increasing division of health care provided by various health care providers, the cost of health care has increased.
items.ex: More specialized providers mean more services, coordination, and duplicated tests, raising costs.
items.ww: Dividing care among many specialists has added to rising health care costs.

alt.q: As health care has been split among more and more types of providers, health care costs have gone up.
alt.ex: More providers mean more services, coordination, and duplicated tests, raising costs.
alt.ww: Dividing care among providers has added to rising costs.

alt.q: Dividing patient care among many different providers has lowered the overall cost of health care.
alt.ex: Increasing division of care among providers has raised health care costs.
alt.ww: More providers and coordination add cost rather than reduce it.

items.q: How many Alzheimer's patients live their last years or months in a nursing home?
items.ex: About two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's spend their final months or years in a nursing home.
w: This is more than 100%, which is impossible.
This is under 7%, far too low.
This would mean all patients; many die at home or elsewhere.

alt.q: About what fraction of people with Alzheimer's disease spend their last months or years in a nursing home?
alt.ex: Roughly 2/3 of Alzheimer's patients spend their final months or years in nursing homes.
w: About one-tenth
Far too low compared with the estimate of two-thirds.
About one-third
Too low; the estimate is two-thirds.
All of them
Many die at home or elsewhere, so not all.

alt.q: A region has 300 people with Alzheimer's disease. About how many are likely to spend their last months or years in a nursing home?
alt.ex: About two-thirds do, and two-thirds of 300 is 200.
w: That is only one-tenth.
That is one-third, below the estimate.
That would be all of them; many die elsewhere.

items.q: Which of the following is true about suicides?
items.a: Most people who die by suicide have a mental health diagnosis.
items.ex: Studies find a mental health condition, most often depression, in most people who die by suicide.
w: Women die by suicide at higher rates than men.
Men die by suicide at roughly four times the rate of women.
Asking someone about suicidal thoughts increases their risk.
This is a myth; asking directly opens the door to getting help.
Most people who die by suicide show no warning signs.
Most people show warning signs, such as talking about death or withdrawing.
tf: Most people who die by suicide have a mental health diagnosis.
Most people who die by suicide have no history of mental illness.
Most suicide deaths involve an underlying mental health condition such as depression.

alt.q: Which statement about people who die by suicide is accurate?
alt.a: A majority of them had a diagnosable mental health condition.
alt.ex: Research finds a mental health condition, most often depression, in most suicide deaths.
w: Women die by suicide more often than men.
Men die by suicide at about four times the rate of women.
Asking someone about suicidal thoughts raises their risk.
This is a myth; asking directly helps a person get help.
Most people who die by suicide give no warning signs.
Most show warning signs, such as talking about death or withdrawing.

alt.q: A nursing student is preparing a suicide-prevention handout. Which fact belongs on it?
alt.a: Most people who die by suicide had a mental health condition, such as depression.
alt.ex: Most suicide deaths involve a mental health diagnosis, so screening and treatment matter.
w: Talking openly about suicide puts the idea in a person's mind.
This is a myth; open questions help people seek help.
Suicide deaths occur mostly among women.
Men die by suicide at much higher rates than women.
People who die by suicide rarely show warning signs.
Most people show warning signs before a suicide attempt.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT true about holistic medicine?
items.a: It does not consider stress to be an important factor in health.
items.ex: Holistic medicine treats the whole person, so stress and emotions are key factors in health.
w: It treats the whole person, including mind, body, and spirit.
True: treating the whole person is the core idea of holistic medicine.
It considers lifestyle and environment as factors in health.
True: holistic care looks at diet, habits, and surroundings, not just symptoms.
It encourages patients to take responsibility for their wellness.
True: holistic medicine stresses the patient's active role in staying healthy.
tf: Holistic medicine considers stress to be an important factor in health.
Holistic medicine focuses only on the physical symptoms of disease.
Holistic medicine treats mind, body, and spirit, not just physical symptoms.
ms: Which of the following are characteristics of holistic medicine? (Select all that apply)
Treats the whole person: mind, body, and spirit
This whole-person view defines holistic medicine.
Considers stress and emotions important to health
Holistic care sees emotional stress as a real health factor.
Encourages patients to take responsibility for wellness
Patients are active partners in holistic care.
Focuses mainly on pathology and curing disease
That describes Western medicine, not holistic medicine.
Ignores lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise
Holistic medicine pays close attention to lifestyle.

alt.q: Which statement does NOT describe holistic medicine?
alt.a: It treats stress as unimportant to a person's health.
alt.ex: Holistic medicine sees stress and emotions as key factors in health.
w: It views the patient as a whole person: mind, body, and spirit.
True: treating the whole person is the core of holistic medicine.
It considers lifestyle and environment when promoting health.
True: holistic care looks at habits and surroundings, not just symptoms.
It asks patients to take an active role in their own wellness.
True: holistic medicine stresses patient responsibility for staying well.

alt.q: A holistic practitioner is planning care for a patient with frequent headaches. Which approach would the practitioner be LEAST likely to take?
alt.a: Ignore the patient's stress level, since stress does not affect health
alt.ex: Holistic medicine considers stress an important factor, so it would not be ignored.
w: Ask about the patient's diet, sleep, and daily habits
Holistic care does consider lifestyle factors like these.
Explore the patient's emotions and sources of stress
Holistic care does look at the mind and emotions.
Encourage the patient to take part in a wellness plan
Holistic care does ask patients to take an active role.

items.q: The work of the National Institutes of Health includes which of the following?
items.ex: The NIH is the federal agency that conducts and funds medical research.
w: Licensing physicians and nurses
Licensing is done by state licensing boards, not the NIH.
Processing Medicare claims
Medicare claims are handled through CMS, not the NIH.
Accrediting hospitals
The Joint Commission accredits hospitals for quality and safety.
tf: The work of the National Institutes of Health includes supporting medical research.
The National Institutes of Health accredits hospitals for quality and safety.
The Joint Commission accredits hospitals; the NIH conducts and funds research.

alt.q: Which activity is part of the role of the National Institutes of Health (NIH)?
alt.ex: The NIH is the federal agency that carries out and supports medical research.
w: Licensing physicians and nurses
State licensing boards license health care workers, not the NIH.
Processing Medicare claims
Medicare claims are handled through CMS, not the NIH.
Accrediting hospitals
The Joint Commission accredits hospitals, not the NIH.

alt.q: A university scientist wants federal money to study a new treatment for heart disease. Which agency would most likely support this study?
alt.ex: Supporting medical research is the core work of the NIH.
w: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
CMS runs Medicare and Medicaid payments, not research grants.
The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission accredits health care organizations for quality and safety.
A state board of nursing
Nursing boards license and regulate nurses, not research.

sections.name: Ethics, Law, Patient Rights, and Legal Responsibilities

items.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the relationship between ethics and law?
items.a: Ethics provide general principles for laws to be based upon.
items.ex: Ethics are principles of right and wrong; many laws are built on those principles.
w: There is no relationship between ethics and law.
Laws often grow out of ethical principles, so they are closely related.
Laws determine what is and is not ethical.
Ethics come first; an action can be legal yet still unethical.
Laws are always moral and ethical.
Some laws have been unjust; legal does not always mean ethical.
tf: Ethics provide general principles on which laws are based.
Laws determine what is and is not ethical.
Ethics guide laws, and something can be legal but still unethical.

alt.q: How are ethics and laws connected?
alt.a: Laws are often built on the general principles that ethics provide.
alt.ex: Ethics are principles of right and wrong that many laws are based on.
w: Ethics and laws are completely unrelated.
Many laws grow out of ethical principles, so they are closely linked.
Whatever the law says decides what is ethical.
Ethics come first; something can be legal yet still unethical.
Every law is moral and ethical.
Some laws have been unjust; legal does not always mean ethical.

alt.q: A state passes a law requiring patient consent before treatment, based on the belief that people should control their own bodies. What does this show?
alt.a: Ethical principles provided the basis for the law.
alt.ex: The law grew out of an ethical principle, showing ethics guide laws.
w: Laws decide what counts as ethical.
Here the ethical belief came first and shaped the law.
Ethics and law have no connection.
The law was based directly on an ethical belief.
Because it is a law, it must be fully ethical.
Laws are not always ethical; being legal is not proof of ethics.

items.q: The second health care professional described by the patient in the video practiced good communication skills and treated the patient with respect. This is an example of which ethical principle?
items.ex: Communicating well and treating patients with respect is acting for their benefit: do good.
w: Do no harm
Do no harm means avoiding injury, such as staying competent and careful.
Be discreet
Be discreet means keeping patient information private.
Be loyal
Loyalty is faithfulness to employer and team, not respectful patient care.

alt.q: A health care worker communicates clearly and treats a patient with respect. Which ethical principle is the worker following?
alt.ex: Respectful, effective communication acts for the patient's benefit, which is doing good.
w: Do no harm
Do no harm is about avoiding injury, such as staying competent.
Be discreet
Be discreet is about keeping patient information private.
Be loyal
Loyalty is faithfulness to the employer and team.

alt.q: A medical assistant explains each step of a procedure in plain language and patiently listens to a nervous patient. Which ethical principle does this show?
alt.ex: Kind, respectful communication benefits the patient, which is the principle of doing good.
w: Be discreet
Be discreet concerns protecting private information, not communication style.
Be loyal
Loyalty concerns faithfulness to employer and coworkers.
Do no harm
Do no harm centers on competence and avoiding injury.

items.q: The patient describes two experiences with two different health care professionals. The patient heard the first health care professional discussing private information about them in the hallway. This is an example of a violation of which ethical principle?
items.ex: Discussing a patient's private information in a hallway violates the duty to be discreet.
w: Do good
Do good is about actively benefiting the patient, not guarding their privacy.
Be honest
Nothing false was said; the problem was where private information was shared.
Be loyal
Loyalty concerns faithfulness to employer and team, not confidentiality.
ms: Which of the following actions violate the principle Be discreet? (Select all that apply)
Discussing a patient's diagnosis in a hallway
Others can overhear private information in public areas.
Leaving a patient's chart open at the front desk
Records left in view expose private information.
Talking about a patient with friends after work
Patient information must never be shared outside of care.
Sharing patient information with the care team
Sharing with those directly caring for the patient is appropriate.
Logging off the computer before walking away
Logging off protects privacy, so it follows the principle.

alt.q: Talking about a patient's confidential information in a public area, such as a hallway, breaks which ethical principle?
alt.ex: Being discreet means sharing private patient information only in proper, private settings.
w: Do good
Do good is about actively benefiting the patient, not privacy.
Be honest
Nothing false was said; the problem was where information was shared.
Be loyal
Loyalty is faithfulness to employer and team, not confidentiality.

alt.q: In a crowded elevator, a pharmacy technician tells a coworker about a customer's new HIV prescription. Which ethical principle is the technician failing to follow?
alt.ex: Discussing private health details where others can hear violates the duty to be discreet.
w: Be honest
The technician said nothing untrue; the issue is privacy.
Be loyal
Loyalty concerns faithfulness to the employer, not patient privacy.
Do good
Do good is about benefiting patients, not guarding their information.

items.q: When an individual or an organization is faced with an ethical dilemma that is especially difficult, what source may assist with the decision?
items.ex: Ethics committees bring together several viewpoints to help resolve especially difficult ethical dilemmas.
w: The patient's insurance company
Insurers decide on payment, not on ethical questions about care.
The organization's billing department
Billing handles charges and claims, not ethical decision-making.
The organization's public relations office
Public relations manages the facility's image, not ethical dilemmas.

alt.q: Which resource can help an organization work through an especially hard ethical dilemma?
alt.ex: Ethics committees bring several viewpoints together to help resolve difficult ethical dilemmas.
w: The patient's insurance company
Insurers decide on payment, not ethical questions about care.
The organization's billing department
Billing handles charges and claims, not ethical decisions.
The organization's public relations office
Public relations manages image, not ethical dilemmas.

alt.q: A hospital care team disagrees about whether to continue life support for a patient whose wishes are unknown. Where should they turn for help?
alt.ex: An ethics committee helps staff resolve especially difficult ethical decisions like this one.
w: The hospital's billing office
Billing deals with charges, not ethical decisions about care.
The patient's health insurance company
Insurers decide payment, not ethical questions about treatment.
The hospital's marketing department
Marketing promotes the hospital and has no role in ethical decisions.

items.q: The purpose of following professional codes of ethics is to:
items.a: ensure a high quality of care.
items.ex: Codes of ethics set standards of conduct so that patients receive high-quality care.
w: increase the profits of the facility.
Codes of ethics focus on patients and conduct, not on income.
protect workers from all lawsuits.
Following a code helps, but it cannot protect workers from all legal action.
replace the need for state laws.
Codes of ethics work alongside laws; they do not replace them.

alt.q: Why do health care professionals follow professional codes of ethics?
alt.a: To ensure patients receive high-quality care
alt.ex: Codes of ethics set standards of conduct so patients get high-quality care.
w: To increase the facility's profits
Codes of ethics focus on patients and conduct, not income.
To protect workers from all lawsuits
Following a code helps but cannot prevent all legal action.
To replace the need for state laws
Codes of ethics work alongside laws; they do not replace them.

alt.q: A new dental hygienist asks why her professional association's code of ethics matters. What is the main reason to follow it?
alt.a: It helps ensure patients receive high-quality care.
alt.ex: The purpose of a professional code of ethics is high-quality patient care.
w: It guarantees she will never be sued.
No code can protect a worker from all lawsuits.
It makes state licensing laws unnecessary.
Codes of ethics do not replace laws.
It helps the practice earn more money.
Codes of ethics focus on conduct and patients, not profit.

items.q: A respiratory therapist's supervisor is in a hurry and asks them to perform a procedure that they have not been trained to do. What should they do?
items.a: Tell their supervisor that they do not have the training and cannot do the procedure
items.ex: Workers must stay within their training and scope of practice, even when a supervisor asks.
w: Perform the procedure carefully since the supervisor approved it
Supervisor approval does not make an untrained worker competent or protect the patient.
Ask a coworker to quickly explain the steps and then do it
A quick explanation is not proper training and puts the patient at risk.
Perform the procedure but document the supervisor's request
Documentation does not excuse working outside one's training.
tf: A health care worker should refuse a procedure they are not trained to do, even if a supervisor asks.
A health care worker may perform an untrained procedure if a supervisor asks, since the supervisor is responsible.
Each worker is responsible for staying within their own training and scope of practice.

alt.q: A supervisor in a rush asks a health care worker to do a procedure they were never trained to perform. What is the correct response?
alt.a: Explain that they lack the training and cannot do the procedure
alt.ex: Workers must stay within their training and scope of practice, even when a supervisor asks.
w: Do the procedure carefully because the supervisor approved it
Approval does not make an untrained worker competent or keep the patient safe.
Have a coworker quickly explain the steps, then do it
A quick explanation is not proper training and risks the patient.
Do the procedure but document the supervisor's request
Documenting the request does not excuse working beyond one's training.

alt.q: A busy charge nurse asks a new patient care technician to start an IV, a skill the technician has never been trained to do. What should the technician do?
alt.a: Tell the charge nurse they are not trained in this skill and cannot do it
alt.ex: Health care workers must refuse tasks they are not trained to perform safely.
w: Start the IV since the charge nurse approved it
Permission from a supervisor does not replace proper training.
Watch a short online video, then start the IV
A short video is not proper training and puts the patient at risk.
Start the IV and chart who asked them to do it
Charting the request does not make working untrained acceptable.

items.q: Which term means the disclosure of unauthorized information about a person that can harm that person's reputation?
items.ex: Defamation of character is sharing information that damages a person's reputation, spoken or written.
w: False imprisonment
False imprisonment is restraining or confining someone without consent.
Breach of contract
Breach of contract is failing to carry out the terms of an agreement.
Malpractice
Malpractice is professional negligence in providing care, not harm to reputation.
tf: Defamation of character is disclosing information about a person that can harm their reputation.
Defamation of character is restraining a person against their will.
Restraining someone without consent is false imprisonment.
ms: Which of the following are forms of defamation of character? (Select all that apply)
Slander
Slander is spoken defamation.
Libel
Libel is written defamation.
False imprisonment
This is confining someone without consent, not harming reputation.
Fraud
Fraud is deliberate deception for gain, such as false billing.

alt.q: What is the legal term for sharing unauthorized information about someone that can damage their reputation?
alt.ex: Defamation of character is spoken or written information that harms a person's reputation.
w: False imprisonment
False imprisonment is confining someone without consent.
Breach of contract
Breach of contract is failing to meet the terms of an agreement.
Malpractice
Malpractice is professional negligence in care, not harm to reputation.

alt.q: A clinic employee tells community members damaging stories about a patient's private life, hurting the patient's reputation. Which legal term describes this?
alt.ex: Sharing information that harms someone's reputation is defamation of character.
w: Negligence
Negligence is failing to use reasonable care, not harming reputation.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment means restraining someone against their will.
Malpractice
Malpractice is negligent professional care that injures a patient.

items.q: A respiratory therapist who works at a children's hospital is careful to keep their technical knowledge and skills up-to-date. What ethical principle is illustrated by their actions?
items.ex: Keeping knowledge and skills current prevents mistakes, so it protects patients from harm.
w: Be discreet
Be discreet is about protecting patient privacy, not skill competence.
Be loyal
Loyalty is faithfulness to employer and team, not keeping skills current.
Be honest
Honesty is about truthfulness; staying competent prevents harm.

alt.q: Keeping one's technical knowledge and skills current is an example of which ethical principle?
alt.ex: Staying competent prevents mistakes, which protects patients from harm.
w: Be discreet
Be discreet is about protecting patient privacy.
Be loyal
Loyalty is faithfulness to employer and team.
Be honest
Honesty is about truthfulness, not skill competence.

alt.q: A radiologic technologist attends yearly training to stay current on new imaging equipment and safety practices. Which ethical principle does this support?
alt.ex: Up-to-date skills help prevent errors that could injure patients.
w: Be discreet
Be discreet concerns keeping patient information private.
Be loyal
Loyalty concerns faithfulness to employer and coworkers.
Be honest
Honesty concerns telling the truth, not staying competent.

items.q: A patient has terminal lung cancer. Their family understands that there is no cure. They signed a document that includes their wish to not have CPR administered. This document is called a(n) _____.
items.ex: A living will is an advance directive stating which treatments, such as CPR, a person does not want.
w: durable power of attorney
This names a person to make decisions, rather than listing treatment wishes.
informed consent
Informed consent is agreeing to a treatment after learning its risks and benefits.
implied consent
Implied consent is shown by actions, not by a signed document.
ms: Which of the following are types of advance directives? (Select all that apply)
Living will
It states in advance which treatments a person wants or refuses.
Durable power of attorney for health care
It names someone to make health care decisions if the person cannot.
Express contract
This is a stated agreement, not a directive about future care.
Implied consent
This is consent shown through actions, not an advance directive.
HIPAA privacy notice
This explains privacy rights, not end-of-life wishes.

alt.q: What is the signed document called in which a person states they do not want CPR or certain other treatments?
alt.ex: A living will is an advance directive listing treatments a person does not want.
w: Durable power of attorney
This names a decision-maker rather than listing treatment wishes.
Informed consent
Informed consent is agreeing to a treatment after learning its risks.
Implied consent
Implied consent is shown by actions, not a signed document.

alt.q: While still able to decide, a patient signs a document saying she does not want to be placed on a ventilator if she cannot breathe on her own. What is this document?
alt.ex: A living will records which life-sustaining treatments a person refuses.
w: Durable power of attorney for health care
That document names a person to make decisions, not specific treatment wishes.
Informed consent form
Informed consent agrees to a specific treatment after explanation of risks.
Implied consent
Implied consent is agreement shown by actions, not a written document.

items.q: A home health aide suspects that her older adult client is being abused by the client's niece. What should they do?
items.a: Report the signs or symptoms of abuse to their supervisor
items.ex: Health care workers must report suspected abuse; the aide reports it through their supervisor.
w: Confront the niece directly about the suspected abuse
Confronting the abuser can endanger the client and the worker.
Wait until they have proof before telling anyone
Suspicion is enough to report; proof is not required.
Keep watching the client and say nothing for now
Delaying a report leaves the client at risk of more abuse.
tf: A home health aide who suspects a client is being abused should report it to their supervisor.
A home health aide should wait for proof of abuse before reporting it.
Suspected abuse must be reported; proof is not required.

alt.q: What should a home health aide do if they suspect a client's relative is abusing the older adult client?
alt.a: Report the signs of suspected abuse to their supervisor
alt.ex: Suspected abuse must be reported, and the aide does this through their supervisor.
w: Confront the relative directly
Confronting the suspected abuser can endanger the client and the aide.
Wait until there is proof before telling anyone
Suspicion is enough to report; proof is not required.
Keep watching and say nothing for now
Delaying a report leaves the client at risk.

alt.q: While bathing an older client, a home health aide sees unexplained bruises, and the client seems afraid of her son. What should the aide do?
alt.a: Report the signs of possible abuse to her supervisor
alt.ex: Health care workers must report suspected abuse promptly through proper channels.
w: Ask the son directly whether he is hurting his mother
Confronting a suspected abuser can put the client and aide in danger.
Wait for proof of abuse before telling anyone
Reporting is required on suspicion; proof is not needed.
Treat the bruises and say nothing for now
Staying silent leaves the client at risk of more abuse.

items.q: Which of the following is the leading cause of medical malpractice lawsuits?
items.a: The lack of good interpersonal relationships between patient and health care provider
items.ex: Patients who feel ignored or disrespected are far more likely to sue, so good relationships matter.
w: Incorrect diagnosis
Errors happen, but the course teaches that poor relationships drive patients to sue.
The high cost of health care
Cost frustrates patients but is not the leading cause of malpractice suits.
Surgical errors
Errors alone are not the leading cause; poor relationships make patients sue.
tf: The leading cause of malpractice lawsuits is a lack of good interpersonal relationships between patient and provider.
The leading cause of malpractice lawsuits is the high cost of health care.
Poor patient-provider relationships, not cost, lead most patients to sue.

alt.q: According to the course, what most often leads patients to file malpractice lawsuits?
alt.a: Poor interpersonal relationships between patients and health care providers
alt.ex: Patients who feel ignored or disrespected are much more likely to sue.
w: Incorrect diagnoses
Errors happen, but poor relationships are what most often lead to suits.
The high cost of health care
Cost frustrates patients but is not the leading cause of suits.
Surgical errors
Errors alone are not the leading cause; poor relationships drive suits.

alt.q: A clinic manager wants to lower the risk of malpractice lawsuits. Based on their leading cause, which step would help most?
alt.a: Train staff to build respectful, caring relationships with patients
alt.ex: Poor provider-patient relationships are the leading cause of malpractice suits.
w: Lower the price of all services
High cost is not the leading cause of malpractice suits.
Limit how much time staff spend talking with patients
Less communication would weaken relationships and raise lawsuit risk.
Buy newer surgical equipment
Surgical errors are not the leading cause of malpractice suits.

items.q: Which of the following illustrates a situation where a release of patient information would be legal?
items.a: The patient's injuries are life-threatening and caused by a shooting.
items.ex: Gunshot wounds must be reported to authorities, so releasing that information is legal.
w: A reporter calls asking about a famous patient's condition.
The media has no right to patient information without consent.
The patient's employer asks why the patient missed work.
Employers cannot get health information without the patient's authorization.
A neighbor asks whether the patient's surgery went well.
Curiosity from neighbors is not a legal reason to share information.
ms: In which situations is releasing patient information without consent legal? (Select all that apply)
Injuries caused by a gunshot
Gunshot wounds must be reported to law enforcement.
Suspected child abuse
Health care workers are mandated reporters of suspected abuse.
Certain reportable communicable diseases
Some diseases must be reported to public health agencies.
An employer asking why a worker was absent
Employers need the patient's written authorization.
A reporter asking about a celebrity patient
The media has no legal right to patient information.

alt.q: In which situation is it lawful to release a patient's information?
alt.a: The patient has life-threatening injuries caused by a shooting.
alt.ex: Gunshot wounds must be reported to authorities, so releasing that information is legal.
w: A reporter asks about a famous patient's condition.
The media has no right to patient information without consent.
The patient's employer asks why the patient missed work.
Employers need the patient's authorization to get health information.
A neighbor asks whether the patient's surgery went well.
Curiosity is not a legal reason to share patient information.

alt.q: An emergency department nurse receives several requests about patients. Which one may legally be answered?
alt.a: Police need a report on a patient with life-threatening gunshot wounds.
alt.ex: Laws require reporting gunshot wounds, so this release of information is legal.
w: A patient's coworker calls to ask about the diagnosis.
Coworkers have no right to health information without the patient's consent.
A TV station asks about a celebrity patient's condition.
The media cannot receive patient information without consent.
A patient's landlord asks when the patient will be discharged.
A landlord has no legal reason to receive patient information.

items.q: A patient is at an appointment for their yearly physical exam. The medical assistant takes their vital signs. What action is the patient entering when they extend their arm for the medical assistant to apply a blood pressure cuff?
items.ex: Extending an arm for the cuff shows agreement through action rather than words: implied consent.
w: Express contract
An express contract is stated in words or writing, not shown by actions.
Informed consent
Informed consent follows a full explanation of risks, usually with a signature.
Battery
Battery is touching without permission; the patient's action gave permission.
tf: A patient who extends their arm for a blood pressure cuff is giving implied consent.
A patient who extends their arm for a blood pressure cuff is entering an express contract.
Express contracts are stated in words; actions that show agreement are implied consent.
ms: Which of the following are examples of implied consent? (Select all that apply)
Extending an arm for a blood pressure cuff
The action shows agreement without words.
Opening the mouth for an oral thermometer
Cooperating with the procedure implies consent.
Rolling up a sleeve for an injection
The patient's action signals permission.
Signing a surgical consent form
A signed form is written, not implied.
Saying "Yes, you may draw my blood"
Stated permission is expressed, not implied.

alt.q: When a patient holds out an arm so a medical assistant can put on a blood pressure cuff, this action is an example of what?
alt.ex: Agreeing through an action rather than words is implied consent.
w: Express contract
An express contract is stated in words or writing, not shown by action.
Informed consent
Informed consent follows a full explanation of risks, usually with a signature.
Battery
Battery is touching without permission; the patient's action gave permission.

alt.q: When a phlebotomist says it is time to draw blood, the patient silently rolls up a sleeve and holds out an arm. What does the patient's action show?
alt.ex: The patient agreed through actions instead of words, which is implied consent.
w: Express contract
An express contract is spelled out in words or writing.
Respondeat superior
This makes employers responsible for employees' actions, not patient agreement.
Defamation of character
Defamation is sharing information that harms a reputation.

items.q: A pharmacist makes an error when filling a prescription because they are not paying full attention to their work. Which of the following words applies to this situation?
items.ex: Negligence is failing to use the care a reasonable person would, such as working inattentively.
w: Fraud
Fraud is intentional deception; this error was careless, not deliberate.
Slander
Slander is spoken statements that harm a person's reputation.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment is confining someone against their will.
tf: A pharmacist who makes an error because they are not paying attention is an example of negligence.
A pharmacist who makes an error because they are not paying attention is committing fraud.
Fraud requires intent to deceive; careless mistakes are negligence.

alt.q: Which term describes a mistake caused by a pharmacist failing to pay proper attention while filling a prescription?
alt.ex: Negligence is failing to use the care a reasonable person would use.
w: Fraud
Fraud is intentional deception; this was careless, not deliberate.
Slander
Slander is spoken statements that harm a person's reputation.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment is confining someone against their will.

alt.q: A medical assistant is texting while preparing an injection and draws up the wrong dose. Which term applies?
alt.ex: Working carelessly instead of with reasonable care is negligence.
w: Fraud
Fraud requires deliberate deception, and this error was careless.
Libel
Libel is written statements that damage a person's reputation.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment is restraining a person without consent.

items.q: Which of the following is the best example of the principle "Be Discreet"?
items.a: Do not leave patient records where others can see them
items.ex: Being discreet means protecting patient privacy, including keeping records out of sight.
w: Keep your technical skills and knowledge up to date
Staying competent illustrates Do no harm, not Be discreet.
Speak kindly and respectfully to every patient
Respectful communication illustrates Do good, not Be discreet.
Refuse procedures you have not been trained to do
This is staying within scope of practice, not protecting privacy.
ms: Which of the following are examples of being discreet? (Select all that apply)
Not leaving patient records where others can see them
Keeps private information out of view.
Not discussing patients in elevators or hallways
Prevents others from overhearing private information.
Logging off the computer when leaving a workstation
Stops others from viewing patient records.
Keeping technical skills up to date
This illustrates Do no harm.
Using good communication skills with patients
This illustrates Do good.

alt.q: Which action best shows a health care worker following the principle "Be discreet"?
alt.a: Keeping patient records out of view of others
alt.ex: Being discreet means protecting patient privacy, including keeping records out of sight.
w: Keeping technical skills and knowledge up to date
Staying competent illustrates Do no harm, not Be discreet.
Speaking kindly and respectfully to every patient
Respectful communication illustrates Do good, not Be discreet.
Refusing procedures one has not been trained to do
This is staying within scope of practice, not protecting privacy.

alt.q: A unit clerk is about to step away from the nurses' station. Which action best follows the principle "Be discreet"?
alt.a: Close the patient chart on the screen so visitors cannot read it
alt.ex: Hiding patient information from others protects privacy, which is being discreet.
w: Sign up for a skills refresher course later that day
Keeping skills current illustrates Do no harm.
Greet the next visitor warmly and respectfully
Respectful treatment illustrates Do good.
Tell the supervisor about a task she was never trained to do
This is staying within scope of practice, not privacy.

items.q: One of the dental assistants employed in a large dental practice caused an injury to a patient while preparing the patient for a procedure. Which legal concept can be used to describe the dentist's responsibility for the actions of the dental assistant?
items.ex: Respondeat superior (let the master answer) makes employers responsible for employees' actions on the job.
w: Good Samaritan laws
These protect people who give emergency help in good faith, not employers.
malpractice
Malpractice describes the injury-causing act, not the employer's responsibility for it.
Negligence
Negligence describes the assistant's careless act, not the dentist's liability for it.
tf: Under respondeat superior, an employer is responsible for the actions of employees on the job.
Under respondeat superior, only the employee who caused an injury can be held responsible.
Respondeat superior extends responsibility to the employer for employees' actions.

alt.q: Which legal concept makes an employer responsible for harm an employee causes while doing their job?
alt.ex: Respondeat superior ("let the master answer") holds employers liable for employees' work actions.
w: Good Samaritan laws
These protect people giving emergency help in good faith.
Malpractice
Malpractice describes the harmful act, not the employer's responsibility for it.
Negligence
Negligence describes the careless act, not the employer's liability.

alt.q: A medical assistant injures a patient while drawing blood. The patient sues the physician who employs the assistant. Which concept supports holding the physician responsible?
alt.ex: Employers are responsible for employees' actions on the job under respondeat superior.
w: Good Samaritan laws
These protect volunteers giving emergency care, not employers.
Implied consent
Implied consent is agreement shown by actions, not employer liability.
Defamation of character
Defamation involves harming reputation, not responsibility for an injury.

items.q: The Patient Care Partnership is a standard form that health care providers use to create written contracts with patients.
items.ex: The Patient Care Partnership is an American Hospital Association brochure explaining patients' rights and expectations.
items.ww: It is an informational guide to patient rights, not a form for writing contracts.

alt.q: The Patient Care Partnership serves as a contract form that providers and patients sign.
alt.ex: It is an informational brochure about patients' rights and expectations, not a contract form.
alt.ww: It is not used to create contracts, so the statement cannot be true.

alt.q: The Patient Care Partnership is an informational guide explaining what patients can expect during a hospital stay.
alt.ex: The American Hospital Association created it to explain patients' rights and expectations.
alt.ww: It is an informational guide, not a contract, so this statement is accurate.

items.q: Denise is a member of a political organization. The organization has a reputation for holding political rallies that include hate speech. The group wants to rent a local high school stadium for a large rally. The school district refuses due to the reputation of the group. The group objects, stating they have a right to free speech. Which term below can be used to describe this situation?
items.ex: An ethical dilemma involves conflicting values, here free speech versus preventing hate speech.
w: Defamation of character
Refusing a rental is not spreading information that harms reputation.
Breach of contract
No agreement was made and broken; the district declined to rent.
Conflict of interest
That involves personal gain influencing decisions, which is not the issue here.

alt.q: A school district will not rent its stadium to a group known for hate speech, and the group claims a right to free speech. What best describes this clash of values?
alt.ex: An ethical dilemma involves conflicting values, here free speech versus preventing hate speech.
w: Defamation of character
Refusing a rental does not spread information that harms reputation.
Breach of contract
No agreement was made and broken; the district declined to rent.
Conflict of interest
That involves personal gain affecting decisions, which is not the issue.

alt.q: A nurse believes a patient should be told about a grim diagnosis, but the family insists the news be withheld. Both sides act from their values. What term describes this?
alt.ex: Competing values with no simple right choice create an ethical dilemma.
w: Defamation of character
No one is spreading information that harms someone's reputation.
Breach of contract
No agreement has been broken in this situation.
Negligence
Negligence is careless failure to use proper care, not a clash of values.

items.q: A patient had hip surgery at a large hospital. They met with the surgeon prior to the procedure, who explained the procedure, answered the patient's questions, and asked them to sign some forms. What term describes the formalized promises made to Robin?
items.ex: Promises formally stated in words and signed forms, like those before surgery, form an express contract.
w: Implied consent
Implied consent is shown by actions, not by formal signed promises.
Implied contract
Implied contracts are understood through actions; these promises were stated and written.
Informed consent
Per the course, formalized promises in signed forms are best described as an express contract.
tf: Formal promises explained by a surgeon and put in signed forms are an example of an express contract.
Formal promises explained by a surgeon and put in signed forms are an example of an implied contract.
Implied contracts come from actions; stated and written promises are express.

alt.q: Before surgery, a surgeon explains the operation, answers the patient's questions, and has the patient sign forms. What term describes these formal promises?
alt.ex: Promises stated in words and signed forms make up an express contract.
w: Implied consent
Implied consent is shown by actions, not formal signed promises.
Implied contract
Implied contracts are understood through actions; these promises were stated and written.
Respondeat superior
This makes employers liable for employees' actions; it is not an agreement.

alt.q: A patient signs a written agreement with a physical therapy clinic stating the services to be provided and their fees. What type of agreement is this?
alt.ex: Terms clearly stated in writing or words form an express contract.
w: Implied contract
An implied contract is understood from actions, not written terms.
Implied consent
Implied consent is agreement shown through actions, not a signed agreement.
Living will
A living will states treatment wishes, not services and fees.

items.q: Two friends who work as registered nurses in an emergency department are at a college football game when a man sitting near them appears to be having a heart attack. Why can they volunteer to assist without being concerned about liability?
items.ex: Good Samaritan laws protect people who give emergency care in good faith from liability.
w: Respondeat superior
This makes employers liable for employees at work; the nurses are off duty.
Affordable Care Act
The ACA concerns health insurance coverage, not liability for rescuers.
Patient Care Partnership
This is a hospital guide to patient rights, not a liability protection.
tf: Good Samaritan laws protect people who give emergency care in good faith from liability.
Good Samaritan laws protect rescuers even when they perform procedures beyond their training.
Rescuers should not perform procedures they lack the skills for, even under these laws.

alt.q: What protects off-duty health care workers from liability when they give emergency help in good faith?
alt.ex: Good Samaritan laws protect people who give emergency care in good faith.
w: Respondeat superior
This makes employers liable for on-duty employees, not off-duty rescuers.
Affordable Care Act
The ACA concerns health insurance coverage, not rescuer liability.
Patient Care Partnership
This is a guide to patient rights, not liability protection.

alt.q: A dental hygienist sees a shopper collapse in a grocery store and begins CPR. What protects her from being sued if she acts in good faith within her skills?
alt.ex: These laws protect rescuers who give emergency care in good faith.
w: HIPAA
HIPAA protects the privacy of health records, not rescuers.
Respondeat superior
This concerns employer liability for employees on the job.
Affordable Care Act
The ACA deals with insurance coverage, not liability for rescuers.

items.q: The policies created by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) are designed to _____.
items.a: protect the privacy of patient medical records
items.ex: HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules control who can see and share patients' health information.
w: set standards for accrediting hospitals
Hospital accreditation is done by The Joint Commission.
regulate the cost of prescription drugs
HIPAA does not set drug prices.
require employers to provide paid sick leave
Sick leave rules come from labor laws, not HIPAA.
ms: Which of the following are covered by HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules? (Select all that apply)
A patient's right to access and copy their medical record
HIPAA gives patients the right to their own records.
Safeguarding electronic health information
The Security Rule protects electronic patient data.
Limits on who can receive patient information
The Privacy Rule restricts disclosure of health information.
Accrediting hospitals for quality and safety
That is the role of The Joint Commission.
Setting prices for prescription drugs
HIPAA does not regulate drug costs.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of the policies set by HIPAA?
alt.a: Protecting the privacy of patients' medical records
alt.ex: HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules control who can see and share health information.
w: Setting standards for accrediting hospitals
Hospital accreditation is done by The Joint Commission.
Regulating the cost of prescription drugs
HIPAA does not set drug prices.
Requiring employers to give paid sick leave
Sick leave rules come from labor laws, not HIPAA.

alt.q: A clinic requires staff to log off computers and limits who can view patient charts. Which law are these policies mainly meant to satisfy?
alt.ex: HIPAA requires safeguards that protect the privacy of patient medical records.
w: Affordable Care Act
The ACA expanded insurance coverage; it is not mainly about record privacy.
Good Samaritan laws
These protect emergency rescuers from liability.
Social Security Act
This law created Social Security and later Medicare, not privacy rules.

items.q: What can a health care professional learn from their profession's code of ethics?
items.a: Guidelines of right and wrong conduct for their profession
items.ex: A code of ethics spells out the standards of right and wrong conduct expected of a profession.
w: Step-by-step procedures for performing clinical skills
Procedures come from training and manuals, not a code of ethics.
The salary range expected for their profession
Codes of ethics address conduct, not pay.
The state laws that license their profession
Licensing laws are separate legal rules, not ethical guidelines.

alt.q: When a health care professional reads their profession's code of ethics, what does it mainly provide?
alt.a: Standards of right and wrong conduct for the profession
alt.ex: A code of ethics spells out the conduct expected of members of a profession.
w: Step-by-step procedures for clinical skills
Procedures come from training and manuals, not a code of ethics.
The expected salary range for the profession
Codes of ethics address conduct, not pay.
The state laws that license the profession
Licensing laws are separate legal rules, not ethical guidelines.

alt.q: A new surgical technologist is unsure whether accepting an expensive gift from a patient is appropriate. Which source gives guidance on right and wrong conduct for her profession?
alt.ex: A professional code of ethics outlines right and wrong conduct for that profession.
w: A procedure manual for surgical instruments
This explains how to handle instruments, not ethical conduct.
A salary survey for surgical technologists
This reports pay, not standards of conduct.
The hospital's billing guidelines
Billing guidelines cover charges and claims, not professional ethics.

items.q: A company submits a claim to Medicare for a wheelchair for which the customer did not qualify. Which of the following terms describes this action?
items.ex: Fraud is deliberate deception for gain, such as billing Medicare for items a patient doesn't qualify for.
w: Negligence
Negligence is careless failure to use proper care, not intentional deception.
Malpractice
Malpractice is professional negligence in giving care, not false billing.
Libel
Libel is written statements that damage a person's reputation.

alt.q: Billing Medicare for a wheelchair that the customer was not eligible to receive is an example of what?
alt.ex: Fraud is deliberate deception for gain, such as billing for items a patient doesn't qualify for.
w: Negligence
Negligence is careless failure to use proper care, not deliberate deception.
Malpractice
Malpractice is negligent professional care, not false billing.
Libel
Libel is written statements that damage a person's reputation.

alt.q: A clinic knowingly bills an insurance company for a lab test that was never performed. Which term describes this?
alt.ex: Knowingly billing for services not provided is deliberate deception for gain: fraud.
w: Negligence
Negligence is carelessness; this billing was done on purpose.
Slander
Slander is spoken statements that harm someone's reputation.
Implied consent
Implied consent is agreement shown by a patient's actions.

items.q: New federal health care laws that were created in 2010 say that a person can no longer be denied coverage because of preexisting medical conditions and that certain preventative health screenings must be provided without extra charge. Which of the following includes these laws?
items.ex: The 2010 Affordable Care Act banned denials for preexisting conditions and covered preventive screenings.
w: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
HIPAA (1996) mainly protects the privacy of patient records.
Social Security Act
This 1935 law created Social Security and later Medicare, not these 2010 rules.
Patient Self-Determination Act
This 1990 law requires informing patients about advance directives.
tf: The Affordable Care Act prevents insurers from denying coverage because of preexisting conditions.
The Affordable Care Act made health insurance affordable for every American.
The ACA expanded coverage, but not every American can afford insurance and care.

alt.q: Which 2010 federal law stopped insurers from denying coverage for preexisting conditions and required certain preventive screenings at no extra charge?
alt.ex: The 2010 Affordable Care Act created these coverage and preventive screening rules.
w: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
HIPAA (1996) mainly protects the privacy of patient records.
Social Security Act
This 1935 law created Social Security and later Medicare.
Patient Self-Determination Act
This 1990 law requires informing patients about advance directives.

alt.q: A new patient learns her insurer cannot refuse her coverage because of her diabetes and must cover a recommended screening at no extra cost. Which law requires this?
alt.ex: The ACA bans coverage denials for preexisting conditions and requires free preventive screenings.
w: Social Security Act
This 1935 law created Social Security, not these coverage protections.
Patient Self-Determination Act
This law concerns informing patients about advance directives.
Good Samaritan laws
These protect emergency rescuers, not insurance coverage.

items.q: A laboratory technician tells a friend that a mutual acquaintance tested positive for HIV at the clinic where they work. As a result, the lab technician and the clinic could be charged with _____.
items.ex: Slander is spoken defamation: telling others information that can harm a person's reputation.
w: libel
Libel is written defamation; this disclosure was spoken.
Fraud
Fraud is deception for gain, such as false billing.
assault
Assault is a threat of harm, not sharing information.
tf: Spoken statements that harm a person's reputation are called slander.
Spoken statements that harm a person's reputation are called libel.
Libel is written; spoken defamation is slander.

alt.q: A lab technician tells a friend that an acquaintance tested positive for HIV at their clinic. With what could the technician and clinic be charged?
alt.ex: Slander is spoken defamation: telling others information that can harm someone's reputation.
w: Libel
Libel is written defamation; this disclosure was spoken.
Fraud
Fraud is deception for gain, such as false billing.
Assault
Assault is a threat of harm, not sharing information.

alt.q: At a party, a medical receptionist tells guests that her neighbor is being treated for a sexually transmitted infection at her clinic. What could she be charged with?
alt.ex: Spoken disclosure that can harm someone's reputation is slander.
w: Libel
Libel is written defamation, but this was spoken aloud.
Fraud
Fraud is deliberate deception for gain, such as false billing.
Assault
Assault is a threat of bodily harm, not sharing information.

items.q: Performing an action that results in the death of a patient to alleviate suffering when there is no hope for recovery is called _____.
items.ex: Euthanasia is deliberately ending a patient's life to relieve suffering when recovery is hopeless.
w: palliative care
Palliative care relieves symptoms and suffering without ending life.
hospice care
Hospice provides comfort care for the dying, not actions that cause death.
living will
A living will is a document stating treatment wishes, not an act.
tf: Euthanasia is performing an action that causes a patient's death to relieve suffering.
Euthanasia is providing comfort care without curative treatment to a dying patient.
Comfort care is hospice or palliative care; euthanasia actively ends life.

alt.q: What is the term for deliberately ending the life of a patient with no hope of recovery in order to relieve suffering?
alt.ex: Euthanasia is intentionally ending a life to relieve suffering when recovery is hopeless.
w: Palliative care
Palliative care relieves symptoms without ending life.
Hospice care
Hospice gives comfort care to the dying, not actions that cause death.
Living will
A living will is a document of treatment wishes, not an act.

alt.q: A family asks a physician to give their terminally ill father a drug that will end his life to stop his suffering. What is this act called?
alt.ex: Acting to cause death to end suffering when there is no hope of recovery is euthanasia.
w: Palliative care
Palliative care eases symptoms but does not end life.
Hospice care
Hospice provides comfort at the end of life without causing death.
Durable power of attorney
This document names a health care decision-maker; it is not an act.

items.q: The purpose of a durable power of attorney for health care is to _____.
items.a: name a person whom an individual wants to make health care decisions for them
items.ex: A durable power of attorney for health care appoints an agent to decide if the patient cannot.
w: state which life-sustaining treatments a person refuses
Listing treatment wishes is the purpose of a living will.
give consent for a single surgical procedure
That is an informed consent form, not a power of attorney.
distribute a person's property after their death
Property is handled by a regular will, not a health care document.
tf: A durable power of attorney for health care names a person to make health care decisions for an individual.
A durable power of attorney for health care is a list of treatments a person refuses, such as CPR.
A list of treatment wishes is a living will; this document names a decision-maker.

alt.q: What does a durable power of attorney for health care do?
alt.a: It names a person to make health care decisions for the individual.
alt.ex: It appoints an agent to make health care decisions if the patient cannot.
w: It lists which life-sustaining treatments the person refuses.
Listing treatment wishes is the purpose of a living will.
It gives consent for a single surgical procedure.
That is an informed consent form, not a power of attorney.
It divides a person's property after death.
Property is handled by a regular will, not a health care document.

alt.q: A patient with early dementia wants her daughter to make medical decisions for her once she can no longer decide. Which document should she complete?
alt.a: Durable power of attorney for health care
alt.ex: This document names the person who will make health care decisions for the patient.
w: Living will
A living will lists treatment wishes but does not name a decision-maker.
Informed consent form
Informed consent agrees to one specific treatment.
Last will and testament
A last will handles property after death, not medical decisions.

items.q: A nurse practitioner is preparing to administer medication to their patient. Before they give the medication to the patient, they check it three times. After they administer the medication, they carefully document it in the patient's record. The health care worker's actions can help them prevent _____.
items.ex: Careful checking and accurate documentation prevent errors and show proper care, reducing malpractice risk.
w: slander
Slander is spoken statements that harm reputation, unrelated to medication checks.
fraud
Fraud is intentional deception, such as false billing, not medication errors.
assault
Assault is a threat of harm, not something prevented by medication checks.

alt.q: Checking a medication three times before giving it and carefully charting it afterward helps a health care worker avoid what?
alt.ex: Careful checks and accurate documentation prevent errors, lowering malpractice risk.
w: Slander
Slander is spoken statements that harm reputation.
Fraud
Fraud is intentional deception, such as false billing.
Assault
Assault is a threat of harm, unrelated to medication checks.

alt.q: A respiratory therapist confirms each patient's identity and order before every treatment and charts each one accurately. These habits mainly help protect against which legal problem?
alt.ex: Careful practice and accurate records prevent the errors that lead to malpractice claims.
w: Slander
Slander involves spoken remarks that damage reputation.
Libel
Libel involves written remarks that damage reputation.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment means confining someone against their will.

items.q: Your family is visiting from out of town, and you decide to go to a local amusement park with them. You did not arrange in advance with your employer, so you call in sick to the clinic where you work. Calling in sick is _____.
items.ex: Lying to an employer by calling in sick when not ill is dishonest and ethically wrong.
w: Ethical dilemma
A dilemma has no clear right choice; lying here is clearly wrong.
ethically acceptable
Deceiving an employer about being sick is dishonest, so it isn't acceptable.
an employee right
Sick leave is for illness; using it under false pretenses is not a right.
tf: Calling in sick to spend a day at an amusement park is ethically wrong.
Calling in sick to spend time with visiting family is an ethical dilemma.
A dilemma has no clear right answer; lying to an employer is clearly wrong.

alt.q: You want to spend the day with visiting relatives, so you tell your clinic you are sick even though you feel fine. How is this best described?
alt.ex: Lying to an employer about being sick is dishonest and ethically wrong.
w: Ethical dilemma
A dilemma has no clear right choice; lying here is clearly wrong.
Ethically acceptable
Deceiving an employer about illness is dishonest, so it is not acceptable.
An employee right
Sick leave is for illness; using it under false pretenses is not a right.

alt.q: A phlebotomist feels fine but calls in sick so she can attend a concert she had not requested time off for. How is her action described?
alt.ex: Claiming illness falsely deceives the employer, which is ethically wrong.
w: Ethical dilemma
There are no competing valid values here; lying is clearly wrong.
Ethically acceptable
Dishonesty with an employer is not acceptable conduct.
An employee right
Sick time is for real illness, not a right to use for fun.

items.q: Feelings and beliefs held by a person that can conflict with situations encountered in the workplace are called _____.
items.ex: Values are personal feelings and beliefs; they can clash with situations met at work.
w: laws
Laws are rules set by government, not a person's own beliefs.
policies
Policies are rules set by an organization, not personal beliefs.
procedures
Procedures are steps for doing tasks, not personal feelings or beliefs.

alt.q: What term describes a person's own feelings and beliefs, which can sometimes clash with situations at work?
alt.ex: Values are personal feelings and beliefs that can conflict with workplace situations.
w: Laws
Laws are rules set by government, not personal beliefs.
Policies
Policies are rules set by an organization, not personal beliefs.
Procedures
Procedures are steps for doing tasks, not feelings or beliefs.

alt.q: A nursing assistant's personal beliefs make her uncomfortable caring for a patient who chose a procedure she opposes. What is conflicting with this work situation?
alt.ex: Personal feelings and beliefs that clash with work situations are values.
w: Her employer's policies
Policies are organizational rules, not her personal beliefs.
State laws
Laws are government rules, not personal feelings.
Clinical procedures
Procedures are steps for tasks, not beliefs.

items.q: The combining form "my/o" refers to which body part?
items.ex: My/o means muscle, as in cardiomyopathy: disease of the heart muscle.
w: Spinal cord
Spinal cord is myel/o, which looks similar to my/o.
Vein
Vein is ven/o or phleb/o.
Mouth
Mouth is or/o or stomat/o.
ms: Which of the following terms contain a word part meaning muscle? (Select all that apply)
Myalgia
My/o (muscle) + -algia (pain): muscle pain.
Myocardium
My/o (muscle) + cardi/o (heart): heart muscle.
Myelogram
Myel/o means spinal cord or bone marrow, not muscle.
Phlebitis
Phleb/o means vein: inflammation of a vein.

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

alt.q: In the term "cardiomyopathy," what tissue does the combining form my/o indicate?
alt.ex: My/o means muscle, so cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle.
w: Spinal cord
Spinal cord is myel/o, which looks similar to my/o.
Vein
Vein is ven/o or phleb/o.
Mouth
Mouth is or/o or stomat/o.

alt.q: A patient is diagnosed with myalgia (-algia means pain). Based on my/o, where is the patient's pain?
alt.ex: My/o means muscle, so myalgia is muscle pain.
w: In the spinal cord

items.q: Most health care occupations do not require the use of math.
items.ex: Nearly every health career uses math, such as dosage calculations, measurements, vital signs, and billing.
items.ww: Nurses calculate doses, convert units, and total intake and output, so math is clearly required.

alt.q: Math skills are rarely needed in most health care careers.
alt.ex: Almost every health career uses math for doses, measurements, vital signs, or billing.
alt.ww: Nurses and assistants calculate doses and measure intake, so math is needed.

alt.q: Nurses routinely use math for tasks such as calculating medication doses and measuring intake and output.
alt.ex: Dosage calculations and intake and output totals are everyday nursing math.
alt.ww: Calling it false ignores that safe medication dosing depends on math.
