sections.name: Anatomy, Physiology, Body Organization, and Body Systems

items.q: The liver is located within which body cavity?
items.ex: The liver sits just below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, mostly on the right side.
w: Pelvic cavity
The pelvic cavity holds the urinary bladder and reproductive organs, below the abdomen.
Cranial cavity
The cranial cavity is inside the skull and holds the brain.
Spinal cavity
The spinal cavity runs through the vertebrae and holds the spinal cord.
tf: The liver is located in the abdominal cavity.
The liver is located in the thoracic cavity.
The liver is below the diaphragm; the thoracic cavity holds the heart and lungs.

sc.title: Julio - abdominal pain
sc.text: Julio arrives at their local urgent care reporting pain in the right upper area of their abdomen. The medical assistant brings Julio back to an exam room to complete the intake. Julio reports eating dinner an hour earlier at the local hamburger restaurant. Julio states that this pain has been on and off for a few weeks, usually around mealtimes, but this time the pain is significantly worse.

alt.q: In which body cavity would you find the liver?
alt.ex: The liver lies just below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity.
w: Thoracic cavity
The thoracic cavity is above the diaphragm and holds the heart and lungs.
Pelvic cavity
The pelvic cavity holds the bladder and reproductive organs.
Cranial cavity
The cranial cavity is inside the skull and holds the brain.

alt.q: A medical assistant is labeling a diagram of body cavities. Which cavity label belongs next to the liver?
alt.ex: The liver is an abdominal organ, sitting mostly on the right below the diaphragm.
w: Thoracic cavity
The thoracic cavity contains the heart and lungs, not the liver.
Spinal cavity
The spinal cavity holds the spinal cord.
Cranial cavity
The cranial cavity holds the brain.

items.q: In which quadrant is Julio experiencing pain?
items.ex: Pain in the right upper area of the abdomen is in the right upper quadrant (RUQ).
w: LUQ
LUQ is the left upper quadrant; Julio's pain is on the right.
LLQ
LLQ is the left lower quadrant, opposite side and lower than Julio's pain.
RLQ
RLQ is the right lower quadrant, below the umbilicus; Julio's pain is upper.

sc.title: Julio - abdominal pain
sc.text: Julio arrives at their local urgent care reporting pain in the right upper area of their abdomen. The medical assistant brings Julio back to an exam room to complete the intake. Julio reports eating dinner an hour earlier at the local hamburger restaurant. Julio states that this pain has been on and off for a few weeks, usually around mealtimes, but this time the pain is significantly worse.

alt.q: Julio's pain is in the right upper part of the abdomen. Which abdominal quadrant does this match?
alt.ex: Right upper abdominal pain falls in the right upper quadrant.
w: LUQ
LUQ is the left upper quadrant; Julio's pain is on the right.
RLQ
RLQ is the right lower quadrant, below the umbilicus.
LLQ
LLQ is the lower left, opposite in both directions.

alt.q: A patient points to pain on their right side, below the ribs and above the navel. Which quadrant should the medical assistant document?
alt.ex: Right side above the umbilicus is the right upper quadrant.
w: LUQ
LUQ is on the patient's left side.
RLQ
RLQ is on the right but below the navel.
LLQ
LLQ is on the left and below the navel.

items.q: The right upper area of the abdomen, just below the ribs, is in which region of the abdomen?
items.ex: Hypochondriac means below the cartilage of the ribs, so the upper right region is right hypochondriac.
w: Epigastric
Epigastric is the upper middle region, just below the sternum.
Right lumbar
Right lumbar lies beside the umbilical region, at waist level.
Hypogastric
Hypogastric is the lower middle region, below the umbilical region.
tf: The right hypochondriac region lies on the upper right, just below the ribs.
The right upper area just below the ribs is the right lumbar region.
Right lumbar is beside the umbilical region; right hypochondriac is just below the ribs.
ms: Which of the following are in the top row of the nine abdominal regions? (Select all that apply)
Right hypochondriac
Upper right region, just below the ribs.
Epigastric
Upper middle region, just below the sternum.
Left hypochondriac
Upper left region, just below the ribs.
Umbilical
The umbilical region is the center of the middle row.
Hypogastric
The hypogastric region is the center of the bottom row.

sc.title: Julio - abdominal pain
sc.text: Julio arrives at their local urgent care reporting pain in the right upper area of their abdomen. The medical assistant brings Julio back to an exam room to complete the intake. Julio reports eating dinner an hour earlier at the local hamburger restaurant. Julio states that this pain has been on and off for a few weeks, usually around mealtimes, but this time the pain is significantly worse.

alt.q: In the nine-region system, the area just under the ribs on the right side of the abdomen is called the:
alt.ex: Hypochondriac means below the rib cartilage, so the upper right region is right hypochondriac.
w: Epigastric
Epigastric is the upper middle region below the sternum.
Right lumbar
Right lumbar is at waist level beside the umbilical region.
Right iliac (inguinal)
Right iliac is the lower right region, near the hip.

alt.q: A provider presses on a patient's abdomen just beneath the right rib cage. Which of the nine regions is being examined?
alt.ex: The region below the right ribs is the right hypochondriac region.
w: Left hypochondriac
Left hypochondriac is below the left ribs, not the right.
Epigastric
Epigastric is centered below the sternum, not off to the right.
Umbilical
Umbilical is the central region around the navel.

items.q: The medical assistant documents that Julio is feeling pain on the front side of their body. The medical term that describes this location is _____.
items.ex: Anterior (ventral) means toward the front of the body.
w: posterior
Posterior (dorsal) means toward the back of the body.
lateral
Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline.
caudal
Caudal means toward the lower end or tail of the body.
tf: Pain on the front side of the body is described as anterior.
Pain on the front side of the body is described as posterior.
Posterior means the back; the front of the body is anterior.

sc.title: Julio - abdominal pain
sc.text: Julio arrives at their local urgent care reporting pain in the right upper area of their abdomen. The medical assistant brings Julio back to an exam room to complete the intake. Julio reports eating dinner an hour earlier at the local hamburger restaurant. Julio states that this pain has been on and off for a few weeks, usually around mealtimes, but this time the pain is significantly worse.

alt.q: Which directional term describes a location on the front side of the body?
alt.ex: Anterior, also called ventral, means toward the front of the body.
w: posterior
Posterior means toward the back of the body.
lateral
Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline.
caudal
Caudal means toward the lower or tail end of the body.

alt.q: A nurse documents a rash on the front of a patient's chest and abdomen. Which term describes this location?
alt.ex: The chest and abdomen front surfaces are anterior, or ventral.
w: posterior
Posterior would describe the back, not the chest.
inferior
Inferior means below, not the front surface.
distal
Distal means farther from a point of attachment, usually on limbs.

items.q: Julio is diagnosed with a liver infection and is admitted to the hospital. The liver is an example of which of the following?
items.ex: An organ is made of several tissue types working together for a function, like the liver.
w: Cells
Cells are the basic units of life; the liver is made of many cells.
Tissues
Tissues are groups of similar cells; the liver contains several tissue types.
Body systems
The liver is one organ within the digestive system, not a system itself.
ms: Which of the following are examples of organs? (Select all that apply)
Liver
Made of several tissues working together, so it is an organ.
Heart
Combines muscle, connective, and nervous tissue to pump blood.
Kidney
An organ of the urinary system that filters blood.
Red blood cell
A single cell, the lowest level of organization.
Digestive system
A body system, a group of organs working together.

sc.title: Julio - abdominal pain
sc.text: Julio arrives at their local urgent care reporting pain in the right upper area of their abdomen. The medical assistant brings Julio back to an exam room to complete the intake. Julio reports eating dinner an hour earlier at the local hamburger restaurant. Julio states that this pain has been on and off for a few weeks, usually around mealtimes, but this time the pain is significantly worse.

alt.q: Within the levels of body organization, the liver is classified as which level?
alt.ex: The liver is made of several tissue types working together, which makes it an organ.
w: Cell
Cells are the smallest units; the liver contains millions of them.
Tissue
A tissue is one group of similar cells; the liver has several tissue types.
Body system
The liver is one part of the digestive system, not a whole system.

alt.q: A student is sorting structures by level of organization. Which of these is an organ, like the liver?
alt.ex: The stomach is built from several tissues working together, so it is an organ.
w: Epithelial tissue
Epithelial tissue is a tissue level, not an organ.
Red blood cell
A red blood cell is a single cell.
Digestive system
The digestive system is a group of organs, a higher level.

items.q: The _____ divides the body from top to bottom through the center of the body and divides it into equal right and left portions.
items.ex: The midsagittal plane runs vertically through the midline, creating equal right and left halves.
w: transverse plane
The transverse plane divides the body horizontally into top and bottom.
posterior plane
Posterior is a directional term meaning back, not a body plane.
frontal plane
The frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into front and back.
tf: The midsagittal plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.
The frontal plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.
The frontal plane separates front from back; midsagittal splits equal right and left.

alt.q: Which plane runs vertically through the center of the body, creating equal right and left halves?
alt.ex: The midsagittal plane runs down the midline, making equal right and left sides.
w: transverse plane
The transverse plane divides the body into top and bottom.
frontal plane
The frontal plane divides the body into front and back.
posterior plane
Posterior is a direction meaning toward the back, not a plane.

alt.q: An imaging slice passes straight down through the center of the nose and navel, splitting the body into matching right and left halves. Which plane is this?
alt.ex: A vertical cut through the midline into equal halves is midsagittal.
w: transverse plane
A transverse cut is horizontal, separating top and bottom.
frontal (coronal) plane
A frontal cut separates the front of the body from the back.
oblique plane
An oblique plane cuts at an angle, not straight down the midline.

items.q: The wrist is _____ to the shoulders.
items.ex: Distal means farther from the point of attachment; the wrist is farther from the trunk than the shoulder.
w: proximal
Proximal means closer to the point of attachment, which describes the shoulder.
superior
Superior means above; the wrist hangs below the shoulder in anatomical position.
cephalic
Cephalic means toward the head; the wrist is farther from the head.
tf: The wrist is distal to the shoulder.
The wrist is proximal to the shoulder.
Proximal means closer to the attachment point; the wrist is farther away, so distal.

alt.q: Compared with the shoulder, the wrist is located in a more _____ position.
alt.ex: The wrist is farther from where the arm attaches to the trunk, so it is distal.
w: proximal
Proximal means closer to the attachment, which describes the shoulder.
superior
Superior means above; the wrist is below the shoulder.
cephalic
Cephalic means toward the head; the wrist is farther from it.

alt.q: A nurse documents a cut on a fingertip and compares its location to the knuckles. Which term describes the fingertip relative to the knuckles?
alt.ex: The fingertip is farther from the limb's attachment point than the knuckles.
w: proximal
Proximal would mean closer to the attachment, which describes the knuckles.
superior
Superior means above; in anatomical position fingertips hang below knuckles.
cephalic
Cephalic means toward the head, which the fingertip is not.

items.q: Ligaments are a type of _____ tissue.
items.ex: Ligaments are dense connective tissue that connect bone to bone and support joints.
w: nervous
Nervous tissue carries electrical impulses through neurons.
epithelial
Epithelial tissue covers and lines body surfaces and organs.
muscle
Muscle tissue contracts to produce movement; ligaments do not contract.
ms: Which of the following are made of connective tissue? (Select all that apply)
Ligaments
Dense connective tissue joining bone to bone.
Tendons
Dense connective tissue joining muscle to bone.
Bone
Bone is a hard, mineralized connective tissue.
Outer layer of the skin (epidermis)
The epidermis is epithelial tissue covering the body.
Neurons
Neurons are nervous tissue that carry impulses.

alt.q: Which tissue type do ligaments belong to?
alt.ex: Ligaments are dense connective tissue that join bone to bone.
w: epithelial
Epithelial tissue covers and lines body surfaces.
muscle
Muscle tissue contracts; ligaments do not contract.
nervous
Nervous tissue carries electrical impulses.

alt.q: An athlete tears a ligament that holds two bones together in the knee. What type of tissue was injured?
alt.ex: Ligaments are connective tissue that support joints by linking bones.
w: muscle
A muscle injury would be a strain, not a ligament tear.
nervous
Nervous tissue transmits signals; ligaments do not.
epithelial
Epithelial tissue lines surfaces; it does not join bones.

items.q: The right and left _____ regions are located below the ribs on either side of the epigastric region.
items.ex: The right and left hypochondriac regions sit below the ribs, flanking the epigastric region.
w: lumbar
The lumbar regions flank the umbilical region, at waist level.
iliac
The iliac (inguinal) regions are in the bottom row, flanking the hypogastric region.
hypogastric
Hypogastric is a single middle region below the umbilical region.

alt.q: On each side of the epigastric region, just beneath the ribs, lie the right and left _____ regions.
alt.ex: The hypochondriac regions sit under the ribs, flanking the epigastric region.
w: lumbar
The lumbar regions flank the umbilical region at waist level.
iliac
The iliac regions flank the hypogastric region in the bottom row.
hypogastric
Hypogastric is a single lower middle region, not a right and left pair.

alt.q: A patient has pain under the left ribs, just beside the epigastric region. Which region should be documented?
alt.ex: The region under the left ribs beside the epigastric region is left hypochondriac.
w: Left lumbar
Left lumbar is lower, at waist level beside the umbilical region.
Left iliac (inguinal)
Left iliac is in the bottom row, near the left hip.
Umbilical
Umbilical is the central region around the navel.

items.q: The _____ take in nutrients and oxygen to create heat and energy.
items.ex: Cells, the basic units of life, use nutrients and oxygen in metabolism to produce heat and energy.
w: Body systems
Body systems are groups of organs; the energy work happens inside cells.
Tissues
Tissues are groups of cells; each cell does its own metabolism.
Organs
Organs are made of tissues; the cells inside them create the energy.

alt.q: Which structures use oxygen and nutrients to produce heat and energy for the body?
alt.ex: Cells carry out metabolism, using nutrients and oxygen to make energy and heat.
w: tissues
Tissues are groups of cells; the energy work happens inside each cell.
organs
Organs are made of tissues; their cells produce the energy.
body systems
Body systems are groups of organs, not energy producers themselves.

alt.q: A patient receives oxygen and IV nutrition. At the most basic level, which structures use these to generate energy and body heat?
alt.ex: Cells are the basic units that turn nutrients and oxygen into energy and heat.
w: Organs
Organs depend on their cells to do this work.
Tissues
Tissues are groups of cells, not the most basic level.
Body systems
Body systems are the highest grouping, made of organs.

items.q: The _____ transports proteins made by the ribosomes.
items.ex: The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of channels that transports proteins made by ribosomes.
w: mitochondrion
The mitochondrion produces energy for the cell, the powerhouse.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi apparatus processes and packages proteins it receives from the ER.
nucleus
The nucleus holds DNA and controls cell activities.
ms: Which statements about cell structures are correct? (Select all that apply)
The mitochondrion produces energy for the cell.
It is called the powerhouse of the cell.
The endoplasmic reticulum transports proteins made by ribosomes.
Its channels move proteins through the cell.
Centrioles play a role in cell division.
Centrioles help organize chromosomes as the cell divides.
The nucleus is the powerhouse of the cell.
The nucleus is the control center; mitochondria are the powerhouse.
Lysosomes control what enters and leaves the cell.
The cell membrane does that; lysosomes digest waste and debris.

alt.q: Which organelle moves proteins produced by the ribosomes through the cell?
alt.ex: The endoplasmic reticulum is a channel network that transports ribosome-made proteins.
w: mitochondrion
The mitochondrion produces energy for the cell.
nucleus
The nucleus holds DNA and directs cell activities.
lysosome
Lysosomes digest waste and worn-out cell parts.

alt.q: In a cell diagram, a student traces a network of channels carrying newly made proteins away from the ribosomes. Which organelle is this?
alt.ex: The ER's channels carry proteins from the ribosomes through the cell.
w: Golgi apparatus
The Golgi packages proteins it receives from the ER.
mitochondrion
The mitochondrion makes energy, not protein transport channels.
centriole
Centrioles help with cell division.

items.q: The right and left _____ regions extend on either side of the umbilical region.
items.ex: The right and left lumbar regions sit at waist level on either side of the umbilical region.
w: hypochondriac
The hypochondriac regions flank the epigastric region, just below the ribs.
iliac
The iliac (inguinal) regions flank the hypogastric region in the bottom row.
hypogastric
Hypogastric is a single middle region below the umbilical region.

alt.q: At waist level, the regions on the right and left of the umbilical region are the _____ regions.
alt.ex: The lumbar regions sit at waist level on either side of the umbilical region.
w: hypochondriac
The hypochondriac regions are higher, under the ribs.
iliac
The iliac regions are lower, flanking the hypogastric region.
epigastric
Epigastric is a single upper middle region, not a pair.

alt.q: A patient has flank pain at waist level, just to the right of the navel region. Which region should be documented?
alt.ex: At waist level beside the umbilical region on the right is right lumbar.
w: Right hypochondriac
Right hypochondriac is higher, just under the ribs.
Right iliac (inguinal)
Right iliac is lower, near the right hip.
Umbilical
Umbilical is the center region, not to the side.

items.q: The _____ play a role in cell division.
items.ex: Centrioles help organize and separate chromosomes when a cell divides.
w: lysosomes
Lysosomes digest worn-out cell parts, debris, and bacteria.
ribosomes
Ribosomes make proteins for the cell.
mitochondria
Mitochondria produce the cell's energy.

alt.q: Which cell structures help the cell divide?
alt.ex: Centrioles organize and separate chromosomes during cell division.
w: lysosomes
Lysosomes digest debris and worn-out parts.
ribosomes
Ribosomes make proteins.
mitochondria
Mitochondria produce the cell's energy.

alt.q: An instructor shows a cell splitting in two and points to the structures helping pull the chromosomes apart. What are they?
alt.ex: Centrioles play a key role in separating chromosomes during cell division.
w: Golgi apparatus
The Golgi apparatus packages proteins.
lysosomes
Lysosomes break down waste inside the cell.
ribosomes
Ribosomes build proteins.

items.q: The _____ plane divides the body horizontally into top and bottom portions.
items.ex: The transverse (horizontal) plane cuts across the body, separating top and bottom portions.
w: frontal
The frontal (coronal) plane separates front and back portions.
sagittal
A sagittal plane runs vertically, separating right and left portions.
midsagittal
The midsagittal plane splits the body into equal right and left halves.
ms: Which of the following are planes used to divide the body? (Select all that apply)
Transverse
Divides the body into top and bottom portions.
Frontal (coronal)
Divides the body into front and back portions.
Midsagittal
Divides the body into equal right and left halves.
Epigastric
Epigastric is an abdominal region, not a plane.
Proximal
Proximal is a directional term meaning closer to the attachment point.

alt.q: Which plane cuts across the body horizontally, separating upper and lower portions?
alt.ex: The transverse, or horizontal, plane separates top and bottom portions.
w: frontal
The frontal plane separates front and back.
sagittal
A sagittal plane is vertical, separating right and left.
midsagittal
The midsagittal plane makes equal right and left halves.

alt.q: A CT image shows a cross-sectional slice at the level of the navel, separating the upper body from the lower body. Which plane is shown?
alt.ex: A horizontal cross-section dividing top from bottom is a transverse plane.
w: frontal
A frontal slice would separate front from back.
sagittal
A sagittal slice is vertical, separating right from left.
midsagittal
A midsagittal slice splits the body into equal right and left halves.

items.q: The _____ is the powerhouse of the cell.
items.ex: Mitochondria convert nutrients and oxygen into usable energy, so they are the powerhouse of the cell.
w: nucleus
The nucleus is the control center that contains DNA.
endoplasmic reticulum
The endoplasmic reticulum transports proteins made by ribosomes.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi apparatus packages and ships proteins.
tf: The mitochondrion is known as the powerhouse of the cell.
The nucleus is known as the powerhouse of the cell.
The nucleus is the control center; mitochondria produce the cell's energy.

alt.q: Which organelle produces most of the cell's energy and is nicknamed its powerhouse?
alt.ex: Mitochondria convert nutrients and oxygen into usable energy.
w: nucleus
The nucleus is the control center holding DNA.
endoplasmic reticulum
The ER transports proteins made by ribosomes.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi apparatus packages proteins.

alt.q: Muscle cells need large amounts of energy. Which organelle would you expect to find in high numbers in them?
alt.ex: Mitochondria are the powerhouses, so energy-hungry cells have many of them.
w: centrioles
Centrioles assist cell division, not energy production.
lysosomes
Lysosomes digest waste, not produce energy.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi packages proteins rather than producing energy.

items.q: The directional term _____ means farther from the reference base point.
items.ex: Distal means farther from the point of reference or attachment, like fingers relative to the elbow.
w: proximal
Proximal is the opposite: closer to the point of reference.
medial
Medial means toward the midline of the body.
superior
Superior means above or toward the head.

alt.q: Which directional term describes a point located farther from the point of reference or attachment?
alt.ex: Distal means farther from the reference or attachment point.
w: proximal
Proximal means closer to the reference point.
medial
Medial means toward the midline of the body.
superior
Superior means above or toward the head.

alt.q: A nurse notes swelling in a patient's toes. Which term describes the toes' location relative to the knee?
alt.ex: The toes are farther from the leg's attachment at the hip than the knee is.
w: proximal
Proximal would mean closer to the hip, which describes the knee.
cephalic
Cephalic means toward the head; the toes are far from it.
superior
Superior means above; the toes are below the knee.

items.q: The _____ cavity contains the gallbladder.
items.ex: The gallbladder sits under the liver in the abdominal cavity, along with the stomach and intestines.
w: epigastric
Epigastric is a region of the abdomen, not a body cavity.
pelvic
The pelvic cavity holds the bladder and reproductive organs.
thoracic
The thoracic cavity, above the diaphragm, holds the heart and lungs.

alt.q: In which body cavity is the gallbladder located?
alt.ex: The gallbladder sits beneath the liver in the abdominal cavity.
w: thoracic
The thoracic cavity holds the heart and lungs.
pelvic
The pelvic cavity holds the bladder and reproductive organs.
cranial
The cranial cavity holds the brain.

alt.q: A patient is scheduled for gallbladder removal. Which body cavity must the surgeon enter?
alt.ex: The gallbladder lies under the liver within the abdominal cavity.
w: thoracic
The thoracic cavity is above the diaphragm, with the heart and lungs.
pelvic
The pelvic cavity is lower, holding the bladder and reproductive organs.
spinal
The spinal cavity contains the spinal cord.

items.q: The directional term meaning toward the midline or center of the body is _____.
items.ex: Medial means toward the midline of the body; its opposite is lateral.
w: distal
Distal means farther from the point of attachment.
proximal
Proximal means closer to the point of attachment, not the midline.
peripheral
Peripheral means toward the outer surface, away from the center.
tf: Medial means toward the midline of the body.
Lateral means toward the midline of the body.
Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline; medial is toward it.
ms: Which pairs of directional terms are opposites? (Select all that apply)
Medial and lateral
Toward the midline versus toward the side.
Proximal and distal
Closer to versus farther from the attachment point.
Anterior and posterior
Front versus back of the body.
Anterior and ventral
These are synonyms; both mean the front.
Medial and proximal
Different references: midline versus attachment point, not opposites.

alt.q: Which directional term means toward the body's midline?
alt.ex: Medial means toward the midline; its opposite is lateral.
w: lateral
Lateral means away from the midline, toward the side.
distal
Distal means farther from the point of attachment.
proximal
Proximal means closer to the attachment point, not the midline.

alt.q: The nose is closer to the center line of the body than the ears are. Which term describes the nose relative to the ears?
alt.ex: Being closer to the midline is described as medial.
w: lateral
Lateral would mean farther from the midline, which describes the ears.
distal
Distal compares distance from a limb attachment, not the midline.
posterior
The nose is in front of the ears, so it is not posterior.

items.q: What is the meaning of homeostasis?
items.a: Tendency to maintain a state of balance
items.ex: Homeostasis is the body's effort to keep a stable internal balance, like temperature and fluids.
w: Clustering of cells into tissues
That describes how tissues form, not homeostasis.
Complexity of the human body
Homeostasis is about stability, not how complex the body is.
Order of the body from cells to organism
That describes the levels of organization.
tf: Homeostasis is the body's tendency to maintain a stable internal balance.
Homeostasis is the order of the body from cells to organism.
That order is the levels of organization; homeostasis means maintaining balance.

alt.q: Which phrase best defines homeostasis?
alt.a: The body's tendency to keep a stable internal balance
alt.ex: Homeostasis is the body keeping conditions like temperature and fluids steady.
w: The order of organization from cells up to the organism
That describes the levels of body organization.
The grouping of similar cells into tissues
That describes how tissues form.
The process of cells dividing to form new cells
That is cell division, not maintaining balance.

alt.q: On a hot day, a patient sweats to keep body temperature near normal. This is an example of which concept?
alt.ex: Sweating to hold a steady temperature shows the body maintaining balance.
w: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is identifying a disease, not a body response.
Levels of organization
Levels of organization describe body structure, not keeping balance.
Anatomical position
Anatomical position is a standard body posture for reference.

items.q: _____ are cells with similar functions grouped together.
items.ex: Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function.
w: Body systems
Body systems are groups of organs working together.
Organs
Organs are made of several different tissue types.
Cells
Cells are the individual units that group together to form tissues.

alt.q: What term describes a group of cells with similar functions working together?
alt.ex: Tissues are groups of similar cells performing a shared function.
w: Organ
Organs are made of several different tissue types.
Body system
Body systems are groups of organs.

w: Cataract
A cataract clouds the lens; it is not caused by eye pressure.
Macular degeneration
Macular degeneration affects the central retina, not via eye pressure.
Hyperopia
Hyperopia is farsightedness and does not damage the optic nerve.

items.q: The sudoriferous glands produce a substance that lubricates and protects the skin.
items.ex: Sudoriferous glands make sweat to cool the body; sebaceous glands make oil (sebum) that lubricates skin.
items.ww: Lubricating, protective oil comes from sebaceous glands, not the sweat-producing sudoriferous glands.

alt.q: The sudoriferous (sweat) glands secrete the oily substance that lubricates and protects the skin.
alt.ex: Sudoriferous glands make sweat; sebaceous glands make the lubricating oil, sebum.
alt.ww: The oil that lubricates skin is sebum from sebaceous glands, not sweat.

alt.q: The sebaceous glands, not the sudoriferous glands, produce the oil that lubricates and protects the skin.
alt.ex: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, an oil that keeps skin lubricated and protected.
alt.ww: Sudoriferous glands make sweat for cooling, so the statement is accurate.

items.q: If a patient complains of angina pectoris, they may be in immediate danger of what event?
items.ex: Angina is chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart, warning that a heart attack may occur.
w: Congestive heart failure
CHF is a gradual weakening of the heart's pumping, not the immediate danger angina signals.
Aneurysm
An aneurysm is a ballooning of an artery wall, not linked to angina.
Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis is plaque buildup that causes angina, not the event it warns of.
tf: Angina pectoris can signal that a patient is in danger of a myocardial infarction.
Angina pectoris signals that a patient is in danger of an aneurysm.
Angina reflects poor blood flow to the heart muscle, warning of a heart attack.

alt.q: Chest pain from angina pectoris is a warning that the patient could soon experience which event?
alt.ex: Angina signals reduced blood flow to the heart, which can lead to a heart attack.
w: Congestive heart failure
CHF is a gradual weakening of pumping, not the immediate danger angina signals.
Aneurysm
An aneurysm is a ballooning artery wall, not linked to angina.
Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis is plaque buildup that causes angina, not the event it warns of.

alt.q: A patient tells the medical assistant they get crushing chest pain when climbing stairs, which the provider diagnoses as angina pectoris. Which emergency is this patient at immediate risk for?
alt.ex: Angina means the heart muscle is short on blood flow, risking a heart attack.
w: Congestive heart failure
CHF develops gradually; it is not the immediate threat angina warns of.
Aneurysm
An aneurysm is a weakened, bulging artery wall, unrelated to angina.
Varicose veins
Varicose veins are swollen leg veins, unrelated to chest pain.

items.q: Which of the following terms means painful menstrual cramps?
items.ex: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation (dys- = painful, men- = month, -rrhea = flow).
w: Menorrhagia
Menorrhagia is abnormally heavy or long menstrual bleeding.
Menses
Menses is the normal monthly menstrual flow.
Amenorrhea
Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation.
tf: Dysmenorrhea is the medical term for painful menstrual cramps.
Amenorrhea is the medical term for painful menstrual cramps.
The prefix a- means without; amenorrhea is absence of menstruation.

alt.q: Which medical term describes menstruation accompanied by painful cramping?
alt.ex: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation (dys- = painful).
w: Amenorrhea
Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation.
Menorrhagia
Menorrhagia is abnormally heavy or long menstrual bleeding.
Menses
Menses is the normal monthly menstrual flow.

w: Amenorrhea
Amenorrhea means no periods, but this patient menstruates monthly.

Menorrhagia describes heavy bleeding, not painful cramps.
Menopause

items.q: Why is sleep apnea a potentially serious condition?

Sleep apnea affects breathing, not body temperature.
It prevents food from being digested.
Sleep apnea is a breathing disorder, not a digestive one.

The danger is pauses in breathing, not vocal cord damage.

alt.q: What makes sleep apnea potentially dangerous to a person's health?
alt.a: Breathing repeatedly stops, depriving the body of oxygen.

w: It raises body temperature during sleep.
Sleep apnea affects breathing, not body temperature.
It prevents food from being digested.

It permanently damages the vocal cords.
The danger is pauses in breathing, not vocal cord damage.

Sleep apnea does not cause dangerous rises in body temperature.
The pauses stop the stomach from digesting food.
Sleep apnea involves breathing, not digestion.
The snoring will permanently damage the vocal cords.
The serious risk is low oxygen, not vocal cord damage.

items.q: Taking a temperature is an example of collecting objective evidence.
items.ex: A temperature is measured by the provider, so it is objective data (a sign).

items.q: Which condition is an age-related condition that causes pressure on the urethra?
items.ex: Prostatic hypertrophy (enlarged prostate) is common with aging and squeezes the urethra, slowing urine flow.

Phimosis is a tight foreskin, not an age-related urethral problem.

Epididymitis

alt.q: As men age, which condition commonly develops and puts pressure on the urethra?

w: Phimosis
Phimosis is a tight foreskin, not an age-related urethral problem.
Orchiditis
Orchiditis is inflammation of a testis.
Epididymitis
Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis, usually from infection.

w: Phimosis

Epididymitis causes scrotal pain and swelling, not urethral pressure.

items.q: An important function of the circulatory system is to regulate body temperature.
items.ex: Blood vessels widen to release heat and narrow to conserve it, helping regulate body temperature.
items.ww: Circulating blood carries heat, and vessel dilation or constriction helps control body temperature.

alt.q: Helping to control body temperature is one of the important jobs of the circulatory system.
alt.ex: Blood vessels widen to release heat and narrow to conserve it.
alt.ww: Blood carries heat, and vessel changes help control temperature, so the statement is true.

alt.q: The circulatory system plays no role in regulating body temperature.
alt.ex: Blood vessels dilate or constrict to release or conserve body heat.
alt.ww: Circulating blood carries heat, so the circulatory system does help regulate temperature.

items.q: Where are the kidneys located?
items.ex: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, lying behind the peritoneum against the back wall of the abdomen.
w: In front of the peritoneum
The kidneys sit behind the peritoneal lining, near the back muscles.
Below the urinary bladder
The bladder is in the pelvis; the kidneys are higher, near the lower ribs.
Inside the thoracic cavity
The thoracic cavity holds the heart and lungs, not the kidneys.
tf: The kidneys are located behind the peritoneum.
The kidneys are located in the pelvic cavity below the urinary bladder.
The kidneys are retroperitoneal near the lower ribs, above the bladder.

alt.q: In relation to the peritoneum, where are the kidneys located?
alt.ex: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum, against the back wall of the abdomen.
w: In front of the peritoneum, beside the intestines
The kidneys are behind the peritoneal lining, not in front of it.
Below the peritoneum, in the pelvic cavity
The pelvic cavity holds the bladder; the kidneys sit higher, near the lower ribs.
Above the diaphragm, in the thoracic cavity
The thoracic cavity holds the heart and lungs, not the kidneys.

alt.q: A medical assistant explaining a kidney ultrasound says the kidneys sit against the back wall of the abdomen, behind the abdominal lining. Which term describes this location?

w: Intraperitoneal
Intraperitoneal organs, like the stomach, are inside the peritoneal lining.
Thoracic
Thoracic refers to the chest cavity with the heart and lungs.
Pelvic
The pelvic cavity holds the urinary bladder, not the kidneys.

items.q: What is the most serious risk for individuals who have osteoporosis?
items.ex: Osteoporosis makes bones porous and brittle, so the biggest danger is fractures, often from falls.
w: Bone infections
Bone infection is osteomyelitis; osteoporosis is loss of bone density.
Joint inflammation
Joint inflammation is arthritis, not the main risk of osteoporosis.
Joint dislocation
Weak bones break; osteoporosis does not mainly cause dislocations.

alt.q: For a person with osteoporosis, what is the greatest danger?
alt.ex: Osteoporosis makes bones porous and brittle, so they break easily.
w: Bone infections
Bone infection is osteomyelitis; osteoporosis is loss of bone density.
Joint inflammation
Joint inflammation is arthritis, not the main risk of osteoporosis.
Joint dislocation
Weakened bones break; osteoporosis does not mainly cause dislocations.

alt.q: An older patient with osteoporosis is going home. Which safety teaching is most important?
alt.a: Prevent falls, because weakened bones fracture easily.
alt.ex: Fractures are the most serious osteoporosis risk, often caused by falls.
w: Avoid crowds, because bone infections spread easily.
Osteoporosis is bone density loss, not an infection.
Rest the joints, because joint inflammation is the main danger.
Joint inflammation is arthritis, not the key osteoporosis risk.
Avoid reaching overhead, because joints dislocate easily.
Osteoporosis mainly causes fractures, not dislocations.

items.q: Which action includes behaviors that promote health?
items.ex: Prevention includes healthy behaviors, like exercise and immunizations, that promote health and stop disease.
w: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is identifying a disease, not promoting health.
Prognosis
Prognosis is the predicted outcome of a disease.
Treatment
Treatment manages an existing illness rather than promoting health beforehand.
ms: Which of the following are examples of prevention? (Select all that apply)
Exercising regularly
Exercise is a health-promoting behavior.
Getting recommended immunizations
Vaccines prevent disease before it starts.
Eating a balanced diet
Good nutrition promotes health.
Taking antibiotics for an infection
This treats an existing illness.
Getting an X-ray to find a fracture
This is part of diagnosis.

alt.q: Healthy behaviors that promote health and keep disease from developing fall under which category?
alt.ex: Prevention includes health-promoting behaviors that stop disease before it starts.
w: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is identifying a disease, not promoting health.
Prognosis
Prognosis is the predicted outcome of a disease.
Treatment
Treatment manages an illness that already exists.

alt.q: A medical assistant encourages a healthy patient to exercise regularly, eat well, and get a yearly flu shot. This counseling is an example of which action?
alt.ex: Exercise, good nutrition, and immunizations are health-promoting preventive behaviors.
w: Diagnosis
Nothing is being identified as a disease, so this is not diagnosis.
Prognosis
Prognosis predicts a disease's outcome; this patient is healthy.
Treatment
Treatment addresses an existing illness, which this patient does not have.

items.q: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a specific disease with a known etiology.
items.ex: COPD is an umbrella term for a group of lung diseases, such as emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
items.ww: COPD is not one specific disease; it groups several chronic lung conditions with varied causes.

alt.q: COPD is one single, specific disease whose cause is clearly known.
alt.ex: COPD is a general term for a group of chronic lung diseases.
alt.ww: COPD includes several conditions, like emphysema and chronic bronchitis, so it is not one disease.

alt.q: COPD is an umbrella term that covers several chronic lung conditions, such as emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
alt.ex: COPD groups several chronic lung diseases rather than naming one specific disease.
alt.ww: COPD is not a single disease, so describing it as an umbrella term is correct.

items.q: How does understanding anatomy and physiology benefit Nurse Practitioner Kayla in assessing and treating Quinn's fractured arm?
items.a: Knowledge of anatomy and physiology allows Kayla to recognize the signs and symptoms of Quinn's injury, facilitating an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Billing is administrative; A&P knowledge is used for clinical assessment and care.
Knowledge of anatomy and physiology lets Kayla skip the X-ray because a fracture can be confirmed by sight alone.
A&P guides assessment, but imaging is still needed to confirm a fracture.
Knowledge of anatomy and physiology is needed only by the radiologist, not by the nurse practitioner treating Quinn.
Every provider assessing and treating patients relies on A&P knowledge.

sc.title: Quinn - fractured forearm
sc.text: Twelve-year-old Quinn was playing basketball with some friends when they fell and landed on their outstretched arm, causing a twisting motion followed by sudden pain. Quinn's parents rush Quinn to the emergency department, where Nurse Practitioner Kayla assesses the injury. X-rays show a fractured radius. Quinn will need a plaster-based cast, prescribed pain medication as needed, elevation of the arm, and cold compresses to reduce swelling.

alt.q: Why is Kayla's knowledge of anatomy and physiology valuable when she evaluates and treats Quinn's broken arm?
alt.a: It helps her recognize Quinn's signs and symptoms so she can make an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.
alt.ex: Knowing normal structure and function lets Kayla spot what is abnormal and plan care.
w: It mainly helps her complete billing and insurance paperwork for Quinn's visit.
Billing is administrative; A&P knowledge is used for clinical assessment.
It lets her skip the X-ray because a fracture can be confirmed by sight alone.
A&P guides assessment, but imaging is still needed to confirm a fracture.
It is needed only by the radiologist, not by the nurse practitioner.
Every provider who assesses and treats patients relies on A&P knowledge.

alt.q: Kayla notices that Quinn's forearm is swollen and that Quinn cannot rotate the wrist normally. What mainly allows Kayla to recognize these findings as abnormal?
alt.a: Her knowledge of normal anatomy and physiology of the arm

Billing knowledge is administrative and does not identify physical findings.

Visitor policies have nothing to do with assessing an injury.
Her knowledge of the cost of cast materials

items.q: Which bodily system plays a role in delivering nutrients and removing waste from Quinn's injured arm?

The nervous system sends signals like pain; it does not transport nutrients.

Integumentary system
The skin protects the body but does not deliver nutrients or remove waste.
tf: In the scenario, the circulatory system delivers nutrients to and removes waste from Quinn's injured arm.
In the scenario, the nervous system delivers nutrients to and removes waste from Quinn's injured arm.
Nerves carry signals; blood vessels transport nutrients and wastes.

Delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
Carries away waste products
Blood removes wastes like carbon dioxide.
Helps regulate body temperature
Vessels dilate or constrict to release or keep heat.
Triggers the fight or flight response
Adrenal gland hormones (endocrine) trigger fight or flight.
Contracts to move the bones
Skeletal muscles move bones.

sc.title: Quinn - fractured forearm

The nervous system sends signals like pain; it does not transport nutrients.

w: Nervous system

Muscular system
Muscles produce movement but do not transport nutrients.

The skin protects the body but does not carry nutrients or wastes.

items.q: When Kayla discusses managing Quinn's pain, Kayla explains the importance of elevating the arm and using cold compresses to reduce swelling. Based on this information, what is the primary reason for Quinn's pain following the fracture?

Muscle atrophy around the fracture
Atrophy develops slowly with disuse, not right after an injury.

Elevation and cold compresses ease Quinn's fracture pain mainly by preventing bone infection.
Elevation and cold target swelling and inflammation, the main source of pain here.

items.q: Based on Quinn's injury, which bone in the forearm was not affected by the fracture?
items.ex: The forearm has two bones, the radius and ulna; the X-ray showed only the radius was fractured.

The X-ray showed the radius was the fractured bone.

The fibula is in the lower leg, not the forearm.

sections.name: Growth, Development, Aging, Grief, and Lifespan Theory

items.q: Based on Piaget's theory of cognitive development, which stage is Antonia likely to be in at 6 years old?
items.ex: Piaget's preoperational stage spans about ages 2 to 7, marked by language, symbolic play, and egocentrism.
w: Concrete operational stage
Concrete operational thinking begins around age 7, after Antonia's age.
Formal operational stage
Formal operational (abstract) thinking starts around age 11 or 12.
Sensorimotor stage
The sensorimotor stage covers birth to about age 2.
tf: At age 5 or 6, Antonia is likely in Piaget's preoperational stage.
At age 5 or 6, Antonia is likely in Piaget's concrete operational stage.
Concrete operational thinking begins around age 7; ages 2 to 7 are preoperational.
ms: Which characteristics fit Piaget's preoperational stage? (Select all that apply)
Rapid language development
Language expands quickly between ages 2 and 7.
Pretend and symbolic play
Using symbols in play marks the preoperational stage.
Egocentric thinking
Preoperational children struggle to see others' viewpoints.
Abstract, hypothetical reasoning
Abstract reasoning belongs to the formal operational stage.
Learning mainly through reflexes and senses
That describes the sensorimotor stage (birth to 2).

sc.title: Antonia - pediatric occupational therapy
sc.text: Occupational therapist Max is working with Antonia, a 5-year-old pediatric patient who was recently diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Antonia's parents are hoping that occupational therapy sessions can assist with Antonia's growth and development. During their therapy sessions, Max engages Antonia in a variety of playful activities designed to assist in healthy growth and development.

alt.q: According to Piaget, a child of Antonia's age (about 5 to 6 years old) is most likely in which stage of cognitive development?
alt.ex: Piaget's preoperational stage spans about ages 2 to 7.
w: Sensorimotor stage
The sensorimotor stage covers birth to about age 2.
Concrete operational stage
Concrete operational thinking begins around age 7.
Formal operational stage
Formal (abstract) thinking starts around age 11 or 12.

alt.q: A 4-year-old pretends a banana is a telephone but insists a tall, thin glass holds more juice than a short, wide glass with the same amount. Which Piaget stage fits this child?
alt.ex: Symbolic play without understanding conservation is typical of the preoperational stage.
w: Sensorimotor stage
The sensorimotor stage ends around age 2, before symbolic pretend play develops.
Concrete operational stage
Concrete operational children, about 7 and up, understand the amounts are equal.
Formal operational stage
Formal operational thinking is abstract reasoning in adolescence.

items.q: How would Max's approach to therapy be different for Antonia compared to an adolescent patient?
items.a: Max should encourage verbalization skills with Antonia.
items.ex: At age 5, language is still developing, so therapy should build verbal skills through play.
w: Max should focus on identity and career planning with Antonia.
Identity and career goals fit adolescents, not a 5-year-old.
Max should rely mainly on written instructions with Antonia.
A 5-year-old cannot rely on reading; written instructions suit older patients.
Max should use abstract reasoning tasks with Antonia.
Abstract reasoning develops in adolescence, beyond Antonia's stage.

sc.title: Antonia - pediatric occupational therapy
sc.text: Occupational therapist Max is working with Antonia, a 5-year-old pediatric patient who was recently diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Antonia's parents are hoping that occupational therapy sessions can assist with Antonia's growth and development. During their therapy sessions, Max engages Antonia in a variety of playful activities designed to assist in healthy growth and development.

alt.q: Compared with how Max would work with an adolescent, what should Max emphasize in Antonia's therapy?
alt.ex: At Antonia's age, language is still developing, so therapy should build verbal skills.
w: Focusing on identity and career planning
Identity and career goals fit adolescents, not a young child.
Relying mainly on written instructions
A young child cannot rely on reading; written instructions suit older patients.
Using abstract reasoning tasks
Abstract reasoning develops in adolescence, beyond a young child's stage.

alt.q: An occupational therapist is working with a 5-year-old during play. Which approach best fits this child's developmental level?
alt.a: Prompting the child to name objects and describe actions out loud
alt.ex: Young children are building language, so therapy should encourage verbalization.
w: Having the child follow written step-by-step instructions
A 5-year-old cannot rely on reading written directions.
Discussing the child's future career goals
Career planning fits adolescents, not a young child.
Asking the child to solve abstract hypothetical problems
Abstract reasoning develops in adolescence.

items.q: How could Max apply Erikson's theory of psychosocial development to support Antonia's therapy?
items.a: By encouraging Antonia to explore the environment and develop a sense of independence
items.ex: Erikson's early childhood stages center on autonomy and initiative, gained by exploring and acting independently.
w: By helping Antonia form an identity and set future career goals
Identity vs. role confusion is Erikson's adolescent stage.
By helping Antonia build close, intimate relationships with peers
Intimacy vs. isolation is Erikson's young adult stage.
By having Antonia reflect on her life accomplishments
Reflecting on life (integrity vs. despair) is Erikson's late adulthood stage.
