alt.q: A hospital clerk smells smoke in a hallway and reports it. Using the text's example, which code would be announced?
alt.ex: In the text's example, code red alerts staff to fire or smoke.
w: Code blue
Code blue is commonly used for a patient in cardiac or respiratory arrest.
Code pink
Code pink is commonly used for an infant or child abduction.
Code silver
Code silver is commonly used for a person with a weapon.

items.q: Alita stayed calm and assisted others to evacuate the office in a calm, controlled manner. Moving safely in an emergency is important because _____.
items.a: it reduces the risk of potential accidents, such as falls.
items.ex: Calm, controlled movement prevents trips, falls, and collisions that cause injuries during an emergency.
w: it allows staff time to collect personal belongings on the way out.
Belongings are left behind; delaying evacuation increases danger.
it is only important when patients are present in the area.
Safe movement matters for everyone, staff included, in any emergency.
it means staff no longer need to account for coworkers outside.
Accounting for everyone is still required after evacuation, as Alita did.

sc.title: Alita - fire and evacuation
sc.text: Alita works as a medical records clerk in a hospital, managing patient records, updating databases, and ensuring the accuracy and confidentiality of medical information. One day, Alita notices the strong odor of smoke coming from the hallway outside of the office door. Alita checks the hospital's emergency response procedures, activates the fire alarm, informs colleagues about the potential fire, and directs them to evacuate safely. Once outside, Alita takes charge of the department's evacuation procedures, ensures everyone is accounted for, assists those who need extra support, and brings the department's emergency preparedness plan.

alt.q: Why is it important to move in a calm, controlled way during an emergency?
alt.a: It lowers the risk of accidents, such as falls
alt.ex: Calm movement prevents trips, falls, and collisions that cause injuries during emergencies.
w: It gives staff time to collect personal belongings
Belongings are left behind; delaying evacuation increases danger.
It matters only when patients are in the area
Safe movement matters for everyone, including staff, in any emergency.
It removes the need to account for coworkers outside
Everyone must still be accounted for after evacuating.

alt.q: During a fire evacuation, a coworker starts running down the stairs and pushing past others. Why should Alita tell them to slow down?
alt.a: Rushing increases the risk of accidents, such as falls
alt.ex: Moving calmly and safely reduces falls and collisions during an evacuation.
w: Running is fine, but only when patients are not present
Running is unsafe for everyone, whether or not patients are present.
Slowing down gives time to grab personal items
Personal items are left behind during an evacuation.
People who move calmly do not need to be counted outside
Everyone must be accounted for regardless of how they evacuated.

items.q: Infectious waste must be handled using _____.
items.ex: Infectious waste can carry pathogens, so it is handled using standard and transmission-based precautions.
w: PASS
PASS is the method for using a fire extinguisher, not handling waste.
the emergency preparedness plan
This plan covers disaster response, not routine infectious waste handling.
incident reports
Incident reports document accidents or errors after they happen.
tf: Infectious waste must be handled using standard and transmission-based precautions.
Infectious waste can be handled like regular trash as long as the bag is tied closed.
Infectious waste carries pathogens and needs standard and transmission-based precautions.

alt.q: Which guidelines must be followed when handling infectious waste?
alt.ex: Infectious waste can carry pathogens, so standard and transmission-based precautions apply.
w: The PASS method
PASS is the method for using a fire extinguisher.
The emergency preparedness plan
This plan covers disaster response, not routine waste handling.
The RACE sequence
RACE is the sequence to follow when a fire is discovered.

alt.q: A medical assistant must discard dressings soaked with a patient's blood. Which guidelines apply?
alt.ex: Blood-soaked dressings are infectious waste, handled with standard and transmission-based precautions.
w: The PASS method
PASS guides fire extinguisher use, not waste handling.
Incident reporting procedures
Incident reports document accidents after they occur.
The RACE sequence
RACE guides the response to a discovered fire.

items.q: A code system for alerting employees in the building to emergencies is done to _____.
items.a: prevent patients and visitors from becoming alarmed
items.ex: Coded announcements like code red alert staff to an emergency without causing panic among patients and visitors.
w: notify the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
OSHA is a federal agency; codes are internal alerts for staff in the building.
notify area law enforcement agencies
Police are contacted by phone or 911, not by overhead codes for employees.
produce an incident report
Incident reports are written documents completed after an event, not emergency alerts.
tf: Hospitals use emergency codes, such as code red, to alert staff without alarming patients and visitors.
Hospital emergency codes are used mainly to notify OSHA that an emergency is happening.
Codes are internal staff alerts designed to prevent panic, not reports to OSHA.

alt.q: Why do hospitals use coded announcements, such as "Code Red," to alert staff to emergencies?
alt.a: To keep patients and visitors from becoming alarmed
alt.ex: Codes alert trained staff without causing panic among patients and visitors.
w: To meet OSHA reporting requirements
OSHA is a federal agency; codes are internal alerts for staff.
To summon local police to the building
Police are called by phone or 911, not by overhead codes.
To create the written incident report
Incident reports are written documents completed after an event.

alt.q: A medical assistant hears "Code Red, third floor" over the intercom instead of "Fire on the third floor." Why is it announced this way?
alt.a: So staff are alerted without causing panic among patients and visitors
alt.ex: Coded language informs employees while keeping patients and visitors calm.
w: So OSHA is automatically notified of the fire
Overhead codes do not notify OSHA; they alert staff inside the building.
So the announcement serves as the incident report
An incident report is a separate written document, not an announcement.
So area law enforcement knows to respond
Outside agencies are contacted directly, not through hospital intercom codes.

items.q: Health care workers who provide constant emotional support, cope with emergency situations, and lack supervisory support are at risk for _____ hazards.
items.ex: Psychosocial hazards affect mental and emotional health, like stress from constant emotional demands and poor support.
w: Social
Social is not a workplace hazard category; emotional strain falls under psychosocial hazards.
Cognitive
Cognitive refers to thinking skills, not a category of workplace hazard.
Intellectual
Intellectual is not a workplace hazard type; the stressors described are psychosocial.
tf: Workers who give constant emotional support and lack supervisory support face psychosocial hazards.
Workers who give constant emotional support and lack supervisory support face mainly physical hazards.
Physical hazards cause tissue injury; emotional strain and stress are psychosocial hazards.

alt.q: Constant emotional demands, frequent emergencies, and little supervisory support are examples of which type of workplace hazard?
alt.ex: Psychosocial hazards harm mental and emotional health through stress and lack of support.
w: Ergonomic
Ergonomic hazards involve body mechanics and workstation design, not emotional strain.
Physical
Physical hazards cause bodily injury, such as fire, falls, or noise.
Biological
Biological hazards are infectious agents like bacteria and viruses.

alt.q: An ER nurse comforts distressed families all shift, handles repeated crises, and rarely gets help from her manager. Which type of hazard is she facing?
alt.ex: Ongoing emotional demands and poor supervisory support are psychosocial hazards.
w: Chemical
Chemical hazards come from hazardous substances, not emotional stressors.
Radiation
Radiation hazards come from sources like x-rays, not emotional demands.
Ergonomic
Ergonomic hazards relate to posture and repetitive motion, not emotional stress.

items.q: Standard precautions must be used when cleaning up a spill involving _____.
items.ex: Blood and body fluids can carry pathogens, so standard precautions like gloves are required for these spills.
w: chemicals
Chemical spills follow the SDS and chemical safety procedures, not infection-control precautions.
flammable liquids
Flammable liquid spills are a fire hazard handled with fire and chemical safety rules.
radiation
Radiation exposure is controlled with shielding like lead aprons, not standard precautions.
ms: Standard precautions must be used when cleaning up which spills? (Select all that apply)
Blood on the floor
Blood can carry bloodborne pathogens, so standard precautions apply.
A patient's vomit
Vomit is a body fluid and may be infectious.
Urine from a spilled specimen
Urine is a body fluid, so treat it as potentially infectious.
Spilled alcohol-based cleaner
This is a flammable chemical spill handled with chemical safety rules.
Spilled mercury from old equipment
Mercury is a hazardous chemical spill requiring chemical cleanup procedures.

alt.q: Cleaning up which type of spill requires the use of standard precautions?
alt.ex: Blood and body fluids may carry pathogens, so standard precautions are required.
w: Cleaning chemicals
Chemical spills are handled using the SDS and chemical safety procedures.
Flammable liquids
Flammable liquid spills are handled with fire and chemical safety rules.
Radioactive materials
Radiation is controlled with shielding like lead aprons, not standard precautions.

alt.q: A patient's IV line disconnects and blood drips onto the floor. What should the health care worker follow while cleaning it up?
alt.ex: Any blood spill requires standard precautions because blood can carry pathogens.
w: Fire safety procedures for flammable liquids
Blood is not flammable; the concern is infection, not fire.
Radiation safety procedures with a lead apron
Lead aprons protect against radiation, not bloodborne pathogens.
No precautions, since the patient has no known infection
Standard precautions apply to all blood regardless of known infection status.

items.q: RACE is the acronym to help remember the proper sequence to follow when a fire is discovered.
items.ex: RACE stands for Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate, the order of actions when fire is found.
items.ww: RACE is the fire-response sequence; PASS is the acronym for using an extinguisher.

alt.q: The acronym RACE helps health care workers recall the correct order of steps to take after discovering a fire.
alt.ex: RACE stands for Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate, the fire-response order.
alt.ww: RACE is exactly the memory aid for the fire-response sequence.

alt.q: PASS, rather than RACE, is the acronym for the order of actions to take when a fire is discovered.
alt.ex: RACE gives the fire-response order; PASS describes how to use an extinguisher.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses PASS, the extinguisher technique, with RACE.

items.q: When using chemicals, you should check the label _____ times.
items.ex: Check the label when taking the chemical from storage, before using it, and when returning it.
w: two
Two checks skips one safety point; the rule is three label checks.
five
Five is not the standard; chemical labels are checked three times.
four
Four is more than the standard rule of three label checks.
tf: A chemical label should be checked three times: when taking it, before using it, and when returning it.
A chemical label needs to be checked only once, right before using the chemical.
One check is not enough; labels are checked three times to prevent mistakes.

alt.q: How many times should you check the label on a chemical container when using it?
alt.ex: Labels are checked when removing the chemical, before using it, and when returning it.
w: One
A single check skips two of the required safety points.
Two
Two checks misses one of the three required label checks.
Five
Five is not the standard; the rule is three label checks.

alt.q: A lab assistant takes a disinfectant from the supply cabinet, uses it, and puts it back. How many label checks should she make in total?
alt.a: Three: when removing it, before using it, and when returning it
alt.ex: The safety rule is to check a chemical label three times.
w: One: just before using it
One check skips the checks at removal and return.
Two: when removing it and when returning it
This skips the check right before using the chemical.
Four: when removing, opening, using, and returning it
The standard rule is three checks, not four.

items.q: When dressing for safety, any type of jewelry is acceptable if it doesn't get in your way as you work.
items.ex: Jewelry should be minimal because it can scratch patients, get caught in equipment, and harbor germs.
items.ww: Even jewelry that seems out of the way can injure patients or carry microorganisms.

alt.q: Health care workers may wear any jewelry they like at work as long as it does not interfere with their tasks.
alt.ex: Jewelry should be minimal because it can injure patients, catch on equipment, and harbor germs.
alt.ww: Even jewelry that seems out of the way can scratch patients or carry microorganisms.

alt.q: Health care workers should keep jewelry to a minimum because it can injure patients, catch on equipment, and harbor germs.
alt.ex: Minimal jewelry reduces injury risk and the spread of microorganisms.
alt.ww: Jewelry poses real safety and infection risks, so limiting it is correct.

items.q: Which of the following statements is true about oxygen administration safety?
items.ex: Oxygen supports combustion, so every listed precaution against sparks, flames, and smoking is correct.
w: Post No Smoking signs where oxygen is in use.
This is true, but it is only one of several correct precautions.
Avoid wool and synthetic fabrics that can cause static sparks.
This is true, but the other precautions are also correct.
Keep open flames and sparking equipment away from oxygen.
This is true, but it is not the only correct statement.
ms: Which of the following are oxygen administration safety precautions? (Select all that apply)
Post No Smoking signs where oxygen is in use
Oxygen makes fire burn faster, so smoking is banned nearby.
Avoid wool and synthetic fabrics that create static
Static sparks can ignite an oxygen-rich area.
Keep open flames away from the oxygen source
Oxygen supports combustion, so flames are a serious fire risk.
Lubricate oxygen fittings with oil or grease
Oil and grease can ignite in the presence of oxygen.
Leave oxygen tanks standing unsecured
Tanks must be secured so they cannot fall and rupture.

alt.q: Which precaution is correct when oxygen is being administered to a patient?
alt.a: Keep open flames and sparking equipment away from the oxygen
alt.ex: Oxygen supports combustion, so flames and sparks must be kept away.
w: Allow smoking if the oxygen flow is turned down low
Smoking is never allowed where oxygen is in use.
Use wool blankets to reduce static electricity
Wool and synthetic fabrics can create static sparks and should be avoided.
Post No Smoking signs only in the operating room
No Smoking signs are posted wherever oxygen is in use.

alt.q: A visitor wants to light a scented candle in the room of a patient receiving oxygen. What should the health care worker do?
alt.a: Explain that open flames are not allowed near oxygen and stop the candle from being lit
alt.ex: Oxygen feeds fire, so any open flame near it is a serious hazard.
w: Allow the candle if it is placed across the room
Any open flame in a room with oxygen is a fire hazard.
Allow the candle if the oxygen is briefly turned off
Oxygen lingers in the room and bedding, so flames remain unsafe.
Cover the patient with a wool blanket for protection
Wool can cause static sparks and adds a fire risk near oxygen.

items.q: Physical hazards are agents that can cause physical injury and tissue damage.
items.ex: Physical hazards, like fire, falls, noise, and radiation, can cause injury and tissue damage.
items.ww: Causing physical injury and tissue damage is exactly how physical hazards are defined.

alt.q: Agents that can injure the body and damage tissue are classified as physical hazards.
alt.ex: Physical hazards, like fire, falls, noise, and radiation, cause injury and tissue damage.
alt.ww: This is the definition of physical hazards, so it is true.

alt.q: Physical hazards affect only a worker's emotional well-being and do not cause tissue damage.
alt.ex: Physical hazards cause bodily injury and tissue damage; emotional harm is psychosocial.
alt.ww: Emotional stressors are psychosocial hazards; physical hazards damage the body.

items.q: Which factor below can put a patient at risk for confusion and forgetfulness?
items.ex: Changes in mental function, from illness, medications, or aging, can leave a patient confused and forgetful.
w: Changes in vision
Vision changes raise the risk of tripping or misreading labels, not confusion.
Changes in balance
Balance problems mainly increase the risk of falls.
Decreased mobility
Limited mobility affects movement and fall risk, not memory or thinking.

alt.q: Which change in a patient increases the risk of confusion and forgetfulness?
alt.ex: Changes in mental function from illness, medication, or aging can cause confusion and forgetfulness.
w: Changes in vision
Vision changes raise the risk of tripping or misreading labels, not confusion.
Changes in balance
Balance problems mainly increase the risk of falls.
Decreased mobility
Limited mobility affects movement and fall risk, not memory.

alt.q: An older patient started a new medication and now often forgets where she is in the hospital. Which safety risk factor does this represent?
alt.ex: Confusion and forgetfulness reflect a change in mental function.
w: A change in vision
Vision changes affect seeing hazards, not memory or orientation.
A change in hearing
Hearing loss affects communication, not memory or orientation.
Decreased mobility
Reduced mobility limits movement but does not cause forgetfulness.

items.q: It is acceptable for health care professionals to wear their uniforms outside of work because someone might need help and would know they are qualified.
items.ex: Uniforms worn outside work can carry pathogens out of, and into, the health care facility.
items.ww: Being recognizable doesn't outweigh the infection risk of wearing uniforms outside work.

alt.q: Health care workers should wear their uniforms in public after work so people needing help can recognize them as qualified.
alt.ex: Uniforms worn outside work can carry pathogens into and out of the facility.
alt.ww: Being recognizable does not outweigh the infection risk of wearing uniforms outside work.

alt.q: Health care workers should avoid wearing work uniforms outside the workplace because uniforms can carry pathogens.
alt.ex: Uniforms can transfer microorganisms between the facility and the community.
alt.ww: Wearing uniforms outside work spreads pathogens, so avoiding it is correct.

items.q: Health care professionals who are overexposed to _____ hazards are at risk for cancer and sterility.
items.ex: Overexposure to radiation, such as x-rays, can damage cells and reproductive organs, causing cancer and sterility.
w: ergonomic
Ergonomic hazards cause musculoskeletal injuries like back strain, not cancer or sterility.
electrical
Electrical hazards cause shocks and burns, not cancer or sterility.
fire
Fire hazards cause burns and smoke inhalation injuries.
tf: Health care workers overexposed to radiation hazards are at risk for cancer and sterility.
Health care workers overexposed to ergonomic hazards are at risk for cancer and sterility.
Ergonomic hazards cause strain injuries; radiation causes cancer and sterility.

alt.q: Cancer and sterility are risks for health care workers who are overexposed to which type of hazard?
alt.ex: Radiation, such as from x-rays, can damage cells and reproductive organs.
w: Ergonomic
Ergonomic hazards cause musculoskeletal injuries like back strain.
Electrical
Electrical hazards cause shocks and burns.
Fire
Fire hazards cause burns and smoke inhalation.

alt.q: An x-ray technician skips protective shielding for months. Which long-term health effects is she most at risk for?
alt.ex: Radiation overexposure is linked to cancer and sterility.
w: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel comes from repetitive motion, not radiation.
Hearing loss
Hearing loss results from noise exposure, not radiation.
Electrical burns
Electrical burns come from contact with faulty equipment or wiring.

items.q: When using a fire extinguisher, where should you aim?
items.a: At the base of the flame
items.ex: Aiming at the base hits the fuel source, which puts the fire out (the A in PASS).
w: At the top of the flame
Spraying the top misses the burning fuel, so the fire keeps going.
At the center of the flame
The middle of the flames is not the fuel source; aim low at the base.
At the smoke above the fire
Smoke is not burning; spraying it wastes the extinguisher.
tf: When using a fire extinguisher, aim at the base of the flame.
When using a fire extinguisher, aim at the top of the flames where they are tallest.
The fuel burns at the base, so spraying the top won't put the fire out.

alt.q: Where should you point a fire extinguisher's nozzle to put out a fire?
alt.a: At the base of the fire
alt.ex: Aiming at the base hits the burning fuel, putting the fire out.
w: At the top of the flames
Spraying the top misses the fuel, so the fire keeps burning.
At the center of the flames
The middle of the flames is not the fuel source.
At the smoke above the fire
Smoke is not burning; spraying it wastes the extinguisher.

alt.q: A small wastebasket fire starts in a clinic break room. After pulling the extinguisher's pin, where should the medical assistant aim?
alt.a: Low, at the base of the flames
alt.ex: The A in PASS means aim at the base, where the fuel is burning.
w: At the tips of the flames
The tips are not the fuel source, so the fire continues.
At the smoke rising from the fire
Smoke is not the fire; spraying it does not extinguish anything.
At the wall behind the wastebasket
The wall is not burning; aim at the fuel at the base.

items.q: The emergency preparedness plan for a facility includes who should report to work, each person's specific duties, and how to communicate during a catastrophe.
items.ex: The plan spells out who reports to work, each person's duties, and how to communicate in a disaster.
items.ww: Staffing, duties, and communication are core parts of an emergency preparedness plan.

alt.q: A facility's emergency preparedness plan states which staff should report to work, each person's duties, and how to communicate during a disaster.
alt.ex: Staffing, assigned duties, and communication are core parts of the plan.
alt.ww: These elements are exactly what an emergency preparedness plan includes.

alt.q: An emergency preparedness plan covers only evacuation routes and does not assign staff duties or communication methods.
alt.ex: The plan also states who reports to work, each person's duties, and communication methods.
alt.ww: The plan goes beyond routes to include staffing, duties, and communication.

items.q: Which class of fire extinguishers are water-based extinguishers?
items.ex: Class A water-based extinguishers are for ordinary combustibles like paper, wood, and cloth.
w: Class C
Class C is for electrical fires, where water would conduct electricity.
Class B
Class B is for flammable liquids like grease and gasoline, which water spreads.

alt.ww: Saying True overstates what time management can do.

alt.ex: Some stress is a normal part of life that planning cannot remove.
alt.ww: Saying False implies time management can remove all stress, which it cannot.

sections.name: Communication, Cultural Competence, Bias, and Patient-Centered Care

items.q: A patient lost their mother to cancer last week. They have visited with a physician twice this week. During the first visit, they became angry when the nurse tried to check them. At the second visit, the patient came in holding a Bible and prayed in the waiting room while waiting. The health care worker knows that these behaviors are the patient's way of _____.
items.ex: Anger and turning to faith are common, normal responses as people cope with grief.
w: seeking safety
Nothing suggests the patient feels physically unsafe; they are grieving.
showing prejudice
Prejudice is a bias against a group; these behaviors are grief responses.
malingering
Malingering is faking illness for gain; this patient is coping with a real loss.

alt.q: A patient whose mother died of cancer last week becomes angry with the nurse at one visit and prays with a Bible in the waiting room at the next. What do these behaviors most likely show?
alt.a: The patient is dealing with loss.
alt.ex: Anger and turning to faith are common, normal responses to grief.
w: The patient is malingering.
Malingering means faking illness for gain, which is not described here.
The patient is showing prejudice.
Prejudice is a preformed judgment about a group, not grief behavior.
The patient is seeking safety.
Safety needs involve physical security, not coping with a death.

alt.q: A man whose wife died recently snaps at the front desk staff, then later asks the chaplain to pray with him. How should the health care worker interpret this?
alt.a: These are normal reactions as he deals with loss.
alt.ex: Anger and seeking spiritual comfort are common ways people cope with grief.
w: He is faking symptoms to gain attention.
Nothing suggests faked illness; his reactions fit grief.
He is showing prejudice toward the staff.
His anger stems from grief, not a judgment about a group.
He should be refused care because of the outburst.
Anger is a normal grief response and calls for understanding, not refusal.

items.q: A patient's father recently abandoned the family and has not contacted them in weeks. To make up for this loss, the patient has started partying and drinking with their teenage friends. This behavior is an example of _____.
items.ex: Compensation is making up for a loss or shortcoming by focusing on another activity or behavior.
w: control
Control is trying to manage every detail of a situation, not replacing a loss.
denial
Denial is refusing to accept that something happened; the patient is substituting behavior.
repression
Repression is pushing painful memories out of awareness, not making up for a loss.
tf: Turning to partying with friends to make up for a parent abandoning the family is an example of compensation.
Turning to partying with friends to make up for a parent abandoning the family is an example of repression.
Making up for a loss with another behavior is compensation; repression is blocking memories.

alt.q: After a teenager's father leaves the family and stops calling, the teen starts partying and drinking with friends to make up for the loss. Which defense mechanism is this?
alt.ex: Compensation is making up for a loss by focusing on another activity or behavior.
w: Denial
Denial is refusing to accept reality; the teen is reacting to the loss, not denying it.
Repression
Repression is pushing painful memories out of awareness, not replacing them with activity.
Control
Control is trying to manage details of a situation to feel less helpless.

alt.q: A student who was cut from the basketball team throws all their energy into becoming the top student in class. This is an example of which defense mechanism?
alt.ex: The student makes up for a disappointment by excelling in another area.
w: Regression
Regression is returning to younger behaviors, not striving in a new area.
Denial
Denial would mean refusing to accept being cut from the team.
Projection
Projection is blaming one's own feelings or faults on others.

items.q: Some children respond to stressful situations, such as serious illness, by demonstrating behaviors usually seen in much younger children. This is an example of _____.
items.ex: Regression is returning to behaviors of an earlier developmental stage when under stress.
w: repression
Repression is unconsciously blocking painful thoughts, not acting younger.
malingering
Malingering is deliberately faking illness for gain, not a stress response.
projection
Projection is blaming others for your own feelings or faults.
tf: A child who acts much younger than their age during a serious illness is showing regression.
A child who acts much younger than their age during a serious illness is showing projection.
Projection is attributing your own feelings to others; acting younger is regression.
ms: Which of the following are defense mechanisms? (Select all that apply)
Regression
Returning to younger behaviors under stress is a defense mechanism.
Denial
Refusing to accept a painful reality protects against anxiety.
Compensation
Making up for a loss with another behavior is a defense mechanism.
Malingering
Malingering is deliberately faking illness, a conscious act, not a defense mechanism.
Empathy
Empathy is understanding another's feelings, a communication skill.

alt.q: When stress causes a child to act in ways usually seen in much younger children, which defense mechanism is involved?
alt.ex: Regression is returning to earlier developmental behaviors under stress.
w: Repression
Repression is blocking painful memories from awareness, not acting younger.
Projection
Projection is attributing one's own feelings or faults to others.
Malingering
Malingering is faking illness for gain, not a stress response.

alt.q: A seriously ill 7-year-old in the hospital starts sucking their thumb and wetting the bed again, habits they had outgrown. This is an example of:
alt.ex: Returning to younger behaviors under stress is regression.
w: Compensation
Compensation is making up for a loss through another activity.
Denial
Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality, such as the illness itself.
Repression
Repression is pushing painful memories out of awareness.

items.q: A patient received a diagnosis of leukemia last month. Their physician discussed the treatment plan and prognosis with them, but they have not returned for any follow-up. The patient's family noticed that the patient doesn't seem to feel well but they tell their family they are "just tired." The patient is using _____ as a defense mechanism.
items.ex: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality, like skipping follow-up and blaming symptoms on being tired.
w: Anger
Anger would show as hostility or blame, not avoiding care and downplaying symptoms.
Bargaining
Bargaining is trying to make deals to change the outcome, which the patient isn't doing.
Acceptance
Acceptance would mean facing the diagnosis and following the treatment plan.
tf: A patient who skips follow-up after a leukemia diagnosis and says they are "just tired" is using denial.
A patient who skips follow-up after a leukemia diagnosis and says they are "just tired" is using bargaining.
Bargaining means making deals for more time; avoiding the reality of the illness is denial.

alt.q: A patient diagnosed with leukemia last month skips all follow-up visits and tells family their symptoms are "just tiredness." Which defense mechanism is the patient using?
alt.ex: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality, such as a serious diagnosis.
w: Acceptance
Acceptance would mean facing the diagnosis and following through with care.
Bargaining
Bargaining is trying to make deals to change the outcome, which is not described.
Compensation
Compensation is making up for a loss through another activity, not avoiding it.

alt.q: A patient newly diagnosed with diabetes keeps eating sweets and tells the nurse, "My blood sugar is fine; the test must be wrong." This patient is using which defense mechanism?
alt.ex: Insisting the diagnosis is wrong is refusing to accept reality, which is denial.
w: Acceptance
Acceptance would mean acknowledging the diagnosis and changing habits.
Regression
Regression is returning to younger behaviors, which is not shown here.
Projection
Projection is blaming one's own feelings on others, not rejecting a diagnosis.

items.q: The foundational beliefs and behaviors of most people in a country or society make up its _____ culture.
items.ex: The dominant culture is the set of beliefs and behaviors shared by most people in a society.
w: minority
A minority culture is held by a smaller group within the society.
individual
Individual refers to one person's own mix of beliefs, not society's majority.
family
Family culture is the traditions of one household, not a whole society.
tf: The foundational beliefs and behaviors of most people in a society make up its dominant culture.
The foundational beliefs and behaviors of most people in a society make up its minority culture.
Beliefs shared by most people form the dominant culture; minority cultures belong to smaller groups.

alt.q: The basic beliefs and behaviors shared by the majority of people in a society are known as its:
alt.ex: The dominant culture reflects the beliefs and behaviors most people in a society share.
w: Minority culture
A minority culture is held by smaller groups within a society.
Individual culture
This refers to one person's beliefs, not the society's majority.
Family culture
This refers to customs within one family, not the whole society.

alt.q: A health care worker notes that belief in democratic government is shared by most people in the United States. This belief is part of the country's:
alt.ex: Beliefs held by most people in a country make up its dominant culture.
w: Minority culture
Minority cultures are held by smaller groups, not most people.
Family culture
Family culture is limited to a single household.
Individual culture
Individual culture applies to one person, not most of the country.

items.q: The first level of Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs consists of _____ needs, which include food, water, and shelter.
items.ex: Physiological needs like food, water, and shelter form the base of Maslow's hierarchy and must be met first.
w: esteem
Esteem needs, like self-respect and recognition, are the fourth level.
love and belonging
Love and belonging, the need for relationships, is the third level.
safety
Safety and security needs are the second level, above physiological needs.
ms: Which of the following are physiological needs in Maslow's hierarchy? (Select all that apply)
Food
Basic survival needs like food form the first level.
Water
Water is a basic survival need at the base of the pyramid.
Shelter
Shelter is listed with food and water as a physiological need.
Friendship
Friendship belongs to the love and belonging level.
Self-respect
Self-respect belongs to the esteem level.

alt.q: Food, water, and shelter make up which level of Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, the base of the pyramid?
alt.ex: Physiological needs are the basic survival needs that must be met first.
w: Safety needs
Safety is the second level, covering security and protection.
Esteem needs
Esteem is a higher level involving self-respect and recognition.
Love and belonging needs
Love and belonging is a middle level about relationships.

alt.q: A social worker helps a patient find food, clothing, and shelter after the patient's house burns down. Which level of Maslow's hierarchy is being addressed?
alt.ex: Food, clothing, and shelter are basic physiological needs.
w: Esteem needs
Esteem involves self-respect and recognition, not basic survival.
Love and belonging needs
This level involves relationships and acceptance.
Self-actualization needs
This top level involves reaching one's full potential.

items.q: Thoughts and feelings that affect how we interact with patients and are unconscious and outside of our immediate intentional control are called _____.
items.ex: Implicit bias is unconscious attitudes and stereotypes that affect how we treat others without our awareness.
w: personal space
Personal space is the physical distance people prefer, not unconscious attitudes.
culture
Culture is shared values and beliefs of a group, not unconscious individual bias.
prejudice
Prejudice is a preconceived opinion a person holds; the key here is that it's unconscious.
tf: Unconscious thoughts and feelings that affect how we interact with patients are called implicit bias.
Unconscious thoughts and feelings that affect how we interact with patients are called cultural competence.
Cultural competence is a skill for working across cultures; unconscious attitudes are implicit bias.

alt.q: Unconscious attitudes that affect how we treat patients without our intentional control are called:
alt.ex: Implicit bias is unconscious attitudes that influence behavior without awareness.
w: Prejudice
Prejudice is a preformed opinion about a group, not specifically unconscious.
Culture
Culture is shared values and beliefs of a group, not unconscious attitudes.
Personal space
Personal space is the physical distance people prefer from others.

alt.q: A nurse who believes she treats everyone equally learns from a self-assessment that she spends less time with older patients without realizing it. This illustrates:
alt.ex: Her unconscious attitude affects her care without her awareness.
w: Dominant culture
Dominant culture is the beliefs shared by most of a society.
Compensation
Compensation is making up for a loss through another activity.
Personal space
Personal space is about physical distance, not unequal treatment.

items.q: Religious and spiritual beliefs influence the health care beliefs of many people in the United States.
items.ex: Religious and spiritual beliefs shape many people's views on illness, treatment, and end-of-life care.
items.ww: Faith influences health choices for many Americans, such as diet, prayer, and treatment decisions.

alt.q: For many people in the United States, religious or spiritual beliefs shape their views about health care.
alt.ex: Faith often shapes views on illness, treatment, and end-of-life care.
alt.ww: Saying False ignores how often faith influences health decisions.

alt.q: Religious and spiritual beliefs rarely affect how people in the United States view health care.
alt.ex: Religious and spiritual beliefs influence the health care beliefs of many Americans.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores the strong role faith plays in health beliefs.

items.q: Which of the following most commonly makes it difficult to integrate into a new culture?
items.ex: Values are deeply held, so clashes between old and new cultural values are the hardest barrier to adapting.
w: Lack of financial resources
Money can be a hardship, but it is not the most common cultural barrier.
Not speaking the language
Language can be learned; deeply held values are harder to reconcile.
Not liking the food
Food preferences are a minor adjustment compared to conflicting values.

alt.q: What is usually the biggest obstacle when a person tries to adjust to a new culture?
alt.ex: Deeply held values are hard to change when they clash with the new culture.
w: Not speaking the language
Language can be learned; conflicting values are harder to reconcile.
Lack of financial resources
Money can be a hardship but is not the most common barrier.
Not liking the food
Food preferences are a minor adjustment compared to values.

alt.q: An immigrant patient has learned English and found a steady job, yet still feels torn adapting to life in her new country. What is the most likely reason?
alt.a: Her traditional values conflict with those of the new culture.
alt.ex: Conflicting values most commonly make integrating into a new culture difficult.
w: She cannot speak the language.
She has already learned English, so language is not the barrier.
She lacks financial resources.
She has a steady job, so money is unlikely to be the main issue.
She dislikes the local food.
Food preferences are a minor issue compared to conflicting values.

items.q: Culture refers only to an individual's ethnic group.
items.ex: Culture includes shared values, beliefs, language, religion, and customs, not just ethnicity.
items.ww: Culture is much broader than ethnicity, including beliefs, values, and practices of any group.

alt.q: A person's culture is defined solely by their ethnic background.
alt.ex: Culture includes values, beliefs, language, religion, and customs, not only ethnicity.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores the many parts of culture beyond ethnicity.

alt.q: Culture includes shared values, beliefs, religion, and customs, not just ethnicity.
alt.ex: Culture is broader than ethnic group and covers shared values and beliefs.
alt.ww: Saying False wrongly limits culture to ethnicity alone.

items.q: Individuals are a unique compilation of their culture, race, experience, genetic make-up, environment, physical characteristics, and more. This compilation is the same for patients and health care professionals.
items.ex: Every person, patient or provider, has a different mix of culture, experience, and genetics.
items.ww: Each person's compilation is unique, so a provider's differs from a patient's.

alt.q: Patients and health care professionals all share an identical mix of culture, experience, genetics, and environment.
alt.ex: Each person has a unique combination of these traits.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that every individual is unique.

alt.q: Every person, whether patient or provider, has a unique combination of culture, experience, genetics, and environment.
alt.ex: No two people share exactly the same mix of influences.
alt.ww: Saying False wrongly suggests everyone has the same makeup.

items.q: Which of following is an example of health beliefs held by various cultural groups?
items.a: All these are examples of health beliefs held by various cultural groups.
items.ex: Ideas about balance, spirits, and faith healing are all real health beliefs held by different cultural groups.
w: Illness results from an imbalance of hot and cold forces in the body.
This is a real cultural health belief, but the others are too, so it is incomplete.
Illness can be caused by evil spirits or the evil eye.
This is a real cultural health belief, but the others are too, so it is incomplete.
Faith and prayer can heal illness.
This is a real cultural health belief, but the others are too, so it is incomplete.

alt.q: Which of the following is an example of a health belief held by some cultural groups?
alt.a: Illness results from an imbalance of hot and cold forces in the body.
alt.ex: Hot and cold balance is a real health belief in several cultures.
w: Smile as you speak unless it is inappropriate.
This is a communication tip, not a cultural health belief.
Use teach-back to check a patient's understanding.
This is a patient education technique, not a cultural health belief.
Up to 70% of a message's meaning is expressed nonverbally.
This is a communication fact, not a cultural health belief.

alt.q: A patient tells the nurse she has her baby wear an amulet because she believes the evil eye causes illness. This is an example of:
alt.ex: Belief that the evil eye causes illness is a health belief held by some cultures.
w: Implicit bias
Implicit bias is a provider's unconscious attitude, not a patient's belief.
Malingering
Malingering is faking illness for gain, which is not described.
A defense mechanism
Defense mechanisms are ways of coping with stress, not beliefs about illness causes.

items.q: Some cultures believe that illness occurs when the body, mind, and spirit are out of balance.
items.ex: Many cultures view health holistically, believing illness results from imbalance among body, mind, and spirit.
items.ww: Holistic health beliefs linking illness to imbalance are common in many cultures.

alt.q: Certain cultures hold that sickness results when the body, mind, and spirit lose their balance.
alt.ex: Many cultures view illness as an imbalance among body, mind, and spirit.
alt.ww: Saying False ignores widely held holistic health beliefs.

alt.q: No cultures link illness to an imbalance of the body, mind, and spirit.
alt.ex: Some cultures believe illness occurs when body, mind, and spirit are out of balance.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores well-known holistic cultural beliefs about illness.

items.q: In most situations, there is one best way to act.
items.ex: Patients' cultures and needs differ, so there are usually several appropriate ways to act.
items.ww: Good care adapts to each patient's culture and situation rather than one fixed approach.

alt.q: Usually there is a single correct way to behave in any given situation.
alt.ex: Patients and situations differ, so several approaches may be appropriate.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores how culture and needs change the best response.

alt.q: Because patients differ in culture and needs, there is often more than one appropriate way to act.
alt.ex: Different people and situations call for flexible, varied responses.
alt.ww: Saying False assumes one approach fits everyone, which is rarely so.

items.q: A patient has just been told they will need to stay in the hospital an additional day for another treatment. The patient owns their own business and has already been in the hospital for a week. They loudly demand to know exactly what time they will be released after the treatment. Which defense mechanism is the patient exhibiting?
items.ex: Control is trying to manage details of a situation to feel less helpless, like demanding an exact release time.
w: compensation
Compensation is making up for a loss with another behavior, not demanding details.
repression
Repression is pushing painful thoughts out of awareness, not seeking control.
denial
The patient accepts the extra treatment; they are trying to control the timing.

alt.q: A business owner hospitalized for a week learns he must stay one more day and loudly insists on knowing the exact time he will be discharged. Which defense mechanism is he showing?
alt.ex: Control is trying to manage details of a situation to feel less helpless.
w: Compensation
Compensation is making up for a loss through another activity.
Repression
Repression is pushing painful thoughts out of awareness.
Denial
Denial is refusing to accept reality; he accepts the extra stay.

alt.q: A patient facing surgery insists on reviewing every step of her schedule and repeatedly asks staff for exact times. This behavior is an example of which defense mechanism?
alt.ex: Managing every detail helps the patient feel less helpless, which is control.
w: Regression
Regression is returning to younger behaviors, which is not shown.
Projection
Projection is blaming one's own feelings or faults on others.
Denial
Denial would mean refusing to accept that surgery is needed.

items.q: Recommendations from The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (United Kingdom) advise health care professionals not to inquire about personal matters, such as a patient's financial needs.
items.ex: NICE advises asking about personal matters like finances because they affect a patient's health and care.
items.ww: Patient-centered care includes asking about social needs like finances that affect health.

alt.q: NICE guidelines in the United Kingdom tell health care professionals to avoid asking about personal matters such as a patient's finances.
alt.ex: NICE advises asking about personal matters because they affect health and care.
alt.ww: Saying True reverses NICE's actual recommendation.

alt.q: UK NICE recommendations encourage health care professionals to ask about personal matters, such as a patient's financial needs.
alt.ex: Personal matters like finances affect health, so NICE advises asking about them.
alt.ww: Saying False contradicts NICE's advice to inquire about personal needs.

items.q: Which of the following health care professionals is demonstrating empathy with the patient?
items.a: Gail tries to understand the patient.
items.ex: Empathy means trying to understand the patient's feelings and situation from their point of view.
w: Maggie tells the patient, "I know just how you feel."
No one truly knows another's feelings; this dismisses the patient's unique experience.
Jan pities the patient.
Pity is looking down on someone's misfortune, not understanding them.
Carolyn feels sorry for the patient.
Feeling sorry for someone is sympathy, not empathy.
tf: Empathy means trying to understand the patient's feelings and point of view.
Empathy means feeling sorry for the patient.
Feeling sorry for a patient is sympathy; empathy is trying to understand them.

alt.q: A health care worker shows empathy toward a patient when she _____.
alt.a: tries to see the situation from the patient's point of view
alt.ex: Empathy means trying to understand the patient's feelings and situation.
w: feels pity for the patient's misfortune
Pity looks down on someone's misfortune rather than understanding them.
tells the patient she knows exactly how he feels
No one truly knows another's feelings; this dismisses the patient's experience.
feels sorry for the patient
Feeling sorry for someone is sympathy, not empathy.

alt.q: A patient tells a medical assistant he is scared about his upcoming surgery. Which response best shows empathy?
alt.a: "It sounds like this surgery worries you. What concerns you most?"
alt.ex: This response tries to understand the patient's feelings from his point of view.
w: "I know exactly how you feel."
Claiming to know his feelings dismisses his unique experience.
"You poor thing, I feel so sorry for you."
Feeling sorry for the patient is pity or sympathy, not empathy.
"Don't worry, everything will be fine."
False reassurance brushes off his fear instead of understanding it.

items.q: If you explain self-care procedures carefully, patients will understand and follow your instructions.
items.ex: Even careful explanations may not be understood or followed, so check understanding with feedback such as teach back.
items.ww: Literacy, language, anxiety, and embarrassment can block understanding no matter how carefully you explain.

alt.q: A careful explanation of self-care steps guarantees that patients will understand and follow the instructions.
alt.ex: Careful explanations can still be misunderstood, so understanding must be checked.
alt.ww: Literacy, language, anxiety, and embarrassment can block understanding despite careful teaching.

alt.q: Even after explaining self-care procedures carefully, a health care professional should check that the patient understood them.
alt.ex: Careful teaching doesn't guarantee understanding, so use feedback such as teach back.
alt.ww: Assuming understanding is risky because many patients misunderstand yet don't say so.

items.q: The percentage of the population of the United States that speaks a language other than English at home is approximately _____.
items.ex: About one in five people in the U.S. speaks a language other than English at home.
w: Too high; the figure is about one in five, or roughly 20%.
Far too high; roughly 20% speak another language at home.
Too low; about twice that, roughly 20%, speak another language at home.

alt.q: Roughly what share of people in the United States speak a language other than English at home?
alt.ex: About one in five people in the U.S. speaks another language at home.
w: About 10%
Too low; the figure is about twice that, roughly 20%.
About 30%
Too high; the figure is about one in five, or 20%.
About 40%
Far too high; roughly 20% speak another language at home.

alt.q: A clinic serves a community that matches the national average. About what fraction of its patients likely speak a language other than English at home?
alt.ex: Nationally, about 20%, or one in five, speak another language at home.
w: About one in ten
Too low; one in ten is only 10%.
About one in three
Too high; one in three is over 30%.
About two in five
Far too high; two in five is 40%.

items.q: Natural, plant-based medicines are regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration with the same requirements as pharmaceutical medications.
items.ex: Herbal and plant-based products are regulated as dietary supplements, with far looser FDA requirements than drugs.
items.ww: Supplements need no FDA proof of safety or effectiveness before sale, unlike prescription drugs.

alt.q: The FDA holds herbal and plant-based remedies to the same approval standards as prescription drugs.
alt.ex: Herbal products are regulated as dietary supplements, with looser FDA requirements than drugs.
alt.ww: Supplements need no FDA proof of safety or effectiveness before sale, unlike drugs.

alt.q: Herbal remedies are regulated less strictly by the FDA than pharmaceutical medications are.
alt.ex: Plant-based products are treated as dietary supplements, which face looser FDA rules.
alt.ww: Drugs must prove safety and effectiveness before sale; supplements do not.

items.q: Which of the following situations are an example of a health care professional working to assist a patient to meet physiological needs in Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
items.a: Adam is assisting a patient with food and clothing after his house burned.
items.ex: Physiological needs are the first level of Maslow's hierarchy: basic survival needs like food, water, and shelter.
w: Beth is explaining fall precautions so a patient feels safe in the hospital.
Feeling safe and secure is the safety level, the second level of Maslow's hierarchy.
Carlos is encouraging a lonely patient to join a cancer support group.
Connection with others meets love and belonging needs, not physiological needs.
Dana is praising a patient for the progress he made in physical therapy.
Praise and recognition support esteem needs, a higher level of Maslow's hierarchy.
tf: Helping a patient get food and clothing after a house fire meets physiological needs in Maslow's hierarchy.
Helping a patient get food and clothing after a house fire meets esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy.
Food, water, and shelter are basic survival needs, the physiological level.
ms: Which of the following are physiological needs in Maslow's hierarchy? (Select all that apply)
Food
Food is a basic survival need, the physiological level.
Water
Water is a basic survival need, the physiological level.
Shelter
The course lists shelter with food and water as physiological needs.
Friendship
Friendship belongs to the love and belonging level.
Self-respect
Self-respect is an esteem need, higher in the hierarchy.

alt.q: Which action by a health care professional helps a patient meet the most basic level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
alt.a: Arranging food and clothing for a patient whose house burned down
alt.ex: Food and clothing are basic survival needs, the physiological level.
w: Explaining fall precautions so a patient feels safe in the hospital
Feeling safe and secure is the safety level, not physiological.
Encouraging a lonely patient to join a support group
Connection with others meets love and belonging needs.
Praising a patient for progress made in physical therapy
Praise and recognition support esteem needs, a higher level.

alt.q: A patient being discharged has not eaten in two days and has no warm clothing. A social worker who arranges meals and a coat is meeting which level of Maslow's hierarchy?
alt.ex: Food and clothing are basic survival needs, the first level of Maslow's hierarchy.
w: Safety and security needs
Safety needs involve feeling protected from harm, the second level.
Love and belonging needs
Belonging needs involve relationships and connection with others.
Esteem needs
Esteem needs involve respect and recognition, not basic survival.

items.q: Which of the following illustrates the BEST way to determine whether a language barrier is present when interacting with a patient?
items.ex: Asking about language preference, watching responses, and using teach back together best reveal a language barrier.
w: Ask the patient which language they prefer to use
A valid method, but only one of several; using all of them is best.
Watch for nodding or answers that do not fit the question
A valid clue, but only one of several; using all of them is best.
Have the patient explain the instructions back in their own words
Teach back is valid, but it is one of several methods; all are best.

alt.q: Which is one effective way to find out whether a language barrier exists with a patient?
alt.a: Ask the patient to explain the instructions back in their own words
alt.ex: Teach back reveals whether the patient truly understood what was said.
w: Speak louder and assume understanding if the patient asks no questions
Volume doesn't reveal a barrier, and silence doesn't prove understanding.
Treat the patient's nodding as proof that they understand
Patients may nod politely even when they do not understand.
Ask "Do you understand?" and accept a yes as confirmation
Patients often say yes out of embarrassment even when confused.

alt.q: A nurse is unsure whether a newly admitted patient understands English well. Which action would best help her detect a language barrier?
alt.a: Asking the patient which language they prefer for health care discussions
alt.ex: Asking about language preference directly reveals whether a barrier is present.
w: Speaking more loudly to see whether the patient responds
Volume tests hearing, not language understanding.
Relying on the patient's smiles and nods as signs of understanding
Smiles and nods can hide confusion and are not proof.
Waiting until discharge to see whether any questions come up
Waiting delays detection and risks unsafe misunderstandings in care.

items.q: A religion-based healing method practiced by some Christians involves _____.
items.ex: Some Christians practice faith healing, relying on faith and prayer to bring about healing.
w: special herbs
Herbal remedies are linked to traditions such as Asian and Native American medicine, not Christian faith healing.
avoiding the evil eye
Belief in the evil eye is a folk belief in some Hispanic and Mediterranean cultures.
restoring harmony
Restoring balance or harmony is central to Native American and Asian healing traditions.

alt.q: Faith healing, practiced by some Christians, relies mainly on _____.
alt.ex: Christian faith healing relies on faith and prayer to bring about healing.

items.q: Which of the following is the best definition of culture?

Religious beliefs
Religion is only one part of culture, not the whole of it.
Language
Language is one element of culture, not its definition.

Culture is best defined as the language a group speaks.
Language is only one element; culture is the group's values and shared beliefs.

alt.q: Culture is best defined as a group's _____.

w: foods, clothing, and holidays
These are outward expressions of culture, not its core definition.
religious beliefs
Religion is only one part of culture, not the whole of it.
language

The religions Americans practice

w: A particular style of dress
Dress varies widely across Americans and is not a foundational belief.

Similar reading preferences

items.q: After teaching a patient how they are to take their medication, the health care professional should use _____ to check for understanding.

examples

active listening
Active listening helps you understand the patient, not verify their understanding.
tf: Teach back, having the patient explain instructions in their own words, checks their understanding.
Active listening is the best way to check that a patient understood medication instructions.
Active listening helps you understand the patient; teach back verifies their understanding.

alt.q: Which technique should a health care professional use to verify that a patient understood newly taught medication instructions?
alt.ex: Teach back has the patient explain or show the instructions, proving understanding.
w: Probing questions
Probing questions gather more detail, not confirm what was learned.

Examples help explain but don't check whether the patient understood.
Active listening
Active listening helps you understand the patient, not verify their learning.

w: Active listening
Active listening focuses on hearing the patient, not checking their skills.
Probing questions
Probing questions ask the patient to expand on a topic.
Reflecting

items.q: Up to _____ of the meaning of messages is expressed nonverbally.
items.ex: Up to 70% of a message's meaning comes from nonverbal cues like body language and tone.

Slightly too high; the course figure is up to 70%.

items.q: During communication, the best action to take when there are periods of silence is to _____.

w: say something to keep the conversation going

encourage the patient to continue speaking

state what you believe the patient wants to say

tf: Periods of silence are a good time to observe the patient's body language.
Periods of silence should be filled quickly to keep the conversation going.
Silence lets patients think and lets you observe nonverbal cues.

alt.q: When a conversation with a patient pauses in silence, what is the most helpful thing to do?
alt.a: Observe the patient's nonverbal cues during the pause

Filling silence can interrupt the patient's thinking.

Pushing the patient to talk can feel pressuring.

items.q: Communication is the process in which _____.

w: messages are sent

messages are transmitted by face-to-face interactions
Communication also occurs by phone, writing, and email, not just face-to-face.
messages are received
Receiving is only half; communication is an exchange between sender and receiver.

alt.q: Which statement best defines communication?
alt.a: An exchange of messages between a sender and a receiver

Receiving is only half; communication is an exchange.

alt.q: A nurse leaves a voicemail with test results, and the patient calls back to confirm she got the message. Why is this an example of communication?

w: A message was sent, which is all communication requires.

items.q: When a patient is anxious about a treatment or procedure and has difficulty focusing, the health care professional should _____.

w: ask the patient to pay attention

ignore the anxiety and proceed with the treatment
Ignoring the patient's feelings is not patient-centered and may increase fear.
tell the patient they have nothing to worry about
This false reassurance dismisses the patient's feelings.
tf: When an anxious patient has difficulty focusing, keep messages simple and reassuring.
When an anxious patient has difficulty focusing, tell them they have nothing to worry about.
That dismisses their feelings; simple, reassuring messages help anxious patients.

alt.ex: Anxiety limits how much a patient can absorb, so brief, calm messages work best.
w: ask the patient to focus harder
Anxious patients can't simply choose to focus; this adds pressure.
ignore the anxiety and begin the procedure
Ignoring the patient's feelings may increase fear.
say there is nothing to worry about
This false reassurance dismisses the patient's feelings.

"Please pay attention so we can get started."
Demanding attention adds pressure; anxious patients can't simply focus.
"There's nothing at all to worry about."
This false reassurance dismisses the patient's fear.

alt.q: Clear communication within the health care team matters just as much as communication with patients.

alt.q: Communication among health care professionals is less important than communication with patients.
alt.ex: Communication among professionals is as important as communication with patients.

items.q: Which of the following questions is most likely to help a nurse learn about the needs of a patient?

w: "You're not in any pain right now, are you?"

"Why didn't you call the nurse sooner?"

"Is your family coming to visit today?"
This question doesn't ask about the patient's care needs.

alt.q: Which question would best help a nurse identify a patient's needs?
alt.a: "What is your pain level on a scale of 0 to 10?"
alt.ex: A pain scale question gives specific, measurable information about a patient need.
w: "You're not in any pain right now, are you?"

"Why didn't you call the nurse sooner?"
This judgmental question makes patients defensive instead of sharing needs.
"Is your family coming to visit today?"

items.q: What type of question is, "What is your date of birth?"

w: Leading
Leading questions suggest the expected answer, such as 'You feel fine, right?'
Open-ended
Open-ended questions invite detailed answers, like 'How have you been feeling?'
Probing
Probing questions dig for more detail, like 'Tell me more about that.'
tf: "What is your date of birth?" is a closed-ended question.
"What is your date of birth?" is an open-ended question.
It has one short, specific answer, which makes it closed-ended.
ms: Which of the following are closed-ended questions? (Select all that apply)
"What is your date of birth?"
Has one short, specific answer.
"Are you allergic to penicillin?"
Can be answered yes or no.
"How do you feel about your upcoming surgery?"
Invites a detailed answer, so it is open-ended.
"Can you tell me more about your headaches?"
Asks for more detail, so it is a probing question.

alt.q: A question asking for a patient's date of birth is an example of which type of question?

w: Leading

Open-ended
Open-ended questions invite detailed answers, like 'How have you been feeling?'
Probing
Probing questions dig for more detail, like 'Tell me more about that.'

items.q: It is important that health care professionals control their facial expressions when working with patients.

alt.q: Health care professionals should be careful to manage their facial expressions around patients.

alt.ex: Patients read faces closely, so expressions strongly affect how they feel.

items.q: Which of the following is the best example of successful communication by a pharmacy technician instructing a customer about how to take a new medication?

The pharmacy technician spoke slowly and the customer nodded as if they understood.

The pharmacy technician gave the customer a detailed printed sheet to read at home.
Written material alone doesn't check understanding, and many patients read at a low level.

alt.a: The technician used feedback to confirm the customer understood the instructions.

Written material alone doesn't check understanding.

This leading question suggests the expected answer.
"Did you take ibuprofen this morning?"

items.q: Today's patients need more education and information from health care professionals than they did in the past.

alt.q: Patients today require more information and teaching from health care professionals than patients did in the past.

alt.q: Patients today need less education from health care professionals than they did in the past.
alt.ex: Patients now handle more of their own care, so they need more education, not less.
alt.ww: More self-care and home treatment increase, not decrease, patients' need for education.

items.q: The use of touch is a common nonverbal form of communication that can be used with all patients to communicate care and interest.

alt.q: Touch is a nonverbal way to show caring that is appropriate for every patient.

alt.q: Raising your voice slightly helps patients who don't speak English understand you better.

items.q: "I think what I hear you saying is that you don't feel any better after taking the medication," is an example of which feedback technique?

alt.q: Restating a patient's message in your own words, such as "So the medicine hasn't helped you," is which feedback technique?
alt.ex: Paraphrasing restates the sender's message in your own words to check understanding.
w: Reflecting
Reflecting focuses on the patient's feelings, such as 'You sound frustrated.'
Evaluating
Evaluating judges what was said rather than restating it.
Requesting an example
Requesting an example asks the patient to illustrate a point.

w: Nonverbal cues are less meaningful than spoken words.

Nonverbal meanings vary across cultures.

items.q: Humor is usually not appropriate for patients who are ill or injured.
items.ex: Used sensitively, humor can relieve tension and help ill or injured patients cope.
items.ww: Appropriate humor can reduce stress and build rapport, even with patients who are ill.

alt.q: Patients who are ill or injured generally should not be exposed to humor.
alt.ex: Used sensitively, humor can relieve tension and help ill patients cope.
alt.ww: Appropriate humor reduces stress and builds rapport, even with ill patients.

alt.q: When used sensitively, humor can help ill or injured patients cope with stress.
alt.ex: Appropriate humor relieves tension and helps patients cope.
alt.ww: Humor is not off-limits for ill patients; used sensitively, it can help.

items.q: Listening and understanding take place at a faster rate than the rate of speech.
items.ex: People think faster than others speak, leaving spare time that can let the mind wander.
items.ww: The mind processes words faster than speech, which is why listeners get distracted.

alt.q: People can listen and understand faster than others are able to speak.
alt.ex: People think faster than others talk, leaving spare time that lets the mind wander.
alt.ww: The mind processes words faster than speech, which is why listeners get distracted.

alt.q: Because people speak faster than listeners can think, a listener's mind rarely has time to wander.
alt.ex: Listening and understanding happen faster than speech, leaving time for the mind to wander.
alt.ww: Thinking outpaces speech, so listeners have spare time and can easily get distracted.

items.q: A patient has just learned they have cancer and is feeling depressed. The best thing to do is to _____.
items.a: invite them to talk about their feelings
items.ex: Inviting the patient to share feelings shows support and lets them express their emotions.
w: tell them everything will be fine
False reassurance dismisses the patient's feelings and may not be true.
change the subject to something cheerful
Avoiding the topic blocks the patient from expressing real feelings.
leave them alone until they feel better
Withdrawing leaves the patient without support when they need it most.
tf: When a patient is depressed after a cancer diagnosis, invite them to talk about their feelings.
When a patient is depressed after a cancer diagnosis, tell them everything will be fine.
False reassurance dismisses feelings; inviting them to talk offers real support.

alt.q: A patient who was just diagnosed with cancer seems depressed. What is the most helpful response?
alt.a: Encourage the patient to talk about how they feel
alt.ex: Inviting the patient to share feelings shows support and lets them express emotions.
w: Tell the patient everything will be fine
False reassurance dismisses feelings and may not be true.
Change the subject to something cheerful
Avoiding the topic blocks the patient from expressing feelings.
Leave the patient alone until they feel better
Withdrawing leaves the patient without support when it is most needed.

alt.q: A medical assistant finds a patient crying after learning of a serious diagnosis. Which response is best?
alt.a: "This must be a lot to take in. Would you like to talk about how you're feeling?"
alt.ex: Inviting the patient to talk about feelings offers support and lets emotions out.
w: "Don't cry, everything will be just fine."
False reassurance dismisses her feelings and may not be true.
"Let's talk about something more cheerful."
Changing the subject blocks her from expressing feelings.
"I'll come back later when you feel better."
Leaving withdraws support when she needs it most.

items.q: The health care professional can enhance a patient's self-esteem by communicating courteously and respectfully.
items.ex: Courtesy and respect show patients they are valued, which supports their self-esteem.
items.ww: Respectful communication helps patients feel valued, so it does support self-esteem.

alt.q: Speaking to patients with courtesy and respect can boost their self-esteem.
alt.ex: Courtesy and respect show patients they are valued, which supports self-esteem.
alt.ww: Respectful communication helps patients feel valued, so it does support self-esteem.

alt.q: How a health care professional speaks to a patient has no effect on the patient's self-esteem.
alt.ex: Courteous, respectful communication can enhance a patient's self-esteem.
alt.ww: Patients feel valued when treated respectfully, so communication does affect self-esteem.

items.q: Which of the following is not a helpful technique for communicating with someone who has dementia?
items.a: Repeat rather than rephrase if the patient does not understand what is being said
items.ex: If a patient with dementia doesn't understand, rephrase in simpler words instead of repeating.
w: Approach the patient from the front and calmly say their name first
This is helpful; it avoids startling the patient and gains their attention.
Use short, simple sentences that express only one idea at a time
This is helpful; simple messages are easier for people with dementia to process.
Give the patient extra time to respond before speaking to them again
This is helpful; people with dementia need more time to process and answer.

alt.q: Which approach is NOT recommended when communicating with a person who has dementia?
alt.a: Repeating the same words instead of rephrasing when the person doesn't understand
alt.ex: If a person with dementia doesn't understand, rephrase in simpler words instead.
w: Approaching from the front and calmly saying the person's name first
This is helpful; it avoids startling the person and gains attention.
Using short, simple sentences with one idea at a time
This is helpful; simple messages are easier to process.
Giving the person extra time to respond
This is helpful; people with dementia need more time to process.

alt.q: A nursing assistant asks a resident with dementia, "Would you like to go to the dining room for lunch now?" The resident looks confused. Which next step is LEAST helpful?
alt.a: Saying the exact same sentence again, word for word
alt.ex: Repeating doesn't help; rephrasing in simpler words is recommended.
w: Rephrasing simply: "Time for lunch. Let's walk together."
This is helpful; simpler rephrasing aids understanding.
Waiting a little longer for the resident to respond
This is helpful; people with dementia need extra processing time.
Gently gesturing toward the dining room while speaking
This is helpful; nonverbal cues support understanding.

sections.name: Computers, Telemedicine, Health Information Technology, and Online Resources

items.q: Telepharmacies are especially beneficial for people who _____.
items.a: live a long distance from a pharmacy
items.ex: Telepharmacies let a remote pharmacist serve rural areas that have no nearby pharmacy.
w: do not have insurance to cover drugs
Telepharmacy solves distance, not drug costs or insurance coverage.
cannot leave their homes
Homebound patients are mainly helped by home delivery or home health, not telepharmacy's main purpose.
have many prescriptions to fill
Number of prescriptions isn't the issue; telepharmacy addresses lack of nearby pharmacies.
tf: Telepharmacies especially benefit people who live a long distance from a pharmacy.
Telepharmacies especially benefit people who have no insurance to cover drugs.
Telepharmacy overcomes distance, not cost or insurance barriers.

alt.q: Who benefits most from telepharmacy services?
alt.a: People who live far from the nearest pharmacy
alt.ex: Telepharmacies let a remote pharmacist serve areas with no nearby pharmacy.
w: People who lack insurance coverage for drugs
Telepharmacy solves distance, not drug costs or coverage.
People who cannot leave their homes
Homebound patients are mainly helped by delivery or home health services.
People who have many prescriptions to fill
The number of prescriptions isn't the issue telepharmacy addresses.

alt.q: Which community would gain the most from opening a telepharmacy?
alt.a: A rural town 60 miles from the nearest pharmacy
alt.ex: Telepharmacy mainly helps people who live a long distance from a pharmacy.
w: A city neighborhood with many uninsured residents
Telepharmacy addresses distance, not insurance coverage.
A suburb where many residents take several medications
Many prescriptions isn't the problem telepharmacy solves.
A large city with pharmacies on almost every block
Nearby pharmacies already exist, so distance isn't a barrier.

items.q: A collection of data organized in a structured way is a _____.
items.ex: A database is a structured collection of data organized for easy searching and retrieval.
w: file
A file is a single stored item, not an organized collection of data.
record
A record is one entry in a database, such as one patient's information.
field
A field is a single piece of data within a record, such as a birth date.
tf: A collection of data organized in a structured way is called a database.
A collection of data organized in a structured way is called a field.
A field is one data item in a record; the whole organized collection is a database.

alt.q: What term describes data that has been gathered and organized in a structured way?
alt.ex: A database is a structured collection of data organized for easy retrieval.
w: File
A file is a single stored item, not an organized data collection.
Record
A record is one entry in a database, such as one patient's information.
Field
A field is a single piece of data within a record.

alt.q: A hospital stores every patient's name, birth date, and visit history in an organized system that staff can search. This system is a _____.
alt.ex: An organized, searchable collection of data is a database.
w: field
A field is one data item, such as a single birth date.
record
A record is one patient's entry, not the whole collection.
file
A file is a single stored item, not a structured collection.

items.q: MedlinePlus is useful for both health care professionals and patients because it _____.
items.a: contains easy-to-understand information about health topics
items.ex: MedlinePlus, from the National Library of Medicine, offers reliable health information in plain language.
w: helps physicians choose effective treatments
Clinical decision support tools do this; MedlinePlus is consumer health information.
contains patient reviews of health care professionals
MedlinePlus is a government health information site, not a review site.
monitors patients in their homes
Home monitoring is done by telemedicine devices, not an information website.

alt.q: Why is MedlinePlus helpful to patients as well as health care professionals?
alt.a: It provides health information that is easy to understand.
alt.ex: MedlinePlus offers reliable health information in plain language.
w: It helps physicians choose effective treatments.
Clinical decision support tools do this, not MedlinePlus.
It contains patient reviews of health care professionals.
MedlinePlus is a health information site, not a review site.
It monitors patients in their homes.
Home monitoring is done by telemedicine devices, not a website.

alt.q: A patient asks a medical assistant where to find plain-language information about her new diabetes diagnosis. Why is MedlinePlus a good suggestion?

alt.ex: MedlinePlus presents reliable health information in language patients can understand.
w: It lists patient reviews of local doctors.

MedlinePlus is an information website, not a monitoring device.
