items.q: One should not include _____ in emails.
items.ex: Tone is hard to read in email, so sarcasm is easily misunderstood and unprofessional.
w: BCC when sending to more than one person
BCC is appropriate; it protects recipients' email addresses from being shared.
a greeting
A greeting is good email etiquette and makes messages courteous.
brief messages
Keeping emails brief and to the point is recommended.
ms: Which of the following should NOT be included in professional emails? (Select all that apply)
Sarcasm
Tone is hard to read in email, so sarcasm is easily misunderstood.
Confidential patient information
Confidential patient information should not be emailed, even to a known recipient.
A greeting
A greeting is courteous and appropriate.
A brief, clear message
Brief, clear messages are recommended.
BCC when emailing a group
BCC protects recipients' addresses and is appropriate.

alt.q: Which of the following should be left out of emails?
alt.ex: Tone is hard to read in email, so sarcasm is easily misunderstood.
w: BCC when sending to several people
BCC is appropriate; it protects recipients' addresses.
A greeting
A greeting is good email etiquette.
Brief, to-the-point wording
Keeping emails brief is recommended.

BCC is appropriate for protecting recipients' addresses.

items.q: _____ is not a strategy that can be used by a health care professional to prevent the computer from being a barrier between them and the patient.
items.a: Looking up as little as possible from the keyboard
items.ex: Keeping your eyes on the keyboard ignores the patient; you should look up and make eye contact.
w: Positioning the screen so the patient can see it as well
This is a good strategy; sharing the screen includes the patient.
Explaining to the patient what you are entering and why
This is a good strategy; it keeps the patient informed and involved.
Making eye contact with the patient before and after typing
This is a good strategy; eye contact keeps the focus on the patient.
ms: Which strategies help keep the computer from being a barrier between you and the patient? (Select all that apply)
Position the screen so the patient can see it
Sharing the screen includes the patient in the visit.
Explain what you are entering into the computer
Explaining keeps the patient informed and involved.
Look up and make eye contact regularly
Eye contact keeps your attention on the patient.
Look up as little as possible from the keyboard
This ignores the patient and makes the computer a barrier.
Keep typing while the patient is talking
This signals you are not fully listening to the patient.

alt.q: Which practice would make the computer a barrier between a health care professional and a patient?
alt.a: Keeping your eyes on the keyboard and rarely looking up
alt.ex: Looking down at the keyboard ignores the patient; you should look up and make eye contact.
w: Positioning the screen so the patient can see it too
This is a good strategy; sharing the screen includes the patient.
Explaining to the patient what you are entering and why
This is a good strategy; it keeps the patient informed.
Making eye contact before and after typing
This is a good strategy; it keeps the focus on the patient.

alt.q: A physician enters notes into an electronic record during a visit. Which action is NOT a good way to keep the computer from coming between her and the patient?
alt.a: Typing continuously without looking up at the patient
alt.ex: Keeping eyes on the keyboard ignores the patient and creates a barrier.
w: Turning the screen so the patient can view it
This is a good strategy; it includes the patient.
Telling the patient what is being entered and why
This is a good strategy; it keeps the patient involved.
Making eye contact before and after typing
This is a good strategy; eye contact keeps focus on the patient.

items.q: _____ make(s) decisions based on real-life information and help(s) health care professionals diagnose and treat specific conditions.

alt.q: Which technology uses real-life information to make decisions that help clinicians diagnose and treat specific conditions?
alt.ex: Artificial intelligence analyzes real-life data to make decisions that aid diagnosis and treatment.
w: Remote diagnostics
Remote diagnostics tests or monitors patients at a distance; it doesn't make decisions.
Fiber optics
Fiber optics carry light through thin fibers, as in endoscopes.
Lasers
Lasers are concentrated light beams used for surgery and treatment.

alt.q: A hospital uses software that analyzes thousands of patient scans and flags likely signs of disease for the radiologist. This is an example of _____.

laser technology

robotic surgery

items.q: _____ is not an obstacle to telemedicine.

ms: Which of the following are obstacles to telemedicine? (Select all that apply)

Provider discomfort limits telemedicine use.
State licensing laws limiting practice across state lines
Licensing rules can block cross-state care.

alt.q: Which of the following is NOT a barrier to using telemedicine?

items.q: A web address ending in .gov is more likely to contain reliable information than one ending in .com.
items.ex: .gov sites are run by government agencies and are usually more reliable than commercial .com sites.

alt.q: Websites with a .gov domain are generally more trustworthy sources than websites with a .com domain.
alt.ex: .gov sites are run by government agencies and tend to be more reliable than commercial sites.
alt.ww: Commercial .com sites are not generally more reliable than government sites.

alt.q: A .com website is generally a more reliable source of health information than a .gov website.
alt.ex: Government .gov sites are usually more reliable than commercial .com sites.

items.q: Many medication errors, resulting in thousands of deaths each year, are the result of incorrect data entry.

items.ww: Incorrect data entry is a well-documented cause of medication errors and patient deaths.

alt.q: Mistakes made when entering data cause many medication errors, leading to thousands of deaths each year.
alt.ex: Data entry errors, like wrong drugs or doses, cause many serious medication errors.
alt.ww: Incorrect data entry is a major, documented cause of medication errors.

alt.q: Incorrect data entry plays almost no role in medication errors.
alt.ex: Incorrect data entry causes many medication errors and thousands of deaths yearly.
alt.ww: Data entry mistakes are a common cause of medication errors, not a minor one.

items.q: It is acceptable to send personal emails from your workplace computer during your break.

alt.q: Using a workplace computer to send personal emails is fine as long as you are on break.

alt.ww: Being on break does not make personal use of a work computer appropriate.

alt.q: Workplace computers should be used for work, not for personal email, even during breaks.
alt.ex: Work computers are meant for job tasks only, regardless of break time.
alt.ww: Personal email on a work computer is inappropriate even on a break.

items.q: Jim receives an email from an unknown source about a topic of interest. It is okay for him to click on the link to see more information.

alt.q: Clicking a link in an email from an unfamiliar sender is safe if the topic interests you.

alt.q: A unit secretary receives an email from an unknown sender with a link to an interesting health article. She should avoid clicking the link.

items.q: Which of the following is defined as the use of medical information exchanged from one site to another via electronic communication to improve a patient's clinical health status?

items.q: It is acceptable to include confidential patient information in an email if you know the recipient.

alt.q: Confidential patient information should not be included in a regular email, even when you know the recipient.

items.q: Health care professionals must be health literate, meaning they need to have the knowledge and skills to efficiently perform the computer tasks required of them.

alt.q: Health literacy means having the knowledge and skills to efficiently perform required computer tasks.

alt.q: Having the knowledge and skills to efficiently perform required computer tasks is called computer literacy.

items.q: Always back up work using a backup system, such as a cloud storage service.

alt.q: Work should always be backed up, for example with a cloud storage service.
alt.ex: Backups protect important work from loss if a computer fails.

alt.q: Backing up work is unnecessary as long as your computer is working normally.

Government sites are generally reliable sources.
MedlinePlus
MedlinePlus is a reputable source of easy-to-understand health information.
A university medical school (.edu) website
Educational institution sites are generally reputable.

alt.q: A patient brings in several printouts about diabetes. Which one should the health care worker treat with the most caution?
alt.a: A post selling a supplement that claims to cure diabetes
alt.ex: It promotes a product, so it is the least likely to be reputable.
w: A diabetes page from MedlinePlus
MedlinePlus is a reputable health information source.
A fact sheet from a .gov health agency
Government sites are more likely to be reliable.
A handout written by the clinic's physician
A handout from the patient's own provider is a trusted source.

items.q: Employers have the right to read and monitor any email messages sent through their computers by any employee.
items.ex: Workplace computers belong to the employer, who may legally read and monitor email sent on them.
items.ww: Employees have no expectation of privacy on employer systems; employers may monitor email.

alt.q: An employer may legally read and monitor any email an employee sends from a work computer.
alt.ex: Work computers belong to the employer, who has the right to monitor their email.
alt.ww: Employees do not have email privacy on employer-owned computers.

alt.q: Emails sent from workplace computers are private, so employers cannot read them.
alt.ex: Employers have the right to read and monitor email sent on their computers.
alt.ww: Work computers belong to the employer, so their email is not private.

items.q: Commercial websites can be good sources of non-biased information.
items.ex: Commercial (.com) sites are not automatically biased; many offer accurate information, but evaluate each source.
items.ww: A commercial domain alone doesn't make information biased; some commercial sites are good sources.

alt.q: Websites run by commercial businesses can provide good, non-biased information.
alt.ex: Commercial sites are not automatically biased; many offer accurate information.
alt.ww: Some commercial sites do provide useful, non-biased information.

alt.q: Information on commercial websites is always biased and should never be used.
alt.ex: Commercial websites can be good non-biased sources, though each should be evaluated.
alt.ww: Not every commercial site is biased; some are good sources.

items.q: Which of the following is a database that contains information on adverse events and medication error reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration?
items.ex: FAERS is the FDA's database of submitted adverse event and medication error reports.
w: Global Infectious Diseases and Epidemiology Network
GIDEON is a database for diagnosing infectious diseases and tracking epidemiology.
computerized provider order entry system
CPOE lets providers enter orders electronically; it isn't an FDA reporting database.
TherapyEdge-HIV
TherapyEdge-HIV is decision-support software for managing HIV treatment.

alt.q: The FDA keeps a database of submitted reports about adverse events and medication errors. What is it called?
alt.ex: FAERS is the FDA database of adverse event and medication error reports.
w: Global Infectious Diseases and Epidemiology Network
This database focuses on infectious diseases, not FDA adverse event reports.
Computerized provider order entry system
CPOE is used to enter orders electronically, not to store FDA reports.
TherapyEdge-HIV
TherapyEdge-HIV supports HIV treatment decisions, not adverse event reporting.

alt.q: A pharmacist wants to review reports of adverse reactions to a drug that were submitted to the FDA. Which resource should she search?
alt.ex: FAERS holds adverse event and medication error reports submitted to the FDA.
w: A personal health record
A personal health record holds one patient's own information.
Computerized provider order entry system
CPOE is for entering orders, not searching FDA reports.
An electronic spreadsheet
A spreadsheet is general software, not the FDA's report database.

items.q: Public Internet access is as secure as private Internet access.
items.ex: Public networks, like free Wi-Fi, are less secure and expose data to interception.
items.ww: Public networks are open to others, so they are less secure than private networks.

alt.q: Using public Internet access is just as safe as using a private Internet connection.
alt.ex: Public networks are less secure and can expose data to interception.
alt.ww: Public access lacks the protection of private connections.

alt.q: Public Internet access, such as free Wi-Fi at a coffee shop, is less secure than private Internet access.
alt.ex: Public networks are easier for others to intercept than private ones.
alt.ww: Public Internet is not as secure as private Internet access.

items.q: Point-of-care charting provides physicians with data they can use to make diagnoses from a distance.
items.ex: Data charted at the point of care is immediately available electronically for physicians to review remotely.
items.ww: Point-of-care data entered electronically can be accessed from a distance to support diagnosis.

alt.q: Physicians can use data recorded through point-of-care charting to make diagnoses even when they are not with the patient.
alt.ex: Point-of-care data is available electronically for physicians to review from a distance.
alt.ww: Point-of-care charting data can be accessed remotely for diagnosis.

alt.q: Data entered through point-of-care charting can only be used by providers physically in the patient's room.
alt.ex: Point-of-care data can be reviewed by physicians at a distance to make diagnoses.
alt.ww: The electronic data is available remotely, not just at the bedside.

items.q: Which type of software should BeWell Clinic choose to create and manage its annual budget?
items.ex: Spreadsheets organize numbers in rows and columns and calculate totals, ideal for budgets.
w: Database
Databases store and organize records, like patient information, not financial calculations.
Word processing
Word processing is for creating text documents such as letters and reports.
Artificial intelligence
AI makes decisions from real-life data to help diagnose and treat, not budget.
tf: An electronic spreadsheet is the best software choice for creating and managing a budget.
Word processing software is the best choice for creating and managing a budget.
Word processing is for text documents; spreadsheets handle calculations like budgets.

alt.q: To create and track its yearly budget, which type of software should BeWell Clinic use?
alt.ex: Spreadsheets organize numbers in rows and columns and calculate totals.
w: Word processing
Word processing is for writing documents, not calculating budgets.
Artificial intelligence
AI helps with decisions like diagnosis, not routine budgeting.
Presentation software
Presentation software creates slides, not budget calculations.

alt.q: An office manager needs to total monthly supply costs and compare them with the planned budget. Which software is the best choice?
alt.ex: Spreadsheets are designed for calculating and comparing financial figures.
w: Word processing
Word processors handle text, not numeric calculations.
Presentation software
Presentation software displays slides, not budget totals.
Email program
Email is for communication, not financial calculations.

sections.name: Medical Records, Documentation, HIPAA, and Charting

items.q: The _____ history is taken as part of the medical history as the medical problems of relatives may show a tendency for problems.
items.ex: The family history records relatives' illnesses that may reveal inherited tendencies toward disease.
w: social
The social history covers lifestyle habits like smoking, alcohol, and drug use.
subjective
Subjective describes information reported by the patient, not a type of history.
physical
A physical exam is the provider's hands-on examination, not relatives' history.
tf: A family history is taken because relatives' medical problems may show a tendency for disease.
The social history records the medical problems of the patient's relatives.
Relatives' illnesses go in the family history; social history covers lifestyle habits.

alt.q: Which part of the medical history records health problems of the patient's relatives because they may show a tendency toward disease?
alt.ex: The family history reveals inherited tendencies through relatives' illnesses.
w: Social history
Social history covers lifestyle habits like smoking and alcohol use.
Chief complaint
The chief complaint is the patient's main reason for the visit.
Physical examination
The physical exam is the provider's hands-on check of the patient.

alt.q: A patient reports that her mother and grandmother both had breast cancer. In which part of the medical history is this recorded?
alt.ex: Relatives' illnesses are recorded in the family history to show disease tendencies.
w: Social history
Social history records lifestyle habits, not relatives' illnesses.
Chief complaint
The chief complaint is the patient's current main problem.
Objective data
Objective data are signs the provider observes or measures.

items.q: If a health care worker has questions about releasing medical information, they should _____.
items.ex: When unsure about releasing information, ask a supervisor to avoid violating patient privacy.
w: consult the patient's medical record
The record holds clinical data but won't answer release-policy questions.
call The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission accredits facilities; it doesn't advise on individual releases.
release the information to the patient's relatives
Releasing to relatives without authorization violates patient privacy.

alt.q: When a health care worker is unsure whether medical information can be released, what is the correct step?
alt.ex: A supervisor can guide the decision and help prevent a privacy violation.
w: Check the patient's medical record for guidance
The record contains care information, not release decisions.
Call The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission accredits organizations and does not approve individual releases.
Give the information to the patient's relatives
Releasing to relatives without authorization may violate privacy.

alt.q: A caller says he is a patient's employer and asks for her test results. The receptionist is not sure this is allowed. What should she do?
alt.a: Ask her supervisor before releasing anything
alt.ex: Questions about releasing information should go to a supervisor.
w: Release the results because the caller knows the patient's name
Knowing a name does not authorize release of health information.
Read the results quickly to avoid delaying the caller
Releasing information without checking risks a privacy violation.
Call The Joint Commission for permission
The Joint Commission does not approve individual information releases.

items.q: Passwords and encryption must be used to secure _____.
items.ex: Electronic medical records must be protected with passwords and encryption to keep data private.
w: SOAP notes
SOAP is a charting format; the security requirement applies to the electronic record system.
personal health records
Personal health records are kept by the patient, not secured by the facility.
progress notes
Progress notes are one part of the record; the electronic record as a whole is secured.

alt.q: Which type of records must be protected with passwords and encryption?
alt.ex: Electronic records need passwords and encryption to keep data private.
w: Paper charts in a locked cabinet
Paper charts are secured physically, not with passwords and encryption.
Printed patient education handouts
General handouts contain no private patient data to encrypt.
Fax cover sheets
A cover sheet is paper and is not secured by encryption.

alt.q: A clinic is switching from paper charts to electronic medical records. Which security measure is required for the new records?
alt.ex: Electronic medical records must be secured with passwords and encryption.
w: Locking the file room door
A locked room protects paper files, not electronic data.
Stamping each page "Confidential"
A label does not secure electronic records.
Using correction fluid on errors
Correction fluid is never acceptable and is unrelated to security.

items.q: A progress note is a written _____ statement about a patient's care.
items.ex: Progress notes document care in time order, showing how the patient's condition changes.
w: history
A history records past health information, not ongoing care over time.
narrative
Narrative is a writing style; progress notes are defined by their chronological order.
diagnostic
Progress notes track care over time rather than state a diagnosis.

alt.q: Progress notes record a patient's care in what kind of order?
alt.ex: Progress notes are written in time order to show changes in the patient's condition.
w: Alphabetical order
Progress notes are not arranged by letter.
Order of importance
Progress notes follow time, not priority.
Order by specialty tabs
Specialty tabs describe source-oriented records, not progress notes.

alt.q: A nurse reads a patient's progress notes to see how his condition changed over three days. Why do the notes show this clearly?
alt.a: They are written as chronological statements of care.
alt.ex: Time-ordered entries show how the patient's condition changed.
w: They list only abnormal findings.
Recording only abnormal findings is charting by exception.
They are grouped by specialty tabs.
Specialty tabs describe a source-oriented record.
They are created by the patient.
Patient-created records are personal health records.

items.q: The "copy and paste" and "smart phrase" features in a health care computerized system must be used _____.
items.a: with caution so the patient's condition or the care provided is not misrepresented
items.ex: Copied or template text may not fit the current patient, so it must be checked for accuracy.
w: freely to save time, since templates are always accurate
Templates may not match the patient's current condition, so they can mislead.
only when documenting a patient's family and social history
These features can be used throughout the record, always with caution.
to copy earlier notes forward unchanged so the record stays consistent
Unchanged copied notes can misrepresent the patient's current condition.

alt.q: Why must copy-and-paste and smart phrase features in electronic charting be used carefully?
alt.a: So the patient's condition or care provided is not misrepresented
alt.ex: Copied or template text may not accurately describe the current patient.
w: Because HIPAA prohibits their use
They are allowed but must be used with caution.
Because they erase earlier entries in the record
These features add text; they do not delete entries.
Because only physicians are allowed to use them
The caution is about accuracy, not who may use them.

alt.q: A nurse copies yesterday's assessment into today's note to save time. What is the main risk?
alt.a: The note may misrepresent the patient's current condition.
alt.ex: Copied text may not match how the patient is doing today.
w: The note will be automatically deleted.
Copied text is not deleted; the risk is inaccuracy.
The patient will lose access to their record.
Copying text does not affect patient access rights.
The entry will be too short to be legal.
The problem is accuracy, not the length of the entry.

items.q: A personal health record is a document maintained by _____.
items.ex: A personal health record is created and maintained by the patient to track their own health information.
w: the Joint Commission
The Joint Commission accredits health care organizations; it keeps no patient records.
the physician
Physicians maintain the medical record, not the patient's personal health record.
the insurance company
Insurers keep claims records, not the patient's personal health record.
tf: A personal health record is maintained by the patient.
A personal health record is maintained by the patient's physician.
The physician keeps the medical record; the patient keeps the personal health record.

alt.q: Who keeps and maintains a personal health record?
alt.ex: A personal health record is created and kept by the patient.
w: The physician
Physicians maintain medical records, not personal health records.
The insurance company
Insurers keep claims records, not personal health records.
The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission accredits organizations and keeps no patient records.

alt.q: A patient's daughter asks who is responsible for updating her mother's personal health record. What is the correct answer?
alt.ex: Personal health records are maintained by the patient.
w: Her primary care physician
The physician maintains the medical record, not the personal health record.
Her insurance company
Insurance companies do not maintain personal health records.
The hospital's records department
Hospital records staff manage the facility's records, not the patient's own.

items.q: A major purpose for the creation of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) was to _____.
items.a: protect the privacy of patient records
items.ex: HIPAA set national standards to protect the privacy and security of patient health information.
w: create electronic health record systems
HIPAA protects health information but did not create EHR systems.
control health care costs
HIPAA's key purpose was protecting patient privacy, not cost control.
increase treatment options
HIPAA regulates information privacy, not the treatments available.
tf: A major purpose of HIPAA is to protect the privacy of patient records.
A major purpose of HIPAA was to increase patients' treatment options.
HIPAA addresses privacy of health information, not treatment choices.

alt.q: HIPAA was created mainly to accomplish which goal?
alt.a: Protect the privacy of patient records
alt.ex: HIPAA set national standards to protect patient health information.
w: Create electronic health record systems
HIPAA protects records but was not created to build EHR systems.
Control health care costs
Cost control was not HIPAA's major purpose.
Increase treatment options
HIPAA deals with privacy, not treatment options.

alt.q: A clinic trains new staff never to discuss patients in public areas like elevators. This supports the main purpose of which law?
alt.ex: HIPAA's major purpose is protecting the privacy of patient information.
w: Good Samaritan laws
These protect people who give emergency aid, not patient records.
Occupational Safety and Health Act
OSHA addresses workplace safety, not patient privacy.
Americans with Disabilities Act
The ADA protects people with disabilities from discrimination.

items.q: Information that is documented in the "o" component of a SOAP chart is called _____.
items.ex: The O (objective) section holds signs: findings the provider observes or measures.
w: assessment
Assessment is the A section, the provider's diagnosis or impression.
chief complaint
The chief complaint is in the patient's words, so it belongs in S.
symptoms
Symptoms are reported by the patient, so they go in the S section.
tf: Information in the O section of a SOAP note is called signs.
Information in the O section of a SOAP note is called symptoms.
Symptoms are patient-reported (S); signs are observed or measured (O).

alt.q: What is the information recorded in the objective ("O") section of a SOAP note called?
alt.ex: The O section holds signs, which the provider observes or measures.
w: Symptoms
Symptoms are what the patient reports and belong in S.
Assessment
The assessment is the provider's conclusion in the A section.
Chief complaint
The chief complaint is the patient's stated reason and belongs in S.

alt.q: A medical assistant measures a temperature of 101°F and sees a rash on the patient's arm. What are these findings called, and where are they recorded?
alt.a: Signs, recorded in the O section
alt.ex: Observed or measured findings are signs, which go in the objective section.
w: Symptoms, recorded in the S section
Symptoms are what the patient reports, not what is measured.
Assessment, recorded in the A section
The assessment is the provider's conclusion, not raw findings.
Plan, recorded in the P section
The plan section holds the treatment plan, not findings.

items.q: The Joint Commission accredits health care organizations that meet its performance standards for _____.
items.ex: The Joint Commission accredits organizations that meet its quality and safety performance standards.
w: cybersecurity and costs
Accreditation focuses on quality of care and patient safety, not costs.
efficiency and privacy
Privacy is regulated by HIPAA; accreditation centers on quality and safety.
records and standardization
Records are reviewed, but the standards measure quality and safety.
tf: The Joint Commission accredits organizations that meet its standards for quality and safety.
The Joint Commission accredits organizations that meet its standards for costs and efficiency.
Joint Commission standards focus on quality of care and patient safety.

alt.q: To earn Joint Commission accreditation, a health care organization must meet performance standards for what?
alt.ex: The Joint Commission accredits organizations that meet its quality and safety standards.
w: Cybersecurity and costs
These are not the focus of Joint Commission standards.
Efficiency and privacy
The Joint Commission's standards focus on quality and safety.
Records and standardization
Accreditation is based on quality and safety, not just records.

alt.q: A hospital is preparing for a Joint Commission survey. What will the surveyors mainly evaluate?
alt.a: Whether it meets standards for quality and safety
alt.ex: Joint Commission accreditation depends on meeting quality and safety standards.
w: Whether it is earning a profit
Profit is not part of Joint Commission accreditation.
Whether its prices are lower than competitors'
Pricing is not what the Joint Commission evaluates.
Whether its staff hold cybersecurity certifications
Accreditation focuses on quality and safety, not cybersecurity credentials.

items.q: Recording observations and information about patients is called _____.
items.ex: Charting is the health care term for documenting observations and information about patients.
w: recording
Recording is a general word; the professional term for patient documentation is charting.
taking a history
Taking a history is gathering past health information, one part of documentation.
noting
Noting is informal; documenting patient information is properly called charting.

alt.q: What is the term for documenting observations and information about patients?
alt.ex: Charting is the health care term for recording patient observations and information.
w: Taking a history
Taking a history is gathering past health information from the patient.
Triage
Triage is sorting patients by how urgently they need care.
Transcription
Transcription is converting dictated reports into written text.

alt.q: After checking on a patient, a nurse enters her observations of his breathing and pain level into his record. What is she doing?
alt.ex: Recording observations about a patient is called charting.
w: Triage
Triage is prioritizing patients by urgency.
Taking a family history
A family history records relatives' illnesses.
Making a referral
A referral sends the patient to another provider.

items.q: Which statement below illustrates the advantage of using electronic medical records in a health care setting?
items.a: Electronic medical record systems can coordinate with other health care services.
items.ex: EMRs can share information electronically with labs, pharmacies, and other services to coordinate care.
w: Electronic medical record systems eliminate the need for passwords and security.
EMRs require passwords and encryption to protect patient data.
Electronic medical records can be viewed by anyone working in the facility.
Access is limited to staff who need the information for their job.
Electronic medical record systems prevent all charting and data entry errors.
Incorrect data entry still occurs and causes many medication errors.
ms: Which of the following are advantages of electronic medical records? (Select all that apply)
They can coordinate with other health care services
EMRs share data across services to coordinate care.
Providers can receive lab and X-ray results from other departments
Results flow electronically between departments and facilities.
They eliminate the need for passwords and security
EMRs must be secured with passwords and encryption.
Any employee in the facility can view them
Access is limited to those who need the information.
They prevent all data entry errors
Incorrect data entry remains a common source of errors.

alt.q: What is one advantage of using electronic medical records in health care?
alt.a: They can coordinate with other health care services.
alt.ex: EMRs can share information electronically with labs, pharmacies, and other services.
w: They do not need passwords or other security.
Electronic records must be protected with passwords and encryption.
They can be shared freely without privacy concerns.
EMRs remain subject to patient privacy protections.
They remove the need for accurate charting.
Accurate charting is still required in electronic records.

alt.q: A physician orders a lab test, and the result appears automatically in the patient's electronic record. Which EMR advantage does this show?
alt.a: Coordination with other health care services
alt.ex: The EMR linked with the lab to share results electronically.
w: No need for encryption
Electronic records still must be encrypted.
Permission to skip late-entry labels
Late entries must still be labeled in any record.
Open access for all facility staff
Access to records is restricted to protect privacy.

items.q: It is acceptable to send a fax to an unattended machine if the cover sheet states, "Confidential Health Information Enclosed."
items.ex: Faxes with health information must go to an attended machine; a cover sheet alone doesn't protect privacy.
items.ww: Anyone could read a fax at an unattended machine, regardless of the cover sheet warning.

alt.q: A cover sheet marked "Confidential" makes it acceptable to fax health information to a machine no one is attending.
alt.ex: Health information faxes must go to an attended machine; a cover sheet is not enough.
alt.ww: A cover sheet alone does not stop others from reading an unattended fax.

alt.q: Faxes containing health information should be sent only to a machine where someone is present to receive them.
alt.ex: An attended machine keeps the health information from being seen by others.
alt.ww: A confidential cover sheet does not make an unattended machine acceptable.

items.q: Having an electronic health record (EHR) system can enable a health care provider to receive information from other departments or facilities, such as lab reports and the results of X-rays.
items.ex: EHR systems let providers receive lab reports, X-ray results, and other data from other departments electronically.
items.ww: Electronic sharing of results between departments and facilities is a key advantage of EHRs.

alt.q: An EHR system lets a provider receive information like lab reports and X-ray results from other departments or facilities.
alt.ex: EHR systems share results electronically between departments and facilities.
alt.ww: EHRs are designed to receive data such as lab and X-ray results.

alt.q: Even with an EHR system, lab and X-ray results from other departments must be delivered on paper.
alt.ex: EHR systems allow lab and X-ray results to be received electronically.
alt.ww: Electronic sharing of results is a key benefit of EHRs.

items.q: Which of the following information would not be included in the "s" component of a chart in SOAP format?
items.ex: Blood pressure is measured by the provider, so it is objective and belongs in O, not S.
w: Chief complaint
The chief complaint is the patient's own words, so it belongs in S.
Patient's description of pain
Pain as described by the patient is subjective, so it goes in S.
Patient's report of nausea
Nausea is reported by the patient, a symptom, so it goes in S.
ms: Which information belongs in the S (subjective) section of a SOAP note? (Select all that apply)
Chief complaint
Stated in the patient's own words, so subjective.
Patient's description of pain
Patient-reported, so subjective.
Patient reports feeling nauseated
A symptom the patient reports, so subjective.
Blood pressure
Measured by the provider, so objective (O).
Temperature of 101 F
A measured sign, so objective (O).

alt.q: Which item does NOT belong in the subjective ("S") section of a SOAP note?
alt.ex: Blood pressure is measured by the provider, so it is objective.
w: The patient's description of her pain
What the patient describes is subjective and belongs in S.
The patient's chief complaint
The chief complaint is stated by the patient and belongs in S.
The patient reports feeling dizzy
A reported feeling is a symptom recorded in S.

alt.q: A medical assistant is writing a SOAP note. Which finding should NOT be placed in the S section?
alt.a: Blood pressure of 150/90 measured by the assistant
alt.ex: A measured blood pressure is objective data for the O section.
w: Patient states she has had a headache for two days
This is the patient's own report, so it belongs in S.
Patient reports nausea after meals
Reported nausea is a symptom and belongs in S.
Patient says she feels tired all the time
Fatigue the patient describes is subjective and belongs in S.

items.q: Which of the following areas would apply to the HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996) Privacy and Security Rules?
items.a: A patient's right to request access to and copies of their medical record
items.ex: HIPAA's Privacy Rule gives patients the right to access and get copies of their records.
w: The accreditation of hospitals for quality and safety
Accreditation for quality and safety is done by The Joint Commission, not HIPAA.
The licensing requirements for health care professionals
Professional licensing is handled by state boards, not HIPAA.
A clinic's annual budget and spending decisions
Budgets are business matters, not protected health information under HIPAA.
ms: Which of the following fall under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules? (Select all that apply)
A patient's right to access and copy their medical record
The Privacy Rule grants patients access to their records.
Securing electronic health records with passwords and encryption
The Security Rule requires safeguards for electronic health data.
Limiting release of health information without patient authorization
HIPAA restricts disclosure of protected health information.
Accrediting hospitals for quality and safety
This is The Joint Commission's role.
Licensing health care professionals
State licensing boards handle this, not HIPAA.

alt.q: Which of the following falls under HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules?
alt.a: A patient's right to request access to and copies of their medical record
alt.ex: HIPAA's Privacy Rule gives patients the right to access and copy their records.
w: Joint Commission quality and safety standards
These are accreditation standards, not HIPAA rules.
Licensing physicians to practice across state lines
State licensing laws govern this, not HIPAA.
Setting prices for medical procedures
HIPAA's rules address privacy and security, not pricing.

alt.q: A patient asks the front desk for a copy of her medical record. Which law gives her the right to request it?
alt.ex: HIPAA's Privacy Rule gives patients the right to access and copies of their records.
w: Good Samaritan laws
These protect people who give emergency aid.
Occupational Safety and Health Act
OSHA covers workplace safety, not record access.
Americans with Disabilities Act
The ADA addresses disability discrimination, not record access.

items.q: Which type of history is the part of the medical history taken to determine if the patient smokes, drinks alcohol, or takes illegal drugs?
items.ex: The social history records lifestyle habits such as smoking, alcohol, and drug use.
w: Psychosocial
Psychosocial refers to psychological and social development, not a history section.
Cognitive
Cognitive relates to thinking and mental abilities, not lifestyle habits.
Intellectual
Intellectual relates to learning and reasoning, not substance use.
tf: Smoking, alcohol, and drug use are recorded in the social history.
Smoking, alcohol, and drug use are recorded in the family history.
Family history covers relatives' illnesses; lifestyle habits go in the social history.
ms: Which information is recorded in the social history? (Select all that apply)
Whether the patient smokes
Tobacco use is a lifestyle habit in the social history.
The patient's alcohol use
Alcohol use is part of the social history.
Use of illegal drugs
Drug use is part of the social history.
The patient's mother has diabetes
Relatives' illnesses go in the family history.
The patient's blood pressure reading
A measured sign is objective exam data, not history.

alt.q: Questions about tobacco, alcohol, and illegal drug use belong in which part of the medical history?
alt.ex: The social history records lifestyle habits like smoking, drinking, and drug use.
w: Familial history
Family history covers relatives' illnesses, not the patient's habits.
Chief complaint
The chief complaint is the main reason for the visit.
Physical examination
The physical exam is the provider's hands-on check, not a history.

alt.q: During intake, a nurse learns that a patient smokes a pack of cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol on weekends. Where is this recorded?
alt.ex: Smoking and alcohol use are lifestyle habits recorded in the social history.
w: Familial history
Family history records relatives' health problems.
Chief complaint
These habits are not the patient's reason for the visit.
Plan section of the SOAP note
The plan section holds treatment plans, not lifestyle history.

items.q: Which of the following should be done if someone charts an entry that occurred after the action that you intended to chart?
items.ex: Labeling it a late entry keeps the record honest about when the documentation was actually made.
w: Insert the entry between the earlier lines
Squeezing entries between lines looks like altering the record.
Backdate the entry to when the action happened
Backdating falsifies the record; the actual charting time must show.
Leave it out since the time has passed
All care must be documented; omitting it makes the record incomplete.
tf: When documenting something after the fact, write "late entry" and then chart it.
A late entry should be dated and timed as if it were charted when the action occurred.

alt.q: What is the SAMPLE mnemonic used for in first aid?
alt.a: Gathering information to understand what happened
alt.ex: SAMPLE collects history: symptoms, allergies, medications, past history, last intake, events.
w: Checking the scene for hazards
Scene safety is checked separately; SAMPLE gathers history.
Getting permission to give care
Consent is asked separately from SAMPLE.
Finding someone to call for help
Calling EMS gets help; SAMPLE gathers information.

alt.q: After checking a fallen patient's breathing and pulse, a nurse asks about allergies, medications, and what they last ate. Which tool is the nurse using?
alt.ex: SAMPLE is used to gather information to understand the situation.
w: RICE
RICE is a treatment method for bone, joint, and muscle injuries.
Good Samaritan law
This is a legal protection for rescuers, not a history tool.
Implied consent
Implied consent is permission to treat, not information gathering.

items.q: Although Good Samaritan laws are written to protect rescuers from liability, you should not perform procedures for which you lack the skills.
items.ex: Good Samaritan laws protect reasonable care within your training, not procedures you lack skills for.
items.ww: Acting beyond your skills can cause harm and may not be protected.

alt.q: Good Samaritan laws do not mean a rescuer should attempt procedures beyond their training.
alt.ex: Rescuers should stay within their skills even though these laws limit liability.
alt.ww: These laws protect reasonable care, not untrained procedures.

alt.q: Because Good Samaritan laws protect rescuers, a bystander may try any procedure, even one they were never trained to do.
alt.ex: Rescuers should not perform procedures for which they lack the skills.
alt.ww: Good Samaritan protection does not justify untrained procedures that may cause harm.

items.q: A tourniquet is rarely used in emergency care because it too often does more harm than good.
items.ex: Tourniquets can damage tissue and cost a limb, so direct pressure is used first.
items.ww: Tourniquets are a last resort because of their serious risks.

alt.q: Tourniquets are seldom used in emergency care since they often cause more harm than benefit.
alt.ex: Tourniquets can damage tissue, so they are rarely used.
alt.ww: Tourniquets are a last resort because of their serious risks.

alt.q: A tourniquet should be the first method tried to stop bleeding from a cut arm.
alt.ex: Direct pressure comes first; tourniquets are rarely used because they often cause harm.
alt.ww: Tourniquets are a last resort, not the first step.

items.q: What is the first step when administering first aid?
items.a: Determine if the victim is breathing and has a pulse
items.ex: Breathing and circulation come first because they are immediately life-threatening.
w: Apply a bandage to any bleeding wounds
Bandaging comes after checking breathing and pulse.
Ask the victim about allergies and medications
This SAMPLE history comes after life-threatening problems are checked.
Move the victim to a more comfortable position
Moving a victim can worsen injuries and is not the first step.

alt.q: Which action comes first when giving first aid to a victim?
alt.a: Checking whether the victim is breathing and has a pulse
alt.ex: Breathing and pulse problems are immediately life-threatening, so they are checked first.
w: Bandaging any bleeding wounds
Bandaging comes after breathing and pulse are checked.
Asking about allergies and medications
This history comes after life-threatening problems are checked.
Moving the victim to a comfortable position
Moving a victim can worsen injuries and is not first.

alt.q: A coworker collapses in the break room. A medical assistant reaches them. Per first aid priorities, what should the assistant do first?
alt.a: Check whether the coworker is breathing and has a pulse
alt.ex: Determining breathing and pulse is the first step in first aid.
w: Look for a Medic Alert bracelet
This helps later, after breathing and pulse are checked.
Ask bystanders what happened
Gathering information comes after life-threatening problems are checked.
Sit the coworker up in a chair
Moving the victim can worsen injuries and is not first.

items.q: The goal of immediate treatment for poisonings is to get the poison out of the body by inducing vomiting.
items.ex: Inducing vomiting can cause more harm; call poison control and follow their instructions.
items.ww: Vomiting can re-injure the throat or cause choking, so it is not routinely induced.

alt.q: Making a poisoned person vomit is the main goal of immediate poisoning treatment.
alt.ex: Inducing vomiting can cause more harm; call poison control and follow instructions.
alt.ww: Inducing vomiting is not the goal and can injure the person.

alt.q: For a suspected poisoning, the rescuer should seek medical help and call poison control rather than induce vomiting.
alt.ex: Poison control gives safe instructions; inducing vomiting can cause harm.
alt.ww: Inducing vomiting is not the goal, so calling poison control is correct.

items.q: Which of the following is a recommended first aid procedure for the injured with heat cramps?
items.ex: Heat cramps come from fluid and salt loss, so replace water and electrolytes.
w: Give salt tablets
Salt tablets can irritate the stomach and are not recommended.
Give aspirin or Tylenol
Pain relievers do not replace lost fluids and electrolytes.
Wrap with blankets to prevent heat loss
The person is overheated; blankets would worsen the condition.
tf: First aid for heat cramps includes giving water and electrolytes.
First aid for heat cramps includes giving salt tablets.
Salt tablets can irritate the stomach; electrolyte fluids are recommended.
ms: Which of the following are recommended first aid for heat cramps? (Select all that apply)
Give water and electrolytes
Replaces the fluid and salt lost through sweating.
Have the person rest in a cool place
Stopping activity and cooling down helps cramps resolve.
Give salt tablets
Salt tablets are not recommended; they irritate the stomach.
Wrap with blankets to prevent heat loss
Blankets trap heat in an overheated person.

alt.q: Which first aid measure is recommended for a person with heat cramps?
alt.ex: Heat cramps come from fluid and salt loss, so both are replaced.
w: Give salt tablets
Salt tablets can irritate the stomach and are not recommended.
Give aspirin or acetaminophen
Pain relievers do not replace lost fluids and electrolytes.
Cover with blankets to keep heat in
The person is overheated; blankets make it worse.

alt.q: A landscaper working in the sun develops painful leg cramps. What should the first aider give?
alt.a: A drink with water and electrolytes, such as a sports drink
alt.ex: Heat cramps are treated by replacing lost water and electrolytes.
w: Salt tablets
Salt tablets are not recommended for heat cramps.
Ibuprofen for the pain
Pain relievers do not replace lost fluids and electrolytes.
A hot drink and a warm blanket
Adding heat worsens a heat-related illness.

items.q: What should you look for if you are attempting to determine what happened and you suspect the ill or injured person may have a specific medical condition?
items.a: A Medic Alert necklace or bracelet
items.ex: Medic Alert jewelry lists conditions like diabetes, epilepsy, or allergies.
w: An implied consent
Implied consent is permission to treat, not medical history.
A copy of the Good Samaritan Act
This law protects rescuers; it tells you nothing about the person.
Help from bystanders
Bystanders may help, but Medic Alert tags identify the condition.
tf: A Medic Alert bracelet or necklace can identify a person's medical condition.
Implied consent can identify a person's specific medical condition.
Implied consent is permission to treat, not medical information.

alt.q: If you suspect an injured person has a particular medical condition, what item could help identify it?
alt.a: A Medic Alert necklace or bracelet
alt.ex: Medic Alert jewelry lists conditions such as diabetes, epilepsy, or allergies.
w: A copy of the Good Samaritan Act
This law protects rescuers; it says nothing about the person.
A first aid kit
A kit holds supplies, not the person's medical information.
The rescuer's CPR certification card
This shows the rescuer's training, not the victim's condition.

alt.q: A man is found confused and sweaty in a parking lot. Which item on him would best tell a rescuer he has diabetes?
alt.a: A Medic Alert bracelet on his wrist
alt.ex: Medic Alert bracelets identify medical conditions like diabetes.
w: His wristwatch
A watch carries no medical information.
A restaurant receipt in his pocket
A receipt does not identify a medical condition.
An empty water bottle nearby
A bottle cannot confirm a specific medical condition.

items.q: Withdrawal from a drug to which an individual has become addicted can result in a life-threatening situation.
items.ex: Withdrawal from substances like alcohol or sedatives can cause seizures and can be fatal.
items.ww: Withdrawal can be dangerous, so it is a medical emergency in some cases.

alt.q: Stopping a drug that a person is addicted to can cause a life-threatening reaction.
alt.ex: Withdrawal from substances like alcohol or sedatives can cause seizures and death.
alt.ww: Withdrawal can be dangerous, so False is wrong.

alt.q: Drug withdrawal may be uncomfortable but is never dangerous to life.
alt.ex: Withdrawal from an addictive drug can be life-threatening.
alt.ww: Withdrawal can cause seizures and death, so 'never dangerous' is false.

items.q: You should always apply ointment to a severe burn.
items.ex: Ointments trap heat and raise infection risk; cover severe burns with a dry sterile dressing.
items.ww: Ointment on severe burns is harmful and should be avoided.

alt.q: Ointment should routinely be put on every severe burn.
alt.ex: Ointments trap heat and raise infection risk on severe burns.
alt.ww: Putting ointment on severe burns is harmful, so True is wrong.

alt.q: Severe burns should not be covered with ointment.
alt.ex: Ointment traps heat and increases infection risk in severe burns.
alt.ww: Ointment on severe burns is harmful, so this statement is true.

sections.name: Health Care Costs, Insurance, Managed Care, and Financing

items.q: _____ incur(s) the highest percentage of health care costs.
items.ex: Chronic conditions need long-term, ongoing care, so they drive most health care costs.
w: Maternal-child care
Pregnancy and child care are costly but much smaller than chronic disease.
Acute injuries and accidents
Acute care is often short-term; chronic care continues for years.
Geriatric care
Older adults cost more largely because of their chronic conditions.
tf: Chronic conditions incur the highest percentage of health care costs.
Acute injuries and accidents incur the highest percentage of health care costs.
Acute care is usually short-term; long-term chronic care costs more.

alt.q: Which category of illness accounts for the largest share of health care spending?
alt.ex: Chronic conditions need long-term care, so they drive most costs.
w: Maternal-child care
Pregnancy and child care cost much less overall than chronic disease.
Acute injuries and accidents
Acute care is usually short-term; chronic care lasts years.
Short-term infections
Brief illnesses cost far less than ongoing chronic care.

alt.q: A hospital finance team wants to focus on its biggest spending area. Which patient group drives the most costs?
alt.a: Patients with long-term chronic conditions like diabetes and heart disease
alt.ex: Chronic conditions incur the highest percentage of health care costs.
w: Patients treated for minor sports injuries
Minor acute injuries are brief and relatively inexpensive.
Healthy patients getting yearly physicals
Preventive visits cost far less than chronic disease care.
Patients in routine prenatal care
Prenatal care costs much less overall than chronic care.

items.q: The type of managed care that allows members to go to an in-network provider for a reduced rate or an out-of-network provider for a higher rate is a(n) _____.
items.ex: Per the course, POS plans let members choose in-network at lower cost or out-of-network at higher cost.
w: preferred provider organization (PPO)
Per the course, a PPO is a network of providers contracted at discounted fees.
exclusive provider organization (EPO)
An EPO generally covers only in-network care, except emergencies.
health maintenance organization (HMO)
An HMO generally covers only in-network care with a gatekeeper PCP.

alt.q: Which managed care plan lets members use in-network providers at a lower cost or out-of-network providers at a higher cost?
alt.ex: Per the course, POS plans allow both choices at different cost levels.
w: Health maintenance organization (HMO)
An HMO generally covers only in-network care.
Exclusive provider organization (EPO)
An EPO covers only in-network care except emergencies.
Capitation arrangement
Capitation is a way of paying providers, not a plan type.

alt.q: Jordan's plan charges a low fee to see network doctors but also lets Jordan see an out-of-network specialist for a higher cost. Per the course, what type of plan is this?
alt.ex: POS plans offer reduced in-network rates and higher out-of-network rates.
w: Health maintenance organization (HMO)
HMOs generally do not cover out-of-network care.
Exclusive provider organization (EPO)
EPOs cover only in-network providers except in emergencies.
Medicare Part D
Part D is prescription drug coverage, not a managed care plan type.

items.q: _____ is a cost-sharing provision stipulating that the insured is to assume a percentage of the costs of covered services.
items.ex: Coinsurance is a percentage split, such as the insured paying 20% of a covered service.
w: Financing
Financing is how care is paid for overall, not a cost-sharing percentage.
Deductible
A deductible is a set amount paid before insurance begins paying.
Copay
A copay is a fixed dollar amount per visit, not a percentage.
tf: Coinsurance means the insured pays a percentage of the cost of covered services.
A copay means the insured pays a percentage of the cost of covered services.
A copay is a fixed dollar amount per visit, not a percentage.
ms: Which of the following are cost-sharing provisions paid by the insured? (Select all that apply)
Coinsurance
The insured pays a percentage of covered costs.
Copay
The insured pays a fixed amount per visit or service.
Deductible
The insured pays a set amount before coverage begins.
Accounts receivable
This is money owed to a provider, not an insurance provision.
Negotiated fee
This is a rate agreed between insurer and provider.

alt.q: What term describes a cost-sharing rule in which the insured pays a set percentage of covered service costs?
alt.ex: Coinsurance is a percentage of covered costs paid by the insured.
w: Deductible
A deductible is a set amount paid before insurance pays.
Copay
A copay is a fixed dollar amount per visit.
Premium
A premium is the regular payment to buy coverage.

alt.q: After meeting the deductible, a patient pays 20% of a covered surgery bill and the insurer pays 80%. What is the patient's 20% share called?
alt.ex: Coinsurance means the insured pays a percentage of covered costs.
w: Copay
A copay is a fixed fee, not a percentage.
Deductible
The deductible was already met before this split began.
Premium
A premium is paid regularly for coverage, not per service.

items.q: Primary care physicians can sometimes provide better care than specialists because they _____.
items.a: may have a more comprehensive view of the patient
items.ex: Primary care physicians see the whole patient over time, not just one body system.
w: can provide more services at a lower cost
Lower cost is not why their care can be better.
are better trained
Specialists have more specialized training, not less.
are easier to access
Access helps, but the advantage is their whole-patient view.
tf: Primary care physicians may have a more comprehensive view of the patient than specialists.
Primary care physicians can give better care because they are better trained than specialists.
Their advantage is a whole-patient view, not more training.

alt.q: Why might a primary care physician sometimes give better care than a specialist?
alt.a: They may see a more complete picture of the patient
alt.ex: Primary care physicians follow the whole patient over time, not one body system.
w: They have more advanced training than specialists
Specialists have more specialized training.
They provide more services at lower cost
Lower cost is not why their care can be better.
They are easier to get appointments with
Access is not the reason given; their whole-patient view is.

alt.q: A patient sees a cardiologist, a dermatologist, and a family doctor. Which advantage does the family doctor most likely have?
alt.a: A fuller view of all of the patient's health issues
alt.ex: Primary care physicians may have a more comprehensive view of the patient.
w: Deeper expertise in heart disease
That is the cardiologist's specialty.
Greater expertise in skin conditions
That is the dermatologist's specialty.
More specialized surgical training
Specialists, not primary care physicians, have specialized training.

items.q: _____ of total health care costs come from patients with chronic conditions.
items.ex: According to the course, about 75% of health care costs come from patients with chronic conditions.
w: Far too low; chronic conditions are the largest cost driver.
Too low; chronic conditions account for most, not a quarter, of costs.
Too low; the course figure is about three-quarters of costs.

alt.q: About what share of total health care costs comes from patients with chronic conditions?
alt.ex: Per the course, about 75% of health care costs come from chronic conditions.
w: Far too low; chronic conditions are the largest cost driver.
Too low; chronic conditions account for most costs.
Too low; the course figure is about three-quarters.

alt.q: Per the course, if the US spent $100 on health care, about how much would go to patients with chronic conditions?
alt.ex: About 75% of total health care costs come from chronic conditions.
w: Far too low; chronic conditions drive most spending.
Too low; chronic care is the majority of costs.
Too low; the course figure is about three-quarters.

items.q: To improve personal efficiency, the greatest time and effort should be spent on _____.
items.ex: Spending effort solving problems at their root prevents repeated inefficiency.
w: corner-cutting
Cutting corners lowers quality and safety, not true efficiency.
evaluation
Evaluation is one step; the course stresses problem-solving overall.
quality assurance
Quality assurance matters, but the focus for personal efficiency is problem-solving.

alt.q: Where should most of your time and effort go if you want to work more efficiently?
alt.ex: Solving problems at their root prevents repeated inefficiency.
w: Corner-cutting
Cutting corners lowers quality and safety.
Evaluation
Evaluation is one step; problem-solving is the main focus.
Quality assurance
Important, but the course stresses problem-solving for personal efficiency.

alt.q: A unit clerk loses time every day to the same scheduling mix-ups. To become more efficient, where should the clerk focus most effort?
alt.a: Solving the problem that causes the mix-ups
alt.ex: Greatest effort should go to problem-solving to improve efficiency.
w: Skipping steps to save time
Corner-cutting hurts quality and does not fix the cause.
Only rating how each day went
Evaluating alone does not fix the underlying problem.
Working longer hours to catch up
Extra hours do not remove the cause of the delays.

items.q: _____ are the most common causes when an employee has difficulty performing efficiently on the job.
items.ex: Most on-the-job inefficiency comes from poor organization, such as poor time and task management.
w: Drug use
Drug use can impair work, but it is not the most common cause.
Alcohol use
Alcohol use can impair work, but it is less common than poor organization.
Family conflict issues
Personal issues can interfere, but poor organization is most common.
tf: Poor organizational skills are the most common cause of employee inefficiency on the job.
Drug use is the most common cause of employee inefficiency on the job.
Poor organizational skills are more common causes than drug use.

alt.q: What is the most common reason an employee struggles to work efficiently?
alt.ex: Poor organization, such as weak time and task management, is the most common cause.
w: Drug use
Drug use can impair work, but it is not the most common cause.
Alcohol use
Alcohol can impair work, but poor organization is more common.
Family conflict
Personal issues can interfere, but poor organization is most common.

alt.q: A medical assistant often misses deadlines and loses track of tasks. Per the course, what is the most likely cause?
alt.ex: Poor organizational skills most often cause on-the-job inefficiency.
w: Drug or alcohol use
Substance use can interfere, but it is not the most common cause.
Conflict at home
Family conflict is less common than poor organization.
Outdated office computers
Equipment is not named as the most common cause.

items.q: 593.401 Sprain of unspecified ligament of the right ankle is an example of _____.
items.a: an International Classification of Diseases code
items.ex: ICD codes classify diagnoses, like a sprained ankle; this is an ICD-10 code (S93.401).
w: a billing code from a private insurance company
Insurers use standard ICD and CPT codes rather than their own.
a Current Procedural Terminology code
CPT codes describe procedures and services, not diagnoses.
a physician's chart note
A chart note is narrative documentation, not a standardized code.
tf: A diagnosis such as an ankle sprain is reported with an ICD code.
A diagnosis such as an ankle sprain is reported with a CPT code.
CPT codes describe procedures; ICD codes describe diagnoses.

alt.q: A code such as S93.401, 'Sprain of unspecified ligament of the right ankle,' belongs to which coding system?
alt.ex: ICD codes classify diagnoses such as an ankle sprain.
w: Current Procedural Terminology (CPT)
CPT codes describe procedures and services, not diagnoses.
A private insurer's own billing code
Insurers use standard ICD and CPT codes.
A physician's chart note
A chart note is narrative documentation, not a code.

alt.q: A billing specialist must code a patient's diagnosis of a sprained right ankle. Which code set describes the diagnosis?
alt.ex: ICD codes are used to report diagnoses.
w: Current Procedural Terminology (CPT)
CPT codes report procedures, not diagnoses.
Diagnosis-related groups (DRGs)
DRGs group hospital stays for payment; they are not diagnosis codes.
A physician's chart note
A chart note documents care but is not a standardized code.

items.q: _____ are health care professionals who serve as the patient's first contact when entering the health care system.
items.ex: Primary care providers are the first contact and coordinate the patient's ongoing care.
w: Managed care planners
These design insurance plans; they don't see patients first.
Diagnostic-related groups (DRGs)
DRGs are a hospital payment classification, not people.
Prepaid planners
Prepaid plans are payment arrangements, not first-contact providers.
tf: Primary care providers serve as the patient's first contact with the health care system.
Diagnostic-related groups serve as the patient's first contact with the health care system.
DRGs are a hospital payment system, not health care professionals.

alt.q: Which health care professionals are usually a patient's first point of contact with the health care system?
alt.ex: Primary care providers are the first contact and coordinate ongoing care.
w: Managed care planners
They design insurance plans and do not see patients first.
Diagnosis-related groups (DRGs)
DRGs are a hospital payment classification, not people.
Hospital administrators
Administrators manage facilities rather than providing first-contact care.

alt.q: Maria has a new cough and wants to start getting care. Under most plans, whom should she see first?
alt.ex: Primary care providers serve as the first contact in the health care system.
w: A lung specialist
Specialists are usually reached by referral from primary care.
The hospital billing office
Billing staff handle payments, not patient care.
An insurance claims adjuster
Adjusters review claims; they do not provide care.

items.q: A strategy for controlling costs is to keep _____ as low as possible.
items.ex: Keeping receivables low means collecting money owed promptly, improving cash flow.
w: accounts payable
Accounts payable are bills the facility owes, not money owed to it.
revenue
Revenue is income; a facility wants it high, not low.
the cost of money
Collecting receivables lowers the cost of money; the strategy targets receivables.

alt.q: To help control costs, a health care facility should try to keep which amount as low as possible?
alt.ex: Low receivables mean money owed is collected promptly, improving cash flow.
w: Revenue
Revenue is income, which a facility wants high.
Number of patients served
Fewer patients lowers income rather than controlling costs.
Collection rate
A low collection rate means less money comes in.

alt.q: A clinic has a large amount of unpaid patient and insurer bills. Which cost-control strategy fits this situation?
alt.a: Collect money owed promptly to lower accounts receivable
alt.ex: Keeping accounts receivable low is a strategy for controlling costs.
w: Let accounts receivable grow to show more income
Unpaid bills are not usable cash and raise costs.
Lower revenue to reduce expenses
Revenue is income; reducing it does not control costs.
Delay sending bills to patients
Delaying bills increases accounts receivable.

items.q: An agreed-upon amount an individual pays to an insurance company for the benefit of having the company pay for a specified amount of future health care costs is called a _____.
items.ex: A premium is the regular payment that buys insurance coverage.
w: coinsurance
Coinsurance is a percentage of each service's cost, paid when care is used.
copay
A copay is a fixed fee paid at each visit.
negotiated fee
A negotiated fee is the rate an insurer agrees to pay providers.
tf: A premium is the agreed amount paid to an insurer for future coverage.
A deductible is the agreed amount paid regularly to an insurer for future coverage.
A deductible is what you pay out of pocket before coverage begins.

alt.q: What is the regular, agreed-upon payment made to an insurer in exchange for coverage of future health care costs?
alt.ex: A premium is the payment that buys insurance coverage.
w: Coinsurance
Coinsurance is a percentage of each service's cost.
Copay
A copay is a fixed fee paid at each visit.
Deductible
A deductible is paid before insurance begins paying for services.

alt.q: Lena pays her insurance company $350 every month, whether or not she sees a doctor. What is this payment called?
alt.ex: A premium is paid regularly to keep coverage, regardless of use.
w: Copay
A copay is paid only when a service is used.
Coinsurance
Coinsurance is a percentage paid when care is used.
Deductible
A deductible is an amount paid for care before insurance pays.

items.q: Treating diabetes cost the United States _____ in 2022.
items.ex: Diabetes cost the US about $413 billion in 2022, in medical costs and lost productivity.
w: $187 million
Far too low; diabetes costs are in the hundreds of billions.
$533 million
Far too low; the figure is in billions, not millions.
$108 billion
Too low; the 2022 total was about $413 billion.
tf: Treating diabetes cost the United States about $413 billion in 2022.
Treating diabetes cost the United States about $108 billion in 2022.
The 2022 figure was about $413 billion.

alt.q: In 2022, about how much did diabetes cost the United States?
alt.ex: Diabetes cost the US about $413 billion in 2022.
w: $187 million
Far too low; the cost is in the hundreds of billions.
$533 million
Far too low; the figure is in billions, not millions.
$108 billion
Too low; the 2022 total was about $413 billion.

alt.q: A health educator wants a 2022 figure showing diabetes is a major US cost driver. Which figure is correct?
alt.ex: The course gives diabetes costs of $413 billion in 2022.
w: About $187 million
Far too low; costs are in the hundreds of billions.
About $533 million
Far too low; the figure is in billions.
About $108 billion
Too low; the 2022 total was about $413 billion.

items.q: Part D is the Medicare Advantage plan that allows people with Medicare Parts A and B to choose to receive all their health care services through a provider organization, such as a health maintenance organization (HMO) or a preferred provider organization (PPO).
items.ex: Part C is Medicare Advantage; Part D covers prescription drugs.
items.ww: Part D is drug coverage, so the description fits Part C instead.

alt.q: Medicare Part D is the Medicare Advantage option that lets people get all their care through an HMO or PPO.
alt.ex: Medicare Advantage is Part C; Part D covers prescription drugs.
alt.ww: This describes Part C, not Part D.

alt.q: Medicare Part C, or Medicare Advantage, lets people with Parts A and B receive care through an organization such as an HMO or PPO.
alt.ex: Part C is Medicare Advantage, offered through plans like HMOs and PPOs.
alt.ww: This correctly describes Part C, so False is wrong.

items.q: Medicare is free and covers all medical expenses.
items.ex: Medicare has premiums, deductibles, and copays and doesn't cover everything, like long-term care.
items.ww: Medicare is not free and leaves many costs uncovered.

alt.q: Medicare pays every medical expense at no cost to the person enrolled.
alt.ex: Medicare has premiums, deductibles, and copays and does not cover everything.
alt.ww: Medicare is not free and leaves many costs uncovered.

alt.q: People on Medicare may still pay premiums, deductibles, and copays, and some services are not covered.
alt.ex: Medicare is not free and does not cover all expenses, like long-term care.
alt.ww: Medicare does leave costs to enrollees, so False is wrong.

items.q: Nonprofit health care institutions are referred to as public health care facilities.
items.ex: Public facilities are government-owned; nonprofits can be privately owned and operated.
items.ww: Nonprofit describes how profits are used, not government ownership.

alt.q: The terms 'nonprofit health care institution' and 'public health care facility' mean the same thing.
alt.ex: Public facilities are government-owned; nonprofits can be privately owned.
alt.ww: Nonprofit describes use of profits, not government ownership.

alt.q: A government-owned hospital is a public facility, while a nonprofit hospital may be privately owned.
alt.ex: Public means government-owned; nonprofit status is about reinvesting profits.
alt.ww: Nonprofits are not automatically public, so this statement is true.

items.q: Health care costs are evenly distributed among all patients.
items.ex: A small share of patients, mostly those with chronic conditions, account for most costs.
items.ww: Costs are concentrated, not spread evenly across patients.

alt.q: Every patient accounts for roughly the same share of health care costs.
alt.ex: A smaller group of patients, mostly with chronic conditions, accounts for most costs.
alt.ww: Costs are concentrated, not spread evenly.

alt.q: Patients with chronic conditions account for a much larger share of health care costs than other patients.
alt.ex: About 75% of health care costs come from patients with chronic conditions.
alt.ww: Costs are not evenly distributed, so False is wrong.

items.q: Health care costs cannot be reduced without decreasing the quality of care.
items.ex: Cutting waste and improving efficiency can lower costs without hurting quality.
items.ww: Efficiency and prevention can reduce cost while keeping quality.

alt.q: Lowering health care costs always means lowering the quality of care.
alt.ex: Cutting waste and improving efficiency can lower costs without hurting quality.
alt.ww: Costs can be reduced while quality is maintained.

alt.q: Reducing waste and improving efficiency can lower health care costs while maintaining quality.
